declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether supply chain risk transmitted through production networks is priced in equity markets. We construct a novel firm-level measure of Network Supply Chain Risk (NSCR) by combining input-output linkages from the Bureau of Economic Analysis with macroeconomic shocks from the Federal Reserve Economic Data database. Using a panel of U.S. firms from 2018 to 2024, we test whether exposure to upstream input shocks affects stock returns. While baseline effects weaken after controlling for standard asset pricing factors, we find strong evidence of heterogeneity. Supply chain risk negatively affects low-exposure firms but positively affects high-exposure firms, consistent with risk compensation and adaptation. These findings contribute to the growing literature on production networks and asset pricing by demonstrating that supply chain risk is not uniformly priced but depends critically on firm exposure, industry structure, and shock magnitude.

title: Board Sustainability Committees: A Shareholders' Perspective
affiliations: , UNSW Business School, University of New South Wales and The University of Sydney

detail.title: Board Sustainability Committees: A Shareholders' Perspective
detail.abstract: With hand-collected information on board sustainability committees for S&P 1500 companies, this paper investigates both the drivers and effects of firms' decisions to establish such committees from the perspective of investor demand for corporate sustainability. We find that firms under pressure to attract institutional investors and enhance environmental and social (ES) reputation are more likely to establish a sustainability committee at the board level. Using a stacked difference-in-differences event study approach, we find that firms adopting a sustainability committee experience an increase in equity ownership by socially responsible institutional investors and a decline in ES-related shareholder proposals after adoption, relative to non-adopting firms matched on the ex-ante adoption propensity. Shareholder responses in adopters can be ascribed to elevated ES reputation and reduced ES risk after adoption. Finally, we find evidence of a lower cost of equity capital for firms with a sustainability committee than for those without. Overall, our findings suggest that firms effectively respond to the growing sustainability demand of socially responsible investors by establishing board-level sustainability committees to provide strategic oversight of sustainability issues.

title: Banking on Rights: A Case Study of Digital Financial Inclusion for Blind Persons in Pakistan

detail.title: Banking on Rights: A Case Study of Digital Financial Inclusion for Blind Persons in Pakistan

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved survey and interview participants. Participants were informed about the purpose of the research, participation was voluntary, and privacy and confidentiality were protected.
declarations.funderStatement: This paper was developed with support from the Interledger Foundation under its 2025 Call for Papers grant programme. The views expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of the Interledger Foundation.

detail.abstract: Access to banking for blind persons is frequently framed as a matter of customer service, technical usability, or special accommodation. This paper contends that such framing is analytically inadequate. In Pakistan, the issue is more productively understood as one of autonomy, privacy, equality, trust, and meaningful participation in the digital economy. The paper traces the evolution of Pakistan's policy framework on banking access for blind persons from 2009 to 2024, evaluates what these reforms achieved, and explains why substantial barriers persist notwithstanding formal regulatory progress. Methodologically, the study employs documentary analysis of banking regulation and disability law, descriptive analysis of an exploratory survey of 120 blind and low-vision respondents, and qualitative thematic analysis of follow-up semi-structured interviews. The paper argues that exclusion has undergone a process of transformation rather than elimination. Legacy barriers—including witness dependence, institutional mistrust, and paternalistic staff attitudes—persist alongside emergent digital barriers such as inaccessible mobile applications, websites, authentication systems, and ATMs. This layered configuration compounds the exclusion experienced by blind persons. Moreover, inaccessibility engenders distinctive trust harms by impeding users' capacity to verify, authorise, and monitor their own financial transactions independently. Drawing on the capability approach, a socio-technical perspective, and the concept of institutional paternalism, the paper demonstrates that the core problematic is not merely deficient access but a systematic failure to convert formal inclusion into substantive financial capability. The paper concludes that meaningful inclusion now necessitates binding digital accessibility obligations, task-based usability testing with blind users, alternative authentication pathways, mandated staff training, accessible grievance redress mechanisms, and disability-disaggregated supervisory monitoring.

title: Fuzzy Logic Based Credit Risk Scoring in Fintech Lending: A Comparative Study of Mamdani and Sugeno Systems

detail.title: Fuzzy Logic Based Credit Risk Scoring in Fintech Lending: A Comparative Study of Mamdani and Sugeno Systems
detail.abstract: Assessing credit risk in fintech lending is not a straightforward task. Borrower data is often incomplete, the variables involved sit on continuous spectra rather than neat categories, and the decisions that come out of any scoring model are increasingly subject to regulatory scrutiny. Standard classification approaches tend to draw hard lines around applicants in ways that do not reflect how risk actually behaves. This paper takes a different approach, building two fuzzy inference systems to score credit risk and comparing how each one performs. The first follows the Mamdani architecture and the second follows the Sugeno architecture. Both systems take the same four inputs: annual income, debt to income ratio, credit history score, and employment stability. These are fuzzified using triangular, trapezoidal, and Gaussian membership functions and passed through a shared rule base of 24 IF-THEN rules. The output in each case is a risk score mapped to one of three categories: Low, Medium, or High. Testing across 8 synthetic borrower profiles showed that both systems classified every applicant correctly and in agreement with each other. Where they differed was in how they produced those results. Mamdani proved more interpretable, with outputs that read naturally as linguistic categories. Sugeno was leaner computationally and produced more precise numerical scores. The paper argues that the two systems are best understood as complementary rather than competing, and that deploying them together would give fintech lenders-including those operating in emerging markets such as sub-Saharan Africa-both the audit trail that regulators expect and the throughput that real-time operations demand.

title: Narrowing the Section 404 Prohibition: A Quantitative Framework for Distinguishing User-Initiated Routing from Disguised Yield Under the Tillis-Alsobrooks Compromise to the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act

detail.title: Narrowing the Section 404 Prohibition: A Quantitative Framework for Distinguishing User-Initiated Routing from Disguised Yield Under the Tillis-Alsobrooks Compromise to the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. The author has no commercial relationship with any stablecoin issuer, money-market-fund operator, or routing-facility provider, and receives no compensation—direct, contingent, or otherwise—from any party with a financial interest in the policy outcome discussed in this report. The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent the views of any current or former employer, including Nanyang Technological University or its Centre in Computational Technologies for Finance.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The report was prepared independently by the author without sponsorship, grant support, or commissioned engagement from any party.

detail.abstract:
Section 404 of the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act (H.R. 3633), as proposed in the Tillis–Alsobrooks compromise text released May 1, 2026 and affirmed final on May 5, prohibits stablecoin payments "economically or functionally equivalent" to bank-deposit interest, while preserving rewards tied to "bona fide activities." The text does not define those activities. It directs the SEC, CFTC, and Treasury Secretary to do so by joint rulemaking within one year of enactment. On May 4, 2026, five major banking trade associations (American Bankers Association, Bank Policy Institute, Consumer Bankers Association, Financial Services Forum, Independent Community Bankers of America) issued a joint statement attacking reward structures based on "duration, balance, and tenure" as a loophole. On May 5, Senators Tillis, Alsobrooks, and Lummis publicly affirmed the text as final and not subject to renegotiation. Senate Banking Committee markup is anticipated the week of May 11, 2026.

This brief addresses the question §404 leaves unresolved: what mechanical standard distinguishes prohibited passive yield from permitted activity-based rewards when users route payment-stablecoin balances into registered tokenized money market funds, such as Franklin Templeton's FOBXX and WisdomTree's WTGXX, both of which the SEC has approved for retail access.

The brief makes three contributions. First, user-initiated routing into registered investment-company shares operates within the existing Investment Company Act of 1940 framework and requires no statutory exemption. The 1940 Act distinction between fund shares and deposits pre-dates §404 by 86 years, and the senators declined to extend §404 to displace it. Second, a threshold test of NAV pass-through integrity, derived from the Reves "family resemblance" doctrine, identifies five conditions a routing architecture must satisfy to fall outside §404: NAV tracking; NAV-based (or dealer-principal) redemption; user-borne loss in adverse fund conditions; per-event risk disclosure; and Form 1099-DIV tax characterization. Third, four on-chain auditable metrics replace the qualitative "user activity" inquiry with ex ante, programmatically verifiable thresholds: the Authorization Density Index, Disclosure Granularity Score, User Control Coefficient, and Activity Coupling Ratio.

The framework responds to the banking-industry critique that "duration, balance, and tenure" rewards recreate deposit-equivalent behavior. The "duration" that concerns the banking trades is the calibration of rewards to idle stablecoin holding. The "duration" that 1940 Act dividend accrual contemplates is the period of record for share ownership in a registered fund. These are different concepts; conflating them is the central interpretive error this brief addresses. The structural transformations that take a routing architecture out of §404's scope are the same transformations that take it out of the deposit-flight concern.

The framework can be incorporated through Committee Report language alone, without modification to the negotiated statutory text — the only path now available after the May 5 affirmation. Quantifiable user protection and on-chain verifiability address the consumer-protection concerns Senate Democrats have raised; ex ante rules and structural conditions address the regulatory-predictability concerns Senate Republicans have raised. The Committee Report is the principal upstream input into the joint SEC/CFTC/Treasury rulemaking that will define "bona fide activities."

title: Emotional and Artificial Intelligence in Intercultural Teams: Building Psychological Safety through AI Tools
affiliations: Hochschule Fresenius - University of Applied Sciences

detail.title: Emotional and Artificial Intelligence in Intercultural Teams: Building Psychological Safety through AI Tools

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Participation in the survey and interviews was voluntary and based on informed consent. All responses were collected anonymously and no personally identifiable information was recorded. The study complied with standard ethical guidelines for social science research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was completed as part of the Master of Science in International Management at Hochschule Fresenius University of Applied Sciences, Berlin.

detail.abstract:
Intercultural and cross-functional teams in consulting and technology-oriented organisations increasingly rely on AI-assisted tools to coordinate work, manage information, and support communication across cultural and professional boundaries. While these tools enhance efficiency and structure, they also shape how individuals interact, express concerns, and experience interpersonal risk. In this context, Emotional Intelligence (EI) remains a critical human capability for sustaining effective collaboration and psychological safety. This thesis examines the role of Emotional Intelligence in intercultural consulting teams, while situating AI-assisted tools as part of the socio-technical context in which communication, collaboration, and psychological safety are experienced, particularly by early-career consultants.


A sequential mixed-methods design was applied. The quantitative phase analysed survey data from 37 professionals working in intercultural, cross-functional project environments. Exploratory factor analysis was used to support construct operationalisation, followed by correlation and regression analyses to examine the relationship between Emotional Intelligence and cross-functional collaboration. The qualitative phase comprised four semi-structured interviews, including three interviews with consulting professionals and one expert interview that provided a conceptual and practice-informed perspective on AI-assisted tools as contextual influences on communication and psychological safety. The interview data were analysed using thematic analysis to explore how emotionally intelligent behaviours, communication practices, and AI-supported work processes are experienced in relation to psychological safety.

 

The findings indicate a positive association between Emotional Intelligence and cross-functional collaboration, suggesting that emotionally intelligent behaviours support coordination and collaborative effectiveness in intercultural team settings. The qualitative analysis further shows that emotional self-regulation, empathy, and inclusive communication practices contribute to psychologically safe interactions, particularly in digitally mediated work environments. AI assisted tools were perceived as supporting clarity and accessibility in communication, while also raising concerns related to emotional distance, over-reliance, and reduced interpersonal nuance. This study contributes to research on Emotional Intelligence and psychological safety by illustrating how emotionally intelligent behaviours operate within contemporary, AI-supported collaboration contexts. From a practical perspective, the findings highlight the importance of combining emotionally intelligent leadership and communication practices with the responsible integration of AI-assisted tools to support psychologically safe collaboration in intercultural teams.

title: A Framework for Recommending Smarter Daily Commutes by Mining Personal Travel Patterns
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and

detail.title: A Framework for Recommending Smarter Daily Commutes by Mining Personal Travel Patterns
detail.abstract: Daily commuters frequently face unpredictable travel conditions, leading to inefficient route choices and wasted time. This paper presents a framework for generating personalized commute recommendations by mining an individual's historical travel patterns from passively collected GPS and mobile network data. Unlike existing systems that rely on real-time traffic broadcasts or aggregated crowd-sourced data-both of which were limited in coverage and accuracy in 2010-our framework builds a personal mobility profile for each user. Using sequence mining and association rule learning, the framework identifies recurring trips, preferred departure times, and typical route choices. When a future commute is detected, the system compares current conditions (time of day, day of week, and basic weather data) against the user's historical patterns and suggests adjustments, such as leaving 15 minutes earlier or taking an alternative arterial road. Evaluation on six months of commute data from 45 participants in a mid-sized European city shows that the framework reduces average commute time by 11% compared to unassisted driving and by 6% compared to using live traffic radio alerts. The results demonstrate that mining personal travel history-without requiring infrastructure-intensive real-time sensors-offers a practical and accessible path toward smarter daily commuting.

title: Structuring an LBO Debt Package: From Classic Syndicated Structures to the Age of Private Credit
affiliations: INSEAD - Singapore, INSEAD, INSEAD and INSEAD

detail.title: Structuring an LBO Debt Package: From Classic Syndicated Structures to the Age of Private Credit

publicationDetails.journalName: INSEAD Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the structural evolution of leveraged buyout (LBO) debt packaging from the classic multitranche bank-syndicated model of the pre-2008 era through the private credit-dominated landscape of 2026. Drawing on a practitioner-oriented analytical framework, the paper traces how three forces-post-GFC regulatory reform (Basel III), a decade of zero interest rate policy (ZIRP), and the growth of collateralised loan obligation (CLO) markets-dismantled the traditional architecture of term loan A/B tranches, high yield bonds, and mezzanine debt, and enabled the rise of direct lending and the unitranche as the defining instruments of modern LBO finance. The paper documents the covenant evolution across three distinct eras: from full quarterly maintenance packages, to cov-lite incurrence-only structures in the broadly syndicated loan (BSL) market, to the single net leverage test that characterises most private credit facilities today. A central contribution is the explicit modelling of interest rate sensitivity across three rate environments-the ZIRP decade (2010-2021), the peak rate shock (2022-2023), and the new normal (2026)-illustrating how SOFR levels directly constrain leverage multiples and equity returns. The paper also analyses the geographic expansion of private credit into European mid-markets and the upmarket shift into large-cap club deals. A structured decision framework for the 2026 deal team is presented, together with an identification of six common structuring pitfalls. The paper concludes that while instruments, market structure, and rate environments have undergone profound transformation, three enduring principles remain unchanged: seniority determines cost, coverage ratios constrain quantum, and leverage amplifies both gains and losses.

title: Value-Based Prototype Libraries for Vehicle Replacement Decisions under Latent Heterogeneity
affiliations: Friedrich Schiller University - Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science

detail.title: Value-Based Prototype Libraries for Vehicle Replacement Decisions under Latent Heterogeneity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: This report studies a vehicle replacement problem in which a fleet manager must decide whether to keep an incumbent vehicle in operation or replace it with a new entrant. The central difficulty is that the future operating performance of the incumbent is unobserved: at any current age, only a partial and noisy history of past net rewards is available. If vehicles differ in latent deterioration patterns, then replacement decisions must be made under both uncertainty and heterogeneity. To study this problem, a simulated population of vehicles is generated from a finite set of latent net-reward trajectories with economically distinct replacement profiles, and a prototype-library approach is developed. Observed histories are represented using spline coefficients, grouped into a finite set of prototype trajectories, and used to match partially observed vehicles to plausible future paths. Replacement decisions are made through an envelope rule that compares the value of continuing with the incumbent against the value of immediate replacement and renewal. The analysis evaluates prototype libraries using value-based regret criteria rather than clustering quality alone. Regret is defined as the value lost relative to the oracle decision that would be taken if the true latent trajectory were known. This distinction is economically important because statistical classification accuracy and decision quality need not coincide. In addition to average performance, the report studies decision stability and early detectability under partial observation by examining how reliability varies with the observed age of the vehicle and how robust the implied action is across candidate library sizes. In the baseline experiment, a library with six prototype types attains the best overall regret performance and the strongest downside-risk control among the candidate libraries considered. Notably, the empirically best decision rule does not coincide with the library that maximises type-classification accuracy, and decision reliability is shown to vary non-monotonically across observation ages. The results therefore support the use of finite prototype libraries as a statistically credible and managerially useful basis for replacement decisions under latent heterogeneity.

title: From Aragalaya to Administration: Governance Failure and Elite Recomposition in Sri Lanka's Post-2022 Transition
affiliations: Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology

detail.title: From Aragalaya to Administration: Governance Failure and Elite Recomposition in Sri Lanka's Post-2022 Transition

keywords: National People's Power (NPP) JEL Classification: D72

detail.abstract: This case study analyzes early governance failures during Sri Lanka's post-2022 transition under the National People's Power (NPP) administration led by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake. Despite an electoral mandate for systemic reform and anti-corruption governance, evidence within months of assuming office reveals politically motivated appointments of unqualified loyalists to senior positions across the Treasury, Central Bank, and public service; suspicious financial transactions involving ten separate Treasury irregularities; a coal procurement scandal investigated through a deflective inquiry extending back to 2009; and a President holding three critical portfolios with each performing poorly. Drawing on the Integrated-Flexible Approach (IFA) and the 10Ps Framework, this study identifies three mediating mechanisms: the paradox of popular mandate under fiscal constraint, whereby IMF conditionalities incentivize patronage appointments over broad-based redistribution; the deflective accountability syndrome, whereby anti-corruption governments lack capacity for credible self-investigation; and coalition management without institutional architecture, enabling factional capture of state resources. The analysis concludes that Sri Lanka's historical pattern of cyclical governance collapse remains undefeated, though three years of the NPP's term remain for potential course-correction contingent on reflexive learning capacities currently underdeveloped.

title: Geopolitical Event Classification and Supply Chain Disruption Propagation: A Quantitative Framework

detail.title: Geopolitical Event Classification and Supply Chain Disruption Propagation: A Quantitative Framework
detail.abstract: The Global supply chains face mounting pressure from an increasingly volatile geopolitical landscape. Trade wars, armed conflicts, sanctions regimes, and pandemic-induced border closures have demonstrated that disruptions originating in one node of a supply network can cascade rapidly and asymmetrically through global production systems. Yet the academic and practitioner literature lacks a unified, quantitative framework that simultaneously (i) classifies geopolitical events by type, severity, and propagation potential; (ii) models how disruptions traverse multi-tier supplier networks; and (iii) estimates downstream economic impact with empirical rigor. This paper develops and validates such a framework. We make three principal contributions. First, we introduce the Geopolitical Event Taxonomy (GET) — a five-dimension classification schema that characterizes events along axes of origin type, geographic scope, sector specificity, duration profile, and substitutability impact. Second, we build a multi-layer propagation model combining agent-based simulation with network-theoretic disruption diffusion equations, calibrated to real supply chain topologies drawn from the Panjiva global trade dataset and OpenSupplyChain network data. Third, we estimate disruption propagation velocities and economic loss amplification factors using a panel regression framework applied to three canonical case studies: the COVID-19 pandemic (2020–2021), the Russia–Ukraine war and associated commodity shocks (2022–2023), and the Suez Canal obstruction caused by the MV Ever Given grounding (2021). Our empirical results reveal that geopolitical disruptions exhibit a power-law propagation structure in which Tier-1 shocks amplify 2.3x–6.8x by the time they reach Tier-3 suppliers, contingent on network topology and event type. NLP-based classification of GDELT and ACLED event streams achieves 87.4% accuracy in predicting supply chain impact severity within 72 hours of event onset. The agent-based model reproduces observed inventory drawdown dynamics with RMSE below 8% for all three case studies. These findings provide actionable early-warning and scenario-planning tools for supply chain managers, policymakers, and financial risk analysts.

title: Kamala Harris and the American presidential elections: An Object-Oriented Ontology of political objecthood

detail.title: Kamala Harris and the American presidential elections: An Object-Oriented Ontology of political objecthood
detail.abstract: In contemporary American politics, representation by the underrepresented has become both a marker of progress and a site of contention, particularly when intersecting with race and gender. This study critically examines Kamala Harris as a political object through which broader societal tensions surrounding power, identity and legitimacy manifest. Drawing from Object-Oriented Ontology (OOO) and critical political communication, the article interrogates how Harris's political trajectory reflects the structural biases that continue to shape perceptions of leadership and authority. As the first female, Black and South Asian Democrat Presidential candidate, Harris occupies a paradoxical position-her historic election to the office of the Vice President initially signified progress, yet the racialized and gendered scrutiny she faced during the 2024 presidential election campaigns illustrates the enduring barriers to true political equity. Through an analysis of media discourse and historical case studies, this study reveals how Harris's struggles on the fronts of colour and gender disrupt, yet simultaneously reinforce, dominant power structures. detail.abstract:
Shazar Stone from Banda, Uttar Pradesh is a unique semi-precious gemstone famous for its naturally occurring abstract patterns and artistic formations. The stone is known for its dendritic designs that resemble natural landscapes, trees, rivers, mountains, and paintings. Due to its rare beauty and artistic appearance, Shazar Stone has gained recognition in both domestic and international markets.
Banda district of Uttar Pradesh is well known for this stone and it has also been recognized under the One District One Product (ODOP) initiative. The abstract appearance of Shazar Stone attracts collectors, artists, designers, and gemstone lovers. Its unique texture and natural patterns make it suitable for premium retail export opportunities and creative product development.

title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Applications for Improving Traffic Safety and Reducing Crashes
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and Public Works Department

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Applications for Improving Traffic Safety and Reducing Crashes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors report no conflicts of interest related to the conduct of the research, authorship, or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: Road traffic crashes kill approximately 1.19 million people annually and impose economic costs exceeding 3% of gross domestic product in most countries, constituting a pressing global public health and safety challenge (WHO, 2023). While traditional traffic safety methods, including empirical crash-frequency modelling, road safety audits, geometric design standards, and enforcement programs, have delivered sustained reductions in high-income settings, they face inherent limitations in real-time responsiveness, high-dimensional data integration, and proactive pre-crash hazard identification. Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, encompassing machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, graph neural networks, reinforcement learning, explainable AI, federated learning, and emerging foundation models, offer complementary capabilities that may support, extend, and strengthen conventional safety engineering practice. This paper presents a structured systematic review of AI applications in traffic and transportation safety, synthesizing evidence from 72 peer-reviewed studies and authoritative reports published between 2001 and 2025 across seven application domains: crash prediction and risk assessment; computer vision for real-time hazard detection; AI-enabled adaptive traffic control; connected and automated vehicle safety systems; driver monitoring and distraction detection; post-crash emergency response optimization; and AI-assisted road infrastructure safety assessment. Results are critically evaluated using a four-level evidence-grading framework that distinguishes model-performance metrics from surrogate safety outcomes and observed crash-reduction evidence. Cross-study synthesis employs a Relative Improvement Index (RII), applied separately within comparable metric families, to enable structured comparison of AI versus conventional baselines across domains. The strongest field-deployment evidence is found for autonomous emergency braking and forward collision warning systems (Grade A; rear-end crash reductions of 38–56% reported in insurance-database studies), certain fleet-level driver monitoring systems (Grade B), and computer-vision incident detection (Grade B). Crash-prediction models, reinforcement learning signal control, and infrastructure assessment AI demonstrate strong computational performance (RII gains of 15–41% on model-accuracy metrics) but primarily Grade C or D safety evidence, underscoring the gap between model accuracy and verified crash reduction. Key implementation barriers include crash-data underreporting and class imbalance, geographic transferability limitations, explainability requirements, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, privacy and surveillance concerns, and algorithmic equity risks. The review concludes with ten recommendations for responsible AI deployment and a research agenda aligned with Safe System principles.

detail.abstract: Chapter 1 THE PROBLEM AND ITS BACKGROUND Rationale Global Perspective Globally, participatory governance has become a defining principle in improving public service delivery, infrastructure development, and community empowerment. International development institutions such as the World Bank, UNDP, and OECD emphasize that local participation strengthens accountability, reduces corruption, and ensures that infrastructure investments respond to genuine community needs (World Bank, 2020; UNDP, 2019; OECD, 2018). Participatory development emerged in the 1990s as a global shift away from purely technocratic planning toward inclusive, community-driven decision-making (Chambers, 1994; Mansuri & Rao, 2013). Across countries, evidence consistently shows that infrastructure projects produced through participatory mechanisms-such as community consultations, school-community partnerships, and local monitoring committees-tend to be more sustainable, cost-efficient, and socially responsive (Fung, 2015; Gaventa, 2006; Cornwall, 2008). Community involvement significantly enhances local ownership and strengthens monitoring, reducing project delays and mismanagement (Joshi & Houtzager, 2012; Brett, 2003). Regional (Asia-Pacific) Perspective In the Asia-Pacific region, participatory planning has become central in decentralization reforms. Countries like Indonesia, Vietnam, and Nepal have demonstrated that local infrastructure projects achieve higher satisfaction and improved service quality when communities participate in planning and monitoring (Smoke, 2015; Heng & Sim, 2021). Studies in rural and urban Asia show that when citizens, teachers, parents, and barangay-level actors are meaningfully included, infrastructure projects align more closely with urgent needs in sanitation, safety, and education (Araral & Hartley, 2016; Park & Kim, 2020). Yet, Asian decentralization also reveals persistent challenges-tokenistic participation, information gaps, and weak coordination between government units and local communities (Crook & Manor, 2018). These issues directly mirror concerns found in Philippine local governance. National (Philippines) Perspective In the Philippines, decentralization under the Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160) intends to devolve planning, budgeting, and infrastructure development to local government units (LGUs).

detail.abstract: This research presents an empirical analysis of demand-and supply-side constraints affecting financial inclusion among micro-enterprises in Manila, Philippines. Access to financial services is essential for sustaining micro-enterprise operations; however, various barriers continue to limit effective financial participation. This research examines whether demand-side and supply-side barriers significantly influence financial inclusion using survey data collected from 400 micro-enterprise owners in Metro Manila. The findings indicate that both demand-side and supply-side constraints have a statistically significant impact on financial inclusion. Specifically, irregular income, limited financial literacy, and lack of trust are identified as significant demand-side barriers. On the supply side, physical access constraints, inappropriate financial products, and policy and regulatory requirements emerge as significant obstacles. This research concludes that most microenterprises in Metro Manila perceive these factors as major barriers to accessing formal credit. This research recommends that current and prospective micro-enterprise owners participate in financial capability programs, such as UPLIFT financial training, and seek financial advice from peers and financial professionals. Furthermore, this research recommends that microfinance institutions tailor financial products and simplify documentation requirements to enhance financial inclusion.

detail.title: From the Mauryan Empire to the Hapsburgs: A Comparative Analysis of Power Dynamics and Human Instinct
detail.abstract: In this book/paper, we are going to discuss the laws and theories of how power, influence and history work/worked. This paper also has various theories on social sciences and human affairs of science. Note that this paper takes examples from various historical events to formulate these theories; these theories are not called laws because human nature is unpredictable, but these theories are mostly accurate  because many historical happenings have proved so. This paper proposes a 12-part framework for analyzing the recurring patterns of political power and historical cycles. By synthesizing theories of information environments (The Suggestion Theory), systemic decay (The Quadrant of Inequality), and historical recurrence (Itihasikā Punarāvitti), I argue that while human behavior is inherently unpredictable, historical events follow observable 'mechanisms' with high frequency. Using cross-cultural case studies from the Iroquois Confederacy and the Mauryan Empire to the Hapsburg Court and the Songhai Empire this work offers a multidisciplinary lens through which to predict systemic outcomes in social and political affairs.

detail.abstract: The real estate sector sits at the centre of the global sustainability challenge, accounting for a substantial share of energy consumption and carbon emissions. While Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) frameworks have gained significant traction in recent years, their practical application within day-today real estate operations remains limited-particularly when comparing different asset classes such as multifamily and commercial properties. Drawing on industry experience and current operational practices, this paper proposes a data-driven framework that integrates ESG metrics with utility consumption and procurement strategies. It further explores how these approaches differ across multifamily and commercial real estate, highlighting variations in consumption behaviour, operational intensity, and efficiency drivers. The study argues that ESG should not be viewed solely as a reporting requirement but rather as a practical lever for improving operational performance and cost efficiency. By linking ESG objectives with real-time data and decision-making processes, this research offers a more grounded and actionable approach for asset managers seeking to align sustainability with financial outcomes.

title: Debt Sustainability as a System Property: A Parsimonious Framework for Structural Monitoring and Resilience

detail.title: Debt Sustainability as a System Property: A Parsimonious Framework for Structural Monitoring and Resilience
detail.abstract: Standard approaches to debt sustainability rely on aggregate ratios and conditions governing debt dynamics, but provide limited guidance on the structural conditions under which it can be sustained. This paper develops a parsimonious framework that treats debt sustainability as a system-level property arising from the interaction between financial burden, income accessibility, income-generating capacity, and the mechanism through which financial imbalances are absorbed. The framework is organized around a minimal state representation defined by structural pressure and the absorption mechanism. Structural pressure summarizes the system's position relative to a feasibility frontier, while dynamic outcomes depend on the joint configuration of financial conditions, credit composition, and the scale of indebtedness. A central implication is that debt dynamics and sustainability are not equivalent: similar debt paths may correspond to different structural configurations, and deterioration may arise even in the absence of debt accumulation. Within the gap region, the framework predicts heterogeneous outcomes governed by financial cost, indebtedness, and composition-weighted exposure. Using a panel of private non-financial sector data, the empirical analysis shows that structural pressure contains systematic but non-deterministic information about future debt dynamics, and that the feasibility frontier provides a non-degenerate partition of the data. The empirical implementation constructs model-consistent proxies from observable aggregates, yielding a reduced-form mapping from a limited set of variables to structural conditions. These elements are integrated into a Structural Debt Monitoring Framework that maps observable conditions into state configurations, forward dynamics, and resilience assessments under counterfactual changes in financial conditions, income accessibility, and credit composition. The results support a reinterpretation of debt sustainability as a configuration-dependent property rather than a unidimensional function of debt levels, and provide a unified and operational basis for monitoring system-level debt dynamics.

detail.abstract: Can financial experts detect potential greenwashing in ESG communications? Using an eye-tracking experiment with 128 professionals, we document a novel attention-detection-recommendation chain. Attention to textual contradictions increases expert detection sensitivity, significantly reducing investment recommendations. Framing impacts this chain in two distinct ways relative to a control condition: ESG exposure amplifies attention to contradictions, heightening detection-a domain-specific focusing effect; but ESG framing partially buffers the detection-to-investment penalty. Additional results reveal a skepticism paradox: media awareness counterintuitively reduces detection. detail.abstract: The Pacific region presents one of the most complex and cost-intensive environments for international development programme monitoring. Spread across approximately 30 million square kilometres of ocean, the Pacific Island Countries and Territories (PICTs) collectively host hundreds of United Nations (UN) and Council of Regional Organisations in the Pacific (CROP) funded development projects. The majority of regional coordination and monitoring activities for these programmes are managed from Suva, Fiji, the designated regional hub for most UN agencies and CROP bodies. This arrangement, widely accepted as operationally logical given Fiji's relative connectivity, has inadvertently institutionalised a costly and increasingly unsustainable model of monitoring: the Fly-In, Fly-Out (FIFO) approach. This paper critically examines the financial and systemic consequences of the FIFO monitoring model in the Pacific context. Drawing on comparative cost analyses, regional programme data, and global evidence on localised monitoring and evaluation (M&E) systems, the paper argues that the substantial resources currently consumed by inter-island air travel should be strategically reinvested into building the M&E capacity of National Statistics Offices (NSOs) and national programme partners. The proposed 'Local First' monitoring framework positions national institutions as the primary agents of programme oversight, with Suva-based regional experts providing remote technical support and periodic strategic verification rather than routine field visits. The paper concludes with actionable recommendations for UN agencies, CROP organisations, and bilateral donors to reform their regional M&E architecture in a manner that is financially sustainable, capacity-generative, and contextually appropriate for Pacific Island development.

detail.abstract: Industrial transformation in the United States is increasingly shaped not only by policy frameworks and technological advancement, but also by entrepreneurial leadership capable of translating innovation into scalable, real-world applications. While the macroeconomic literature has extensively examined the roles of state investment and corporate capital in manufacturing renewal, the microeconomic mechanisms through which founders drive structural change remain undertheorized. This paper examines the role of innovation-driven founders in advancing sustainable manufacturing through the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), localized production systems, and circular economy principles. Drawing on recent industry data, entrepreneurship research, and economic evidence, the study argues that entrepreneurial leadership functions not as a complementary force to industrial policy, but as a necessary precondition for its effective implementation, bridging the critical gap between strategic frameworks and operational outcomes. This perspective is informed not only by economic analysis and industry data, but also by direct experience in building and operating textile manufacturing systems across different markets. The findings contribute to emerging scholarship on the entrepreneurial ecosystem's role in U.S. competitiveness, with particular relevance for policy designers seeking to accelerate sustainable manufacturing adoption at scale.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how escalating geopolitical tensions in the Strait of Hormuz have transformed the operation and scope of war risk insurance in maritime trade. The Strait of Hormuz, a narrow chokepoint through which roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil transits, has increasingly become an active conflict zone. With at least sixteen vessels having been attacked or damaged since the conflict began, the scale of disruption has become increasingly evident. These tensions have directly contributed to a heightened risk environment for commercial shipping in the region. The constant risk of sudden attacks, detentions, or disruptions has forced shipping companies to rethink their routes, adjust schedules, and adopt more cautious risk management strategies. These developments have, in turn, brought renewed attention to the importance of war risk insurance, highlighting its evolving role in managing modern maritime threats and ensuring the continuity of global trade. Accordingly, this paper will examine the impact of these rising tensions on maritime trade and the growing risks faced by commercial shipping in the region.

detail.title: CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF DANGEROUS GOODS DOCUMENTATION AND ITS IMPACT ON AIR CARGO SAFETY: An Empirical Study of Documentation Practices and Error Patterns
detail.abstract: This study investigates the role of dangerous goods (DG) documentation in air cargo safety. Dangerous goods-including flammable liquids, gases, toxic substances, radioactive materials, and lithium batteries-must be documented in accordance with ICAO Technical Instructions (Doc 9284) and IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR). In spite of these well-established rules, documentation errors continue to be a recurring problem in day-today cargo operations. Data were gathered through a structured questionnaire administered to 50 respondents-cargo staff and MBA aviation students in Chennai-along with interviews with seven cargo documentation practitioners. The results indicate that only 24% of respondents have full knowledge of IATA DGR; 62% come across documentation errors on a regular basis; just 44% consistently follow the mandatory DG checklist; and 56% point to time pressure as a direct reason for mistakes. Based on these findings, the study calls for wider adoption of digital documentation tools, more frequent and structured training, and tighter internal audit routines.

detail.abstract:
The fast pace of digitalization in the healthcare system, especially in the context of national initiatives in India, has led to the swift implementation of Hospital Information Systems (HIS). But translating these technology investments into better clinical and operational outcomes remains patchy, largely due to the lack of alignment in processes, governance and user preparedness. The study examines the role of Quality Management Systems (QMS) in supporting structured and sustainable adoption of Health Information Systems (HIS) in healthcare organizations.

Drawing on established technology adoption frameworks and quality management principles, the research conceptualizes the alignment of key QMS components—document control, training and competency, internal audits, corrective and preventive actions (CAPA), and risk management—with critical phases of the HIS lifecycle, including selection, configuration, testing, implementation, and post-deployment monitoring. The study adopts a practice-oriented approach to analyze how such integration influences system usability, user acceptance, and operational stability.

The findings indicate that QMS-driven governance significantly enhances the effectiveness of HIS implementation by reducing workflow disruptions, improving data reliability, and fostering continuous performance monitoring. The study contributes to the existing literature by proposing a structured, integrative framework that bridges the gap between healthcare operations and information technology. It offers actionable insights for healthcare administrators, quality managers, and policymakers aiming to achieve safe, efficient, and scalable digital transformation in resource-constrained settings.

detail.abstract: The book explores the complete life cycle of illumination products, from manufacturing and usage to end-of-life management. It presents advanced recycling methodologies, including hydrometallurgical recovery of rare-earth elements, pyrolysis and plasma based detoxification, cryogenic and mechanical separation of composite LED materials, and glass and metal valorization techniques. title: Tracking Artificial Intelligence Sentiment in the U.S. Labor Market
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh - Katz Graduate School of Business, University of Pittsburgh - Katz Graduate School of Business, Michigan State University and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - School of Accountancy

detail.title: Tracking Artificial Intelligence Sentiment in the U.S. Labor Market
detail.abstract: This study aims to track U.S. labor market sentiments toward artificial intelligence (AI) from multiple aspects by using large-scale datasets of employee reviews from Glassdoor, executive disclosures from earnings conference calls, individual-level career profiles from LinkedIn, and firm-level job postings, spanning 2021 to 2025. Through a textual analysis of employee job reviews, we find that employee sentiment towards AI is significantly more negative than their overall sentiment towards firms. Importantly, we document a strong positive association between firm productivity and employee AI sentiment. In contrast, management AI sentiment (measured based on management discussions of AI in conference calls) is highly optimistic but does not explain productivity, suggesting that employee AI sentiment plays an important role in unlocking the benefits of AI. By analyzing the contents of employee reviews, we discovered several factors contributing to the negative impact of AI on employee sentiment, among which concerns about job security have the most negative impact. AI-related layoffs negatively affect employee AI sentiment and thus could offset the benefits of adopting AI. Consistent with employee concerns, we find that firms with more AI-skilled employees have a higher overall turnover rate, lower hire rate, and slower employment growth. These results are also true for firms without excessive hiring after the COVID pandemic, suggesting that the effects are not mainly due to AI washing. Finally, we document a significant and increasing wage premium and greater upward mobility for skilled AI employees, suggesting a talent war for skilled AI employees among firms and significant rewards for AI skills in the labor market. Overall, the study provides a comprehensive analysis of AI's impact on the U.S. labor market by using the most recent data.

title: The Bot Tax: Why AI Systems Should Pay Social Security on the Wages They Replace — A Labor Displacement Levy Proposal with Empirical Case Study

detail.title: The Bot Tax: Why AI Systems Should Pay Social Security on the Wages They Replace — A Labor Displacement Levy Proposal with Empirical Case Study
detail.abstract:
Abstract

Social Security's trust fund is projected to be depleted by 2033 — triggering an automatic 23% benefit cut — a projection calculated at today's 4.3% unemployment rate. AI-driven labor displacement threatens to accelerate that date by eroding the payroll tax base that exclusively funds Social Security and Medicare. Unlike corporate profits, which flow to the general fund, FICA contributions are ring-fenced: when AI replaces a worker, that revenue does not get redirected — it disappears.

This paper quantifies that displacement using a verifiable empirical case study: a production-grade SaaS application built in 13 calendar days by one non-engineer directing an AI assistant, equivalent to approximately 1,600 developer-hours of traditional professional labor. The human equivalent would have generated $33,742 in tax revenue, of which $14,806 represents FICA contributions directly funding Social Security and Medicare. The AI-assisted build generated zero. Approximately 35 cents of every dollar in AI-replaced labor value represents tax revenue that never reaches government.

We propose a Labor Displacement Levy (LDL) — a 25–35% levy on AI vendor API and subscription revenue, collected at the billing layer and ring-fenced for Social Security and AI workforce transition programs. We argue this is the only mechanically viable collection point before displaced value disperses into corporate margins, and we model its projected yield against the scale of displacement currently underway.

title: The Capacity-Adoption Paradox: Managing Workforce Bottlenecks During Rapid Technology Deployment
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Kenan-Flagler Business School

detail.title: The Capacity-Adoption Paradox: Managing Workforce Bottlenecks During Rapid Technology Deployment
detail.abstract: When automation displaces workers, the natural response is to expand retraining. But retraining programs have finite throughput (limited seats, instructors, and completion capacity), and expanding that throughput can backfire. We show how this happens. Faster retraining drains workers from declining skills, tightens the labor market for legacy tasks, and makes automation more attractive, sending still more displaced workers into the very bottlenecks that were expanded. We call this the capacity-adoption paradox. To study it, we model workforce conversion as a network of capacity-limited pathways and couple it to technology adoption that responds to labor scarcity. The model yields three main results. First, we characterize a pacing region: deployment is sustainable if and only if the required outflow from every set of declining skills stays within the throughput of pathways leaving that set. When this condition fails, no reallocation of workers across existing pathways can prevent backlogs from growing. Second, a cut-level feedback elasticity determines when expanding capacity is destabilizing. It decomposes into four measurable channels: displacement footprint, adoption leverage, labor-cost sensitivity, and wage response to added throughput. Third, the welfare-optimal policy combines capacity investment targeted at binding bottlenecks with a task-specific congestion price that slows deployment where it loads the scarcest pathways most heavily. For workforce planners, the central message is that the binding constraint on AI deployment is not aggregate training budgets but the throughput of specific conversion pathways, and deployment pace must be calibrated accordingly.

title: RESEARCH PROJECT REPORT On "Workplace stress and its impact on employee performance"

detail.title: RESEARCH PROJECT REPORT On "Workplace stress and its impact on employee performance"
detail.abstract:
Workplace stress has emerged as a significant concern in modern organizations, directly
influencing employee performance, productivity, and overall organizational effectiveness. This
research report examines the causes, effects, and implications of workplace stress on employee
performance across different organizational settings.
The study identifies key sources of stress, including excessive workload, tight deadlines, role
ambiguity, lack of job security, and poor work-life balance. It highlights how prolonged exposure to
stress can lead to decreased job satisfaction, reduced efficiency, increased absenteeism, and higher
employee turnover.
The findings suggest that while a moderate level of stress may enhance motivation and
performance, excessive stress negatively impacts employees’ physical and mental well-being,
ultimately lowering productivity. The research also emphasizes the importance of supportive
management, effective communication, and stress management practices in minimizing workplace
stress.
The report concludes that organizations must adopt proactive strategies such as employee wellness
programs, flexible work arrangements, and clear role definitions to reduce stress levels and
improve employee performance. Addressing workplace stress not only benefits employees but also
contributes to sustainable organizational growth and success.

detail.abstract: Organizations are increasingly turning to AI as a means of conducting their business activities...and making decisions. As a result, many companies are benefiting from increased efficiency, productivity, and data-driven decision making when they hire new employees. Many companies have also implemented AI technologies quickly; however, many organizations have been criticized for their inability to provide adequate support for mental health issues faced by workers jumping into the modern age. One of the most common problems resulting from AI implementation is employee anxiety. While anxiety may come from a variety of sources, employees commonly express fears of losing their job, being subject to workplace monitoring and fearing the unknown regarding AI technology. It is therefore imperative from a managerial psychology perspective to understand how AI has impacted employee's mental health through the lens of sustaining high levels of mental health and the effectiveness of the organization as a whole. The purpose of this paper is to explore the link between AI in the workplace and employee anxiety through examining the detrimental psychology factors that influence stress levels during instances of technological changes within an organization, as well as to examine the positive psychology factors that assist with easing employee anxiety and assisting with employee adjustment to the technological advances of AI through an analysis of the actions of management (i.e. communication techniques, training and support) on employee stress levels. The importance of this project is to identify and establish a balance between the advancement of technology and the employees of an organization for the purpose of providing a safe, psychologically healthy and sustainable work environment.

detail.title: Цифровая карта задержки при обработке грузов в морском терминале как ИТ-модель события, подтверждающего факт задержки.
detail.abstract: This article develops a model of a digital delay card for cargo handling operations at a seaport terminal. The study treats a delay as an operational event that should enter an information system in a structured form suitable for subsequent evidentiary use. The methodological basis of the article is A. O. Butrim's approach to recording delays in maritime cargo handling, which focuses on the legal qualification of deviations from an agreed operational schedule, the documentation of delay causes, and the reduction of evidentiary risks. Building on this methodology, the article proposes an IT model that converts a delay into a digital event with fixed time parameters, a process stage, a classified cause, a related participant, a data source, supporting documents, a responsible user, and an audit trail. The article argues that such a model can help a terminal connect operational data with internal control, claims management, and legal risk management. The proposed digital delay card does not replace the terminal operating system. It works as a dedicated module that consolidates legally relevant data from existing operational systems, electronic document flow, event logs, service records, notices, and internal reports.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the central tension of AI-driven economic transformation: the paradox where corporate efficiency gains from artificial intelligence may ultimately undermine the consumer demand that sustains them. Companies adopt AI to reduce costs — primarily labor — but fewer workers mean fewer consumers, triggering a self-reinforcing feedback loop of declining demand and further cost-cutting.

Drawing on data from Goldman Sachs, McKinsey, the World Economic Forum, PwC, and Stanford's AI Index, the paper documents the speed and scale of AI adoption (78% of organizations by early 2026), the emerging evidence of labor market disruption (55,000 AI-attributed U.S. layoffs in 2025, a hiring collapse for young workers in AI-exposed occupations), and the macroeconomic transmission channel through which productivity gains that accrue to capital rather than labor can reduce aggregate consumption even as output rises.

Building on the task-based framework of Acemoglu (2024) and Acemoglu-Restrepo (2018, 2019, 2022), a formal model grounded in differential marginal propensities to consume (labor income vs. capital income) generates three testable scenarios: a benign equilibrium, a consumption squeeze, and an economic bifurcation. The paper introduces the Centaur Economy as a macroeconomic equilibrium in which augmentation-based human-AI collaboration serves as the structural mechanism that maintains aggregate demand. The analysis surveys AI's divergent impacts across the United States, Europe, Asia, and Romania, and outlines five scenarios — from augmentation-centered prosperity to an Icarus-cycle bust — for how the tension between productivity and demand may resolve.

The analysis is informed by the author's direct experience running technology companies in Romania. AI tools were used for research assistance, brainstorming, and English language editing; all analysis, arguments, and conclusions are the author's own.

title: Ex-Ante Structural Diagnosis of Climate Project Performance: VERA-TCV™ Framework Applied to 15 GCF Projects

detail.title: Ex-Ante Structural Diagnosis of Climate Project Performance: VERA-TCV™ Framework Applied to 15 GCF Projects

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study analyzes publicly available project documentation. No human subjects research was conducted. Ethics approval is not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
The structural conditions that determine climate project performance are present in funding proposal documents at the point of GCF Board approval. They are readable before implementation begins. This report provides the quantitative foundation for that claim across fifteen GCF-funded projects spanning four continents, five thematic areas, and an average of 5.7 years of Annual Performance Report records.

VERA-TCV™ applies four computationally independent models — VERA™, ToC:f(x)™, C-FAIR™, and VORTA™ — to funding proposal documents alone, before any implementation data is reviewed. Across 313 assessable signal-year cells, the portfolio-weighted directional consistency rate is approximately 92%. No unresolved material pathway contradiction was recorded across the evaluated portfolio. Thirteen independent evaluation documents converged directionally with framework signals in every comparable case.

Four structural patterns account for all fifteen cases: Design–Environment Separation (8 projects), Internal Mechanism Failure (2), Measurement Architecture Gap (3), and ToC-Level Constraint (2). Three portfolio-level findings emerge that no individual case can produce alone: C-FAIR™ Grade C is the structural justification for concessional climate finance; VORTA™ VCS Grade F conceals six structurally distinct causes; and the absence of ToC:f(x)™ TIER I is a structural feature of multi-actor climate programmes, not a design failure.

Structure before execution. Diagnosis before capital.

detail.abstract: Online Dispute Resolution (ODR), an online variant of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR), is the process of resolving disagreements between parties via the use of technology, including the internet and digital platforms. Through video conferencing, secure messaging, and document sharing, it enables negotiation, mediation, and arbitration, offering a quicker, less expensive, and more convenient substitute for conventional court litigation. It can be effectively incorporated into the commercial jurisprudence of Uzbekistan while maintaining procedural efficiency and fairness at the same time. Specifically, in this paper it will be argued that ODR must be considered as a process reform which allows for more efficient and less costly dispute settlement processes while having built-in protections against potential unfairness that might emerge from ODR solutions. In order to achieve this goal, the article will outline an efficiency-equity framework that will define (i) efficiency-by-design factors, such as online case management and remote participation tools, on one hand, and (ii) equity-by-design considerations, including effective notice, response opportunities, impartiality, evidence handling procedures, reasoning explanation, and enforceability, on the other hand.

title: SME Vulnerability Mapping System under Crisis Conditions A Multi-Layer Diagnostic Framework for SMEs

detail.title: SME Vulnerability Mapping System under Crisis Conditions A Multi-Layer Diagnostic Framework for SMEs
detail.abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are highly exposed to systemic shocks in environments characterized by geopolitical instability, macroeconomic volatility, and supply chain disruption (World Bank, 2020; OECD, 2021). This paper proposes a structured vulnerability mapping system designed to identify and operationalize enterprise-level fragility under crisis conditions. The framework integrates multi-domain risk exposure (operations, finance, supply chain, workforce, information systems) with a failure-mode diagnostic layer and a resilience scoring mechanism. By translating dispersed crisis signals into a unified diagnostic index, the model enables early identification of enterprise stress points and supports decision-making under uncertainty (OECD, 2023). The contribution lies in bridging macro-level instability with firm-level vulnerability assessment through a structured, implementable framework suitable for both policy and applied research contexts.

title: Powering the Digital Economy: The Global Expansion of Data Centres and its Energy Implications
affiliations: Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: Powering the Digital Economy: The Global Expansion of Data Centres and its Energy Implications
detail.abstract: The expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud computing is turning data centers into a strategic component of the global economy. This paper provides an empirical assessment of the global expansion of data centers and its energy implications, focusing on the United States and Europe. We combine facility-level data with electricity consumption data and document a sharp rise in global data-center capacity over the past fifteen years, with the United States remaining the leading market in terms of both number of facilities and computational capacity. While data-center electricity consumption remains relatively limited at the global level, it is growing rapidly and already has notable implications in some areas for local electricity demand, grid congestion, and electricity prices, especially in the United States. These dynamics are generating political tensions and have spurred a broad policy debate on grid access, cost allocation, energy security, and strategic autonomy.

title: Una filiera nucleare europea per il 2050 - Oltre la decarbonizzazione: le ragioni strategiche del consolidamento continentale - This paper is also available in English

detail.title: Una filiera nucleare europea per il 2050 - Oltre la decarbonizzazione: le ragioni strategiche del consolidamento continentale - This paper is also available in English
detail.abstract:
Il dibattito europeo sul nucleare è oggi inquadrato prevalentemente come questione di decarbonizzazione del settore elettrico. Questo inquadramento mette in competizione tecnologie con cinetiche di sviluppo molto diverse — fonti rinnovabili rapidamente dispiegabili e nucleare con tempi industriali quindicennali — e oscura le ragioni propriamente strategiche per cui una filiera nucleare europea continua ad avere senso. Il saggio propone di disgiungere i due piani. La decarbonizzazione fino al 2040 sarà guidata da FER, accumulo, interconnessioni e gas di transizione; la nuova capacità nucleare europea opererà a regime tra il 2042 e il 2080, con un ruolo che si configura come strumento di autonomia continentale, politica industriale, stabilità dei prezzi per la manifattura energy-intensive e continuità del know-how verso la fusione.

Il saggio si colloca nel filone della letteratura tecnica internazionale (MIT 2018 e 2024, IEA, OECD/NEA, BloombergNEF, Clean Air Task Force, Bruegel, ITIF) e aggiunge tre contributi originali. Primo, applica la metodologia dei system costs della NEA al caso italiano utilizzando i dati TERNA 2025 prodotti su mandato ARERA (Delibera 392/2024), quantificando l’insostenibilità economica dello stoccaggio stagionale (LCOS a 4.000 €/MWh al 2050), il gap di generazione invernale (115–130 TWh su quattro mesi) e il requisito residuale di capacità programmabile (almeno 30 GW per adeguatezza). Secondo, propone un’architettura istituzionale concreta articolata in cinque pilastri (ENFCA, ERPF, ENRA, Compact, Skills Programme) costruita su meccanismi esistenti (URENCO, Orano, ENSREG, IPCEI, modello EASA). Terzo, tratta il nucleare come politica industriale e sovranità anziché come variabile di ottimizzazione del sistema elettrico.

Il saggio combina rigore analitico con riconoscimento esplicito dei trade-off. Applica la metodologia NEA dei system costs per quantificare i costi di integrazione oltre l’LCOE; differenzia per Technology Readiness Level tra fissione Gen III/III+ (commercialmente disponibile), SMR Gen III+ e Gen IV (ancora da validare industrialmente) e fusione (fase di ricerca); stima il costo della non-scelta italiana in ordini di grandezza (175–380 mrd€ cumulati 2030–2060); propone un’architettura ENRA articolata su due livelli (Lite entro il 2030 con mutuo riconoscimento volontario delle Generic Design Assessment, Full dal 2032 con poteri di certificazione vincolanti su modello EASA); e struttura la roadmap di implementazione in forma probabilistica su tre scenari (Consolidamento, Geometria Variabile, Frammentazione Persistente) con eventi-trigger e scelte robuste identificabili sotto incertezza profonda. Le obiezioni vengono affrontate in modo simmetrico: il nucleare viene presentato come tecnologia che trasferisce il rischio dal mercato al bilancio pubblico anziché come tecnologia priva di rischio; il nodo critico degli SMR viene individuato nel modello industriale-economico non ancora validato e non nella sola maturità tecnologica; al principale possibilità di fallimento (failure mode) interno di ENRA (l’implementazione incompleta) viene nominato e disciplinato nella proposta stessa; e un caveat di non-monocausalità riconosce che il nucleare non è l’unica soluzione a ciascuno dei problemi individuati, ma è l’unica tecnologia che contribuisce simultaneamente a tutti e sei. Il saggio conclude che la finestra decisionale italiana è 2026–2028, che il rinvio è esso stesso una scelta costosa, e che la partecipazione effettiva all’architettura europea è condizionata alle precondizioni istituzionali domestiche sviluppate nel documento parallelo.

title: AI-Augmented Quantum Entanglement Communications for Department of Defense Operations: Capabilities, Adversarial Risks, and a Governance Architecture

detail.title: AI-Augmented Quantum Entanglement Communications for Department of Defense Operations: Capabilities, Adversarial Risks, and a Governance Architecture

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants or animal subjects and therefore did not require ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Quantum entanglement distribution is transitioning from laboratory demonstration toward engineered network services, raising questions about its role in U.S. Department of Defense (DOD) operations. At the same time, machine learning has become integral to quantum-system control, while national policy has shifted toward post-quantum cryptography under NSA and NIST guidance.

This paper synthesizes research in quantum networking and machine learning with U.S. policy to assess where entanglement-based communications may offer operational value. It combines literature review, capability mapping, and adversarial scenario analysis to evaluate both benefits and risks.

The findings suggest that entanglement-based systems will not replace classical cryptographic infrastructure in the near term, but may provide advantages in specific domains such as timing, coalition key management, and secure sensor links. However, the integration of AI introduces new failure modes not addressed by existing assurance frameworks.

To address this gap, the paper proposes a four-layer governance architecture, including a structured AI auditability framework, to support defensible deployment in mission-critical environments.

title: The Deprivation: A Structural Analysis of States Failure in Fulfilling the Fundamental Human Rights to Food, Shelter, and Clothing
affiliations: Swiss School Of Business and Management
