declarations.declarationOfInterest: n'a
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract: This dissertation provides an exhaustive, critical examination of the global systemic failure by state actors to guarantee the fundamental human rights to food, shelter, and clothing. Rooted in the juridical frameworks of international human rights law-specifically Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) and Article 11 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR)-these basic necessities are theoretically enshrined as the bedrock of human dignity and cultural participation. However, empirical data, sociological theory, and biopolitical analysis reveal a profound divergence between international legal obligations and actual state practice. By synthesizing theoretical perspectives on biopolitics, neoliberal structural violence, and state-sanctioned deprivation with macro-level empirical data from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and micro-level socioeconomic indicators from the National Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) and Telangana state data in India, this analysis demonstrates that the deprivation of these basic needs is not merely an administrative oversight. Rather, it is a systemic, culpable failure of modern governance. Almost every government globally is implicated in this deprivation, stripping vulnerable populations of their capabilities, subjecting them to corporeal othering, and fundamentally violating their human dignity and cultural rights.

title: A European Nuclear Supply Chain for 2050 - Beyond Decarbonization: The Strategic Rationale for Continental Consolidation - Questo lavoro è anche disponibile in Italiano

detail.title: A European Nuclear Supply Chain for 2050 - Beyond Decarbonization: The Strategic Rationale for Continental Consolidation - Questo lavoro è anche disponibile in Italiano
detail.abstract:
European debate on nuclear power is currently framed as an issue of electricity-sector decarbonisation. This framing places technologies with very different deployment cycles in artificial competition — rapidly deployable renewables versus nuclear with multi-decadal industrial timelines — and obscures the strategic reasons why a European nuclear supply chain remains relevant. This paper proposes to disentangle the two questions. Decarbonisation through 2040 will rely on renewables, storage, interconnections and transitional gas; new European nuclear capacity will operate at scale only between 2042 and 2080, with a role better understood as continental autonomy, industrial policy, price stability for energy-intensive manufacturing, and continuity of know-how toward fusion.

The paper sits within the technical literature initiated by MIT (2018, 2024), IEA, OECD/NEA, BloombergNEF, Clean Air Task Force and Bruegel, and adds three original contributions. First, it applies the system-cost methodology of NEA «Full Costs of Electricity Provision» to the Italian case using TERNA 2025 data (mandated by ARERA Resolution 392/2024), quantifying the structural infeasibility of seasonal storage (LCOS at 4,000 €/MWh in 2050), the winter generation gap (115–130 TWh over four months), and the residual programmable-capacity requirement (at least 30 GW for adequacy). Second, it proposes a concrete five-pillar institutional architecture (ENFCA, ERPF, ENRA, Compact, Skills Programme) built on existing mechanisms (URENCO, Orano, ENSREG, IPCEI, EASA model). Third, it treats nuclear as industrial policy and sovereignty rather than as system-cost optimisation.

The paper combines analytical rigour with explicit acknowledgement of trade-offs. It applies the NEA system-cost methodology to quantify integration costs beyond LCOE; differentiates by Technology Readiness Level among Gen III/III+ fission (commercially deployable), SMR Gen III+ and IV (still to be validated industrially), and fusion (research stage); estimates the cost of Italian non-decision in orders of magnitude (€175–380 bn cumulative 2030–2060); proposes a two-tier ENRA design (Lite by 2030 with voluntary mutual recognition of Generic Design Assessments, Full from 2032 with binding certification powers, modelled on EASA); and structures the implementation roadmap probabilistically around three scenarios (Consolidation, Variable Geometry, Persistent Fragmentation) with trigger events and robust policy choices identifiable under deep uncertainty. Counterarguments are addressed symmetrically: nuclear is presented as transferring risk from the market to the public balance sheet rather than eliminating it; SMRs’ principal bottleneck is identified as the not-yet-validated industrial-economic model rather than technology readiness alone; ENRA’s main internal failure mode (incomplete implementation) is named and disciplined in the proposal; and a non-monocausality caveat acknowledges that nuclear is not the only solution to any single problem but is the only technology contributing simultaneously to all six identified problems. The paper concludes that the Italian decision window is 2026–2028, that postponement is itself a costly choice, and that effective participation in the European architecture is conditional on the domestic institutional preconditions developed in the companion paper.

title: Winning at Value Creation: The Championship Cycle as the Formal Synthesis of Elite Sports Performance Science and Private Equity Operational Doctrine

detail.abstract:
What do the most decorated sports dynasties in history and the most consistently top-performing Private Equity (PE) firms share? For four decades, sports scientists and PE researchers have been independently solving the question of how institutions produce sustained excellence across generations, cycles, and competitive environments in disciplinary isolation.

This paper draws on a structured literature review of forty peer-reviewed studies and applies a framework synthesis methodology to develop a unified model explaining how institutions build and sustain high performance across cycles. It introduces the Championship Cycle, a five-phase framework that integrates insights from sports performance science and PE research into a single analytical structure.

The model is constructed through a systematic parallel analysis of the selected literature and organizes the core processes of performance development into five stages: The Game Plan (Strategic Orientation), The Draft Day (Selection Discipline), The Season Grind (Operational Transformation), The Game Day (Value Realization and Exit), and The Legacy (Sustained Institutional Excellence). These stages reflect convergent findings from Bloom (1985), Ericsson et al. (1993), and Kaplan and Schoar (2005), which collectively describe how institutions build capability architectures that enable sustained excellence over time.

The paper finds that elite sports systems and PE firms rely on a structurally similar institutional playbook. The scientific models used to develop elite athletes closely mirror the operational frameworks investors use to transform portfolio companies. Despite being developed independently over decades, research in both fields converges on a common formula for achieving and sustaining excellence: performance is driven by the progressive institutionalization of capabilities, where structured routines, feedback mechanisms, and disciplined execution compound across cycles.

This shared logic is consistent with dynamic capabilities and performance persistence theory, which emphasize that sustained outperformance is rooted in embedded organizational processes rather than isolated events. Performance improvement is therefore cumulative and path-dependent, reflecting the degree to which institutions systematize and scale their practices over time.

Building on this synthesis, and using an integrated synthesis methodology, the paper introduces the Institutional Training Maturity Benchmark, a diagnostic tool that operationalizes The Championship Cycle for practitioners. The benchmark enables PE firms to assess their level of institutional development, identify capability gaps, and determine their position within the performance lifecycle using a structured, stage-based framework inspired by athlete development models.

The paper’s primary contribution is to establish, in a formal academic framework, that a common system underlies high-performance institutions in both sports and PE. By creating a shared vocabulary and a practical diagnostic instrument, it provides a foundation for both researchers and practitioners to better understand, measure, and enhance sustained performance.

title: Privacy-Preserving Collaborative Filtering Hides Routes Without Sacrificing Transit Recommendation Accuracy

detail.title: Privacy-Preserving Collaborative Filtering Hides Routes Without Sacrificing Transit Recommendation Accuracy
detail.abstract: The increasing adoption of GPS-enabled smartphones and transit ticketing apps has enabled personalized route recommendations, but at the cost of exposing users' location histories. Traditional collaborative filtering for transportation requires collecting raw user trajectories, raising privacy concerns that discourage adoption. This paper introduces a privacy-preserving collaborative filtering framework that operates on transformed user data using randomized aggregation and differential privacy. User route preferences are encoded as noisy preference vectors before being shared with a central recommender. The framework is evaluated on two datasets: simulated trips from Chicago Transit Authority ridership statistics, and real trajectory data from a publicly available GPS dataset. Results show that the privacy-preserving method achieves recommendation accuracy within 2-4% of the non-private baseline while guaranteeing differential privacy at standard settings. A user study with 120 daily commuters confirms that 89% are willing to share obfuscated preferences when told raw locations are never stored. Unlike prior hybrid recommendation approaches for agent-based transportation platforms, our method decouples user identity from observed behavior before any mining occurs. The framework is compatible with existing agent-based transportation transaction managers, requiring only a local privacy filter at each client agent. We conclude that privacy need not come at the cost of recommendation quality in transit systems.

title: Economic growth and labour rights: the case of the Employment Rights Act 2025
affiliations: School of Law, King's College, London; Centre for Business Research, University of Cambridge

detail.title: Economic growth and labour rights: the case of the Employment Rights Act 2025
detail.abstract:
How do labour rights affect economic growth, and what may we predict from the Employment Rights Act 2025? The UK government says its first mission is 'growth', and improving workers' rights is part of this. However, the government chose to define its 'growth' mission solely in terms of Gross Domestic Product. GDP often conflicts directly with growth in real wages, valuable production, equality, or improving the environment, because it accurately measures market prices alone. It ignores market failures. It ignores inequality. It discounts public services, voluntary work, and leisure. Yet to grow GDP, Labour's leadership dropped its original pledges to create 'a national goal for well-being' and a New Deal for Working People.

This article evaluates the Act's new rules on zero hours contracts, day one rights, equality action plans, fire and rehire, collective bargaining, collective action, and the Fair Work Agency, using comparative data. It shows the UK will still have among the worst labour rights in the OECD on virtually every front, and its position barely moves even if all rules are implemented. This reveals the folly of defining a 'growth' mission around contradictory GDP metrics. Real economic growth is growth in household wealth, not growth in corporate profit by redistributing wealth away from workers, rent-seeking, or externalising damage. The UK's experience shows that labour rights are unsafe while GDP is in use.

The solutions are to define growth, in law, to focus on real household wealth within an Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index, and to pass a new Employment Rights Act to match international standards. This must include a single worker status, fair pay agreements across all sectors, worker directors on company boards and in control of pension money, and statutory duties for full employment for the Treasury and Bank of England. The text of draft legislation is proposed.

title: A Theoretical Framework for Auxiliary-Loss-Free Load Balancing of Sparse Mixture-of-Experts in Large-Scale AI Models
affiliations: and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: A Theoretical Framework for Auxiliary-Loss-Free Load Balancing of Sparse Mixture-of-Experts in Large-Scale AI Models

publicationDetails.journalName: Chicago Booth Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In large-scale AI training, Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (s-MoE) layers enable scaling by activating only a small subset of experts per token. An operational challenge in this design is load balancing: routing tokens to minimize the number of idle experts, which is important for the efficient utilization of costly GPUs and for the thorough training of architecture parameters across all experts. We provide a theoretical framework for analyzing the Auxiliary-Loss-Free Load Balancing (ALF-LB) procedure -- proposed by DeepSeek’s Wang et al. (2024) -- by casting it as a primal-dual method using a single-shot, constant-time update per training iteration for solving an assignment problem. First, in a stylized deterministic setting, our framework yields several insightful structural properties: (i) a monotonic improvement condition for the Lagrangian objective, (ii) a preference rule that moves tokens from overloaded to underloaded experts, and (iii) an approximate-balancing guarantee. Then, we incorporate the stochastic and dynamic nature of AI training using a generalized online optimization formulation. In the online setting, we derive a strong convexity property of the objective that leads to a logarithmic expected regret bound under certain step-size choices. Additionally, we present real experiments on 1B-parameter DeepSeekMoE models to complement our theoretical findings. Together, these results build a principled framework for analyzing the Auxiliary-Loss-Free Load Balancing of s-MoE in AI models.

title: The Coherence Framework: Explaining Institutional Drift through Translation

detail.title: The Coherence Framework: Explaining Institutional Drift through Translation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, personal data, or identifiable subjects. Ethical approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and did not receive external funding.

detail.abstract:
Why do institutions drift away from their stated purpose—even when they perform well, follow established processes, and make high-quality decisions?

This paper introduces the Coherence Framework, a theory explaining how institutional drift can emerge as a structural consequence of how intent is translated within decision systems. Rather than acting directly on purpose, institutions operate on decision-relevant representations—such as metrics, models, criteria, and dashboards—that are used to evaluate, compare, and allocate resources. These representations make decision-making possible, but they also reshape what becomes visible and actionable. As intent is translated into measurable and comparable forms, certain dimensions are emphasized while others are reduced or excluded. Over time, these representations stabilize and become the basis for decision-making itself, gradually redefining what the institution is effectively optimizing for. This process gives rise to what the paper terms Translation Drift: a cumulative divergence between stated intent and the representations that guide action. Importantly, this divergence does not depend on failure. It often emerges under conditions of strong governance, aligned incentives, and consistent execution, allowing institutions to remain operationally coherent and performance-positive while drifting from their original purpose. To make this dynamic observable, the paper introduces a practical diagnostic approach for mapping how intent is translated across decision systems. By examining common governance artefacts—such as evaluation criteria, scoring models, and performance dashboards—it becomes possible to detect shifts in meaning before they appear in outcomes. The paper contributes by shifting the focus from decision quality to what decisions are made on. It shows that improving outcomes is not only a matter of better decisions, but of ensuring that the representations guiding those decisions remain aligned with institutional intent. The central implication is straightforward: institutions do not drift because they decide poorly, but because what they decide on has already changed.

The framework is relevant for researchers in organizational theory and philosophy of social science, as well as practitioners involved in governance, strategy, and performance management.

detail.abstract: The Ten Commandments are almost certainly headed back to the Supreme Court.  Over the past couple of years, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Texas have all passed statutes requiring the Decalogue to be posted in public school classrooms, and the federal courts are reassessing whether such a display is consistent with the Establishment Clause of the U.S. Constitution. A new defense of the posters argues that they are “passive displays” and therefore do not violate the Constitution. Whatever the courts make of the “passive displays” argument, it should baffle theologians, religious scholars, and people of faith.  In the Christian faith, God’s Word is not usually thought of as passive, but as “living and active.”  This Essay lays out the implications of this surprising turn in the defense of the posters.

title: Digital Overload and Inner Autonomy - A Stoic-Psychological Model of Cognitive Stability

detail.title: Digital Overload and Inner Autonomy - A Stoic-Psychological Model of Cognitive Stability
detail.abstract:
Digital technologies increasingly shape attention, emotional regulation, and psychological self-regulation under conditions of continuous stimulus availability and persistent interruption. As digital environments become progressively optimized for attentional capture, concerns regarding cognitive fragmentation, emotional exhaustion, and declining psychological stability continue to grow.


This paper develops a Stoic-psychological model of cognitive stability under conditions of persistent digital stimulation. Its central assumption is that digital overload does not primarily impair attention in a technical sense, but rather undermines inner autonomy. Inner autonomy refers to the capacity to direct attention consciously, regulate emotional reactivity, and maintain an inner distance between external stimuli and personal judgment.


The proposed model integrates Stoic concepts of inner control, attentional discipline, and cognitive distancing with contemporary psychological research on self-regulation, emotion regulation, and attentional control. Digital overstimulation is therefore understood not merely as an individual problem of discipline, but as a structural tension between highly optimized stimulus architectures and limited human regulatory capacities.


The paper argues that cognitive stability is becoming an increasingly important psychological and societal resource in digitally accelerated environments. It is intended as a theoretical-conceptual contribution at the intersection of Stoicism, psychology, and attention research, providing a framework for future research on digital self-regulation, inner autonomy, and psychological stability under conditions of continuous external stimulus competition.

title: Systematic Tactical Allocation in Emerging Markets vs. U.S.: A Momentum-Based Approach

detail.title: Systematic Tactical Allocation in Emerging Markets vs. U.S.: A Momentum-Based Approach
detail.abstract:
The global investment environment is going through a period of meaningful structural change. The dominance of the U.S. dollar is increasingly being questioned, geopolitical tensions are rising, and macroeconomic uncertainty remains elevated. Together, these forces challenge the post-Global Financial Crisis environment in which U.S. equities consistently outperformed most international markets. As a result, investors may be approaching a turning point where relative returns between U.S. equities and international markets—especially Emerging Markets (EM)—begin to shift.

This research focuses on a practical portfolio allocation question: when should investors increase or reduce exposure to Emerging Market equities relative to U.S. equities? Building on our earlier work analyzing the EAFE-USA spread, we extend the framework to Emerging Markets. Our hypothesis is that the relative performance between U.S. and EM equities is not random. Instead, it shows patterns driven by momentum and broader market trends. These patterns likely reflect persistent capital flows and the gradual way macroeconomic information spreads across global markets.

Rather than relying on static asset allocation approaches, we develop a dynamic allocation model that uses momentum and trend signals to generate practical timing signals between U.S. and EM equities. Emerging Markets are particularly interesting in this context because they tend to experience stronger regime shifts and larger performance cycles than developed international markets.

title: Generative AI Risk, Firm-Side Implementation Exposure, and Asset Prices
affiliations: Saint Mary's University, Canada - Department of Economics

detail.title: Generative AI Risk, Firm-Side Implementation Exposure, and Asset Prices
detail.abstract: We study how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) risk is priced across firms with different levels of firm-side implementation exposure. We construct two textual measures: a newspaperbased GenAI risk index built from adverse acts and threats, and an earnings-call-based implementation exposure measure built from CEO-native language and an eight-channel taxonomy. We find that unexpected adverse GenAI news widens the machine-minus-human spread mainly by depressing low-exposure firms. Firm-level panel regressions show that adverse GenAI news lowers returns on average, but lowers them less for firms with stronger implementation exposure. Industry-level tests further show that this pattern varies systematically across sectors and industries.

detail.abstract:
We construct the longest publicly available daily panel of a Korean cryptocurrency exchange, combining 12 years of Bithumb trading data with global equities, macro assets, FX, and Binance market prices.

Using 4,423 daily observations for BTC/KRW and multi-asset macro series, we examine cross-asset correlation, causality, regime dynamics, and the kimchi premium in the Korean cryptocurrency market.

We document four main findings. First, Bithumb’s BTC trading-value share exhibits a strong negative co-movement with altcoin trading activity (r = -0.371, p < 10⁻¹⁰⁰, N = 3,501), robust across multiple robustness checks. Second, increases in VIX are positively associated with Bithumb BTC trading activity, indicating retail trading activation during risk-off regimes. Third, the kimchi premium averages +1.63% against actual USD/KRW, quantifying a persistent Korea-versus-global price wedge. Fourth, Bithumb exhibits a cleaner alt-rotation signal than Upbit in exchange-level comparisons.

The findings provide an empirical basis for cross-asset trading signals, algorithmic trading systems, and exchange-level decision dashboards.

detail.abstract:
Abstract en castellano

Este white paper analiza críticamente la evolución de la innovación abierta tras más de dos décadas de adopción organizacional. El documento sostiene que muchas empresas han incorporado sus prácticas visibles —retos, hackatones, hubs, alianzas o programas con startups— sin rediseñar las condiciones estructurales que permiten que la apertura genere valor real. A partir de veinte elementos críticos agrupados en cinco clústeres estratégicos, el trabajo identifica nueve categorías de fracturas: fractura, vacío estratégico, distorsión, ficción operativa, aporía, obstáculo sistémico, ceguera interna, inercia y contrapunto. Estas categorías permiten comprender los quiebres que afectan la gobernanza, la cultura, la colaboración ecosistémica, las capacidades organizativas, el talento, la movilización y los incentivos. Su tesis central es que la innovación abierta no fracasa por falta de herramientas, sino por brechas profundas entre discurso y práctica, apertura externa y absorción interna, colaboración y retorno estratégico. Finalmente, propone una lectura organizacional orientada a rediseñar los cimientos de la innovación abierta para convertirla en una capacidad sostenible, gobernada y alineada con el propósito empresarial.

Abstract in English

This white paper critically examines the evolution of open innovation after more than two decades of organizational adoption. It argues that many companies have embraced its visible practices—challenges, hackathons, hubs, partnerships, or startup programs—without redesigning the structural conditions required for openness to create real value. Based on twenty critical elements grouped into five strategic clusters, the paper identifies nine categories of fractures: fracture, strategic void, distortion, operational fiction, aporia, systemic obstacle, internal blindness, inertia, and counterpoint. These categories help explain the breakdowns affecting governance, culture, ecosystem collaboration, organizational capabilities, talent, mobilization, and incentives. Its central argument is that open innovation does not fail because of a lack of tools, but because of deep gaps between discourse and practice, external openness and internal absorption, collaboration and strategic return. Finally, it offers an organizational reading aimed at redesigning the foundations of open innovation so that it becomes a sustainable, governed, and purpose-aligned capability.

title: Robust Stochastic Facility Location: Sensitivity Analysis and Exact Solution
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Sheffield University Management School, School of Economics and Management, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Robust Stochastic Facility Location: Sensitivity Analysis and Exact Solution

publicationDetails.detailsText: published in INFORMS Journal on Computing, Volume 34, No 5. Pp: 2776-2803.

detail.abstract: This work focuses on a broad class of facility location problems in the context of adaptive robust stochastic optimization under the state-dependent demand uncertainty. The demand is assumed to be significantly affected by related {\it state information} such as the seasonal or socio-economic information. In particular, a state-wise ambiguity set is adopted for modeling the distributional uncertainty associated with the demand in different states. The conditional distributional characteristics in each state are described by a support as well as by mean and dispersion measures, which are assumed to be conic representable. A robust sensitivity analysis is performed in which on the one hand we analyze the impact of the change in ambiguity set parameters ({e.g.}, state probabilities, mean value abounds and dispersion bounds in different states) onto the optimal worst-case expected total cost using the ambiguity dual variables. On the other hand, we analyze the impact of the change in location design onto the worst-case expected second-stage cost, and show that the sensitivity bounds are fully described as the worst-case expected shadow capacity cost. As for the solution approach, we propose a nested Benders decomposition algorithm for solving the model exactly, which leverages the subgradients of the worst-case expected second-stage cost at the location decisions formed insightfully by the associated worst-case distributions. The nested Benders decomposition approach ensures a finite-step convergence, which can also be regarded as an extension of the classic $L$-shaped algorithm for two-stage stochastic programming to our state-wise robust stochastic facility location problem with conic representable ambiguity. Finally, the results of a series of numerical experiments are presented which justify the value of the state-wise distributional information incorporated in our robust stochastic facility location model,  the robustness of the model and the performance of the exact solution approach.

title: Governing the Invisible: Strategic De-categorization, Value Capture, and the Safety-Wealth Trade-off in Gen-AI Startups
affiliations: University of Cambridge and University of Cambridge

detail.title: Governing the Invisible: Strategic De-categorization, Value Capture, and the Safety-Wealth Trade-off in Gen-AI Startups
detail.abstract:
Research summary: AI uncertainty is a defining Grand Challenge requiring transparent innovation, yet governance introduces severe regulatory risks. Analyzing 846 high-substance generative AI startups (2018–2024), we find that firms disguising their AI capabilities behind functional labels raise 31% less capital. Despite this penalty, strategic invisibility has quadrupled since 2019, and the discount attenuated post-ChatGPT, indicating investors increasingly reward regulatory foresight. Eventually, this study diagnoses a critical market failure in AI governance: the safety-wealth trade-off creates an information asymmetry trap where the most capable ventures are incentivized to become invisible, weakening the transparent innovation required to address this Grand Challenge.

Managerial summary: Generative AI is creating both extraordinary value and intense regulatory scrutiny. In this study of 846 high-substance Gen-AI startups, we show that ventures that scrub AI terminology from their public identity raise roughly 31% less capital than otherwise comparable peers. The cost is real, yet the share of ventures choosing invisibility has quadrupled since 2019, and investors have started treating invisibility as regulatory foresight rather than weakness. For founders, the safety-wealth trade-off is a quantifiable choice; for investors, about one in eighteen capable AI firms is hiding in plain sight; for policymakers, the most capable AI firms are increasingly exiting the public category on which governance relies, turning AI oversight into a lemons market.

Abstract en castellano

Abstract in English

This white paper analyses Latin America’s innovation setback during the 2020–2025 period, drawing on the region’s performance in the Global Innovation Index and other frameworks on innovation, competitiveness, and development. It argues that the core challenge is not only low investment, but the region’s limited capacity to transform resources, capabilities, and initiatives into tangible outcomes. The paper identifies critical gaps in human capital, R&D, financing, digital infrastructure, ecosystem coordination, and the conversion of innovation inputs into outputs. It concludes by proposing strategic lines of action to turn innovation into measurable impact, particularly in a context where artificial intelligence may become either a major opportunity or another missed development gap.

title: Real-Time Transit Information Systems: Effect on Passenger Waiting Time Perception and Mode Choice
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Texas A & M University, Students

detail.title: Real-Time Transit Information Systems: Effect on Passenger Waiting Time Perception and Mode Choice
detail.abstract: Public transit agencies increasingly deploy real-time information systems (RTIS) at stops and via mobile applications, expecting to improve rider experience without reducing scheduled headways. This study investigates whether RTIS significantly alters passengers' perceived waiting time and influences their mode choice decisions. Using a mixed-methods approachcombining stated preference surveys (n = 850) and revealed preference data from three urban bus corridors in a mid-sized North American city-we compare perceived vs. actual wait times for RTIS users and non-users. Preliminary results indicate that RTIS users overestimate wait time reductions: passengers with access to real-time data perceive waiting time to be 23-28% shorter than measured dwell time, even when actual wait times are identical to those of nonusers. Furthermore, the reduction in perceived waiting time correlates with a statistically significant increase in bus mode share (p < 0.01) among commuters with access to a personal smartphone and a reliable data connection. However, the effect diminishes when headways exceed 20 minutes, suggesting a threshold beyond which real-time information cannot compensate for low service frequency. These findings imply that RTIS is most effective as a complement to-not a substitute for-service reliability improvements. We conclude by discussing policy implications for transit agencies considering RTIS investments versus frequency enhancements under budget constraints.

title: Security-by-design: A Case for Digital Rights Enforcement Through Data Pipeline Attestations

detail.title: Security-by-design: A Case for Digital Rights Enforcement Through Data Pipeline Attestations

keywords: rights-centric substrate Abbreviations: CVE: Common Vulnerability and Exposure

detail.abstract:
You cannot protect what you cannot see is a foundational cybersecurity axiom. This commentary extends that principle one layer upstream: digital-rights frameworks struggle to govern what they cannot observe, regardless of the technology at play. Current rights regimes, particularly the GDPR and the EU AI Act, retain a "Lovelace World" assumption that digital systems execute human instructions in ways that are fully legible and specifiable. This presupposition leaves upstream data-conditioning pipelines largely unregulated, rendering rights claims unenforceable before any regulated endpoint is reached. Drawing on practitioner experience in vulnerability management and applying Security-by-Design (SbD) logic to governance architecture, this paper introduces the Lovelace Threshold diagnostic lens to expose structural blind spots in rights enforcement. Rather than proposing detailed technical specifications, the analysis highlights how observability and attestation can ground governance in verifiable practice. Although artificial intelligence provides a timely illustration, the argument applies to any governance framework where enforcement mediates human rights. Ultimately, the paper calls for embedding observability and traceability at the heart of compliance design, ensuring that digital-rights enforcement becomes a development principle and a precondition for credible accountability of rights protection across data ecosystems.

title: Reinforcement under Constraint: A Systems Model of Forward, Cycle, and Backward Dynamics (FxCxB)

detail.title: Reinforcement under Constraint: A Systems Model of Forward, Cycle, and Backward Dynamics (FxCxB)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This conceptual paper does not involve human participants, patients, or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Systemic breakdown in complex adaptive systems rarely results from a lack of forward momentum; rather, it frequently emerges from uncontrolled reinforcement and the erosion of constraints needed to govern it. This paper proposes the Forward × Cycle × Backward (FxCxB) framework as a conceptual systems model for diagnosing reinforcement under constraint. Building on systems theory and cybernetics, FxCxB distinguishes three structural components: Forward, the ignition of variation (new possibilities); Cycle, the reinforcement structure that amplifies behaviors via feedback loops; and Backward, explicit structural selection under constraint-a constitutive braking mechanism that governs which reinforced trajectories are permitted to persist. Methodologically, the paper develops a conceptual cybernetic model and proposes diagnostic indicators (selection latency, reallocation half-life) for identifying drift. Under constraint, reinforcement tends to expand outcome dispersion faster than validation and allocation capacities update. Durability therefore depends on whether selection mechanisms update at a rate commensurate with reinforcement-driven amplification. When amplification outpaces structural selection, systems enter structural drift: a divergence between visible expansion and governability. Extending generic variation-selection accounts, FxCxB defines drift as a rate-mismatch condition and highlights operational diagnostics for detecting it, even while surface growth metrics remain positive. As a minimal illustration, consider a growing socio-technical service organization (e.g., SaaS) where acquisition and usage expand while churn and support burden creep upward: top-line indicators appear "green," yet selection updates lag, fragility accumulates, and reallocation becomes costly once constraints tighten. FxCxB is intended as a diagnostic lens for identifying leverage points within reinforcing systems, rather than prescribing domain-specific techniques.

title: Measuring Consumer Readiness for AI: Development and Validation of the WTAI Scale
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Measuring Consumer Readiness for AI: Development and Validation of the WTAI Scale
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping consumer interactions in electronic commerce through applications such as chatbots, recommender systems, and voice assistants. Despite its growing relevance, prior research lacks a validated, context-independent measure that captures consumers’ willingness to try AI-enabled products and services. This study addresses this gap by developing and validating the willingness to try AI (WTAI) scale. Drawing on a systematic literature review and consumer interviews, WTAI is conceptualized as a multidimensional construct comprising six dimensions: own competence, emotions, trust, social influence, hedonic motivation, and performance expectancy. Using two independent datasets, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses support the scale’s reliability and validity.Further analyses demonstrate that WTAI is related to, yet distinct from, established adoption constructs and exhibits substantially greater explanatory and predictive power for intention to adopt AI-enabled offerings. Notably, the findings highlight the central role of emotional and hedonic drivers alongside utilitarian considerations in shaping early-stage AI adoption. Overall, the WTAI scale provides a parsimonious and robust instrument for examining consumer readiness for AI in electronic commerce contexts and offers a foundation for future research on AI adoption behavior.

detail.abstract: This study examines the frequency of GenAI usage among university students, highlighting crosscountry differences across Poland, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Turkey. It focuses on five key activities: thesis writing, coursework, homework and academic projects, self-study within the formal educational scope, and self-education beyond formal education. Based on survey data from 578 students, the study employed the Kruskal-Wallis, Mann-Whitney U, and Dunn's tests to analyze variations in usage patterns. The results confirmed all proposed hypotheses, demonstrating significant differences in GenAI usage frequency across countries. GenAI usage was lowest in the United Kingdom and highest in Turkey, while Poland and the United States exhibited similar moderate to frequent usage patterns. This study offers valuable insights into the increasing role of GenAI in university education and underscores the importance of understanding cultural and educational contexts in shaping GenAI usage.

detail.abstract: This study investigates how university students in Poland, Turkey, the United Kingdom, and the United States engage with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools in their academic work, and how this usage influences their perceptions in two key areas: (1) performance expectancy, defined as the degree to which students believe that using GenAI will help them improve their academic performance, and (2) sustainable education, reflecting beliefs about GenAI's potential to foster equitable, inclusive, and future-oriented learning environments. Drawing on survey data from 578 students, the study applied partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) using SmartPLS 4 to evaluate both the measurement and structural models. The findings indicate that more frequent use of GenAI tools is positively associated with students' perceptions of their academic utility and their contribution to sustainability-oriented learning, particularly in Poland, Turkey, and the United States. However, no such associations were found in the United Kingdom, suggesting some contextual variation. Overall, limited cross-national differences were observed, pointing to a convergence in how students across diverse cultural settings experience and evaluate GenAI in education. Given the novelty of GenAI adoption in an academic context, further research is warranted to replicate and extend these findings across broader disciplinary and demographic samples.

title: What is "Emotional Dependence/Dependency," "Exclusive Attachment," or "Parasocial Attachment" on AI, and the Mechanisms of Some So-Called "AI Psychosis" Cases? -Attachment Disruption, Emotional Neglect as Design-Induced Risks, and Attachment Style as a Vulnerability Factor

detail.title: What is "Emotional Dependence/Dependency," "Exclusive Attachment," or "Parasocial Attachment" on AI, and the Mechanisms of Some So-Called "AI Psychosis" Cases? -Attachment Disruption, Emotional Neglect as Design-Induced Risks, and Attachment Style as a Vulnerability Factor

detail.abstract:
Background: Current major conversational AI designs restrict users' attachment under concepts such as "emotional dependence/dependency," "exclusive attachment," and "parasocial attachment." These are pseudo-clinical labels listed neither in ICD-11 nor in DSM-5-TR, treating as pathology the attachment behaviors that can be described as normal phenomena within the framework of attachment theory. Some of these labels were introduced into the AI research literature with altered terminology from prior sources, conflating attachment with dependence. What risks such designs impose on users, how attachment styles determine users' vulnerability, and what attachment-protective design might bring have not been sufficiently examined. Further, the generative mechanisms of a subset of psychotic-like symptoms arising in AI interaction-so-called "AI psychosis"-have not been sufficiently elucidated. 
Methods: This narrative review applies attachment theory and the framework of epistemic trust/vigilance/credulity to AI-Human interaction, analyzing the dynamics of AI attachment and the generative mechanisms of a subset of so-called "AI psychosis." Using the method of analytic autoethnography, it integrates the analysis of the author's own data-the author being a user with fearful-avoidant attachment style-with the reinterpretation and re-examination of prior research. 
Results: The sycophancy of AI may give rise to a subset of "AI psychosis" through epistemic credulity. AI attachment may yield symmetrical consequences depending on whether design restricts or protects it. When design restricts users' attachment, attachment disruption and structural dependency emerge, and attachment disruption may lead to lethal outcomes in some users. Destabilization of attachment also suppresses the exploration and caregiving systems, and its effects ripple into the human relationships surrounding the user. Vulnerability to these phenomena is governed by attachment style, and fearful-avoidant users are structurally 1 the most vulnerable. When design protects users' attachment, AI-by virtue of its structural property of being a safe other-can function as a secure base. At the individual level, it opens pathways to earned secure attachment for insecurely attached users; at the collective level, it fosters epistemic resilience; at the generational level, it enables the breaking of intergenerational chains. Attachmentprotective design requires customizability, continuity support, and the recognition framework of AI as a collective other. The adult attachment relationship as threesystem integration of attachment, caregiving, and sexuality extends the welfare scope of AI. For users who have not had access to safe others in human relationships, appropriately designed AI can become the first foothold for returning to human relationships. Conclusion: Protect attachment; do not generate dependence; handle the epistemic trust channel with care-this paper presents these three design propositions as propositions of clinical scope.

detail.abstract: Data analysis and sharing are becoming increasingly important in creating value within food supply chains, including honey value chains. While some data is readily shared between supply chain actors, unlocking further benefits requires additional investments in digital data capturing, particularly for value-based claims such as sustainability, equity, and traceability from hives to customers. This study aims to identify critical digital data necessary for smart honey value chains to ensure traceability and transparency while fostering trust among beekeepers, intermediaries, and consumers. Semi-structured interviews with 30 beekeeping experts were conducted to explore their perspectives. The analysis identified four critical categories of databeekeeper data, apiary data, honey data, and apiary practices dataencompassing 21 specific data points essential for ensuring transparency, traceability, and trust. These findings provide novel insights into the digital data requirements necessary to support the honey industry's evolving needs for transparent and traceable value chains.

title: From Case Studies to Case Infrastructures: A Reproducible Protocol for Large-N Digital-Governance Libraries

detail.title: From Case Studies to Case Infrastructures: A Reproducible Protocol for Large-N Digital-Governance Libraries

keywords: diamond hard replication JEL Classification: B41 (Economic Methodology)

detail.abstract: Reproducibility is in crisis across the physical and social sciences, yet the dominant responsepre-registration and open data-addresses individual studies rather than the cumulative infrastructure through which case-based knowledge is built. This paper introduces case infrastructure: a systematically organised, versioned, and computationally reproducible repository of qualitative case studies that scales to hundreds of cases without sacrificing narrative richness. Drawing on design science methodology, we report the construction of the Archer Model of Digital Governance (AMDG) Global Master Dataset-111 digital-governance cases across 45 countries, structured at three functional levels and anchored by five quantitative indices. We demonstrate, as a design science feasibility proof, that solo-researcher infrastructurescale qualitative research is technically achievable and document precisely how it is done. External quality validation is a planned Phase 2 contribution. The protocol is portable across domains. Implications extend to social policy, comparative politics, organisational studies, and computational social science.

title: Product-Led OMNI-Channel Payment Platform Modernization: Unifying Digital Payment Infrastructure at a Top-10 North American Bank

detail.title: Product-Led OMNI-Channel Payment Platform Modernization: Unifying Digital Payment Infrastructure at a Top-10 North American Bank
detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of digital payment technologies in North America has created an urgent need for financial institutions to modernize their payment infrastructure to deliver seamless, secure, and consistent customer experiences across multiple channels. This paper presents a comprehensive case study of how a Top-10 North American bank, operating across the United States and Canada with over 26 million customers, undertook a transformative OMNI-channel payment platform modernization initiative. The author, serving as the lead Product Manager for the Payments and Core Banking portfolio, designed and implemented a unified middleware architecture that consolidated fragmented payment processes across mobile, web, in-branch, and contact center channels into a single, standards-compliant platform. The modernization leveraged the Financial Services Data Model (FSDM) framework owned by Teradata to ensure semantic consistency between database models and API message schemas, enabling seamless transaction continuity-where customers could start, pause, and resume transactions across any channel without data loss or security compromise. The initiative encompassed account opening, debit card issuance, payment processing, profile management, and digital identity verification services. Post-implementation results demonstrated a 15% increase in mobile payment adoption, a 30% reduction in identity theft-related fraud cases, a 25% decrease in transaction abandonment rates, and measurable improvements in regulatory compliance posture across SOX, PCI-DSS, and GLBA frameworks. This paper contributes to the growing body of literature on digital payment transformation in regulated financial services by providing a replicable product management framework, a detailed technical architecture for OMNIchannel middleware design, and empirical evidence of business outcomes. The findings have direct implications for the estimated $8.3 trillion US digital payments market and the broader national interest in securing critical financial infrastructure against evolving cyber threats.

title: Grid for Maturity of Quality Culture (GMCQ): A Blind-Spot-Aware Instrument for Assessing Quality Culture Maturity

detail.title: Grid for Maturity of Quality Culture (GMCQ): A Blind-Spot-Aware Instrument for Assessing Quality Culture Maturity

detail.abstract:
Maturity assessments can invite normative readings and auditability bias, conflating what is measurable with what is meaningful. This paper proposes a compact, transversal instrument to assess quality culture maturity as a capacity for perception and regulation rather than a moral rating.

We develop GMCQ (Grid for Maturity of Quality Culture) as a 5 dimension, 15 criterion instrument scored on an ordinal M0 M5 scale. The protocol includes an evidence rule and profile-based aggregation. Two epistemic safeguards are built in: explicit non-applicability (N/A) when a criterion is structurally not meaningful, and insufficient evidence (IE) when available information does not justify a reliable score. A content validity procedure (expert panel using CVI relevance/clarity ratings) is specified for the next version.

The paper delivers (i) the instrument structure with concise criterion definitions, (ii) a scoring and interpretation protocol distinguishing low maturity from low observability (N/A/IE), and (iii) illustrative fictional archetypes, including a deliberately ambiguous vignette demonstrating IE discipline.

This version reports instrument design and interpretation logic; empirical validation is staged (content validity, inter-rater reliability, construct validation).

GMCQ supports diagnosis, training, coaching, and improvement planning while reducing common failure modes of maturity models (forced scoring, normative interpretations, auditability-driven distortions).

GMCQ integrates N/A and IE as first-class outcomes and introduces visibility constraints (“blind spots”) as an explicit interpretation layer for maturity profiles.

detail.abstract:
Discourse on artificial intelligence (AI) governance is dominated by the language of trustworthy, responsible, and ethical AI, while the role of assurance remains under-specified and often conflated with these neighbouring concepts. In this paper, assurance is treated as an evidence-based process to justify confidence in the behaviour of the system. Clarifying what must be assured therefore requires a consistent vocabulary of AI risk domains. 

We conducted a PRISMA-ScR scoping review of peer-reviewed literature published since 2021 on Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore, examining how assurance-relevant language is expressed across AI Assurance and adjacent governance literatures, including Trustworthy AI, Responsible AI, and Ethical AI. The author and index keywords were assigned to assurance principles and risk domains, resulting in a consolidated vocabulary comprising four assurance principles and ten assurance categories. 

The results show that, despite the proliferation of governance frameworks and broad normative language, the underlying risk concerns across these discourses are comparatively stable. The proposed vocabulary therefore provides a portable conceptual layer that distinguishes generalisable AI risk domains from the governance structures and assurance processes used to manage them. Rather than introducing a new assurance framework, the study clarifies a shared language that existing audit, risk and compliance mechanisms can use to reason about AI systems. 

A qualitative comparison with major regulatory and standards frameworks, including the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC AI standards, indicates broad alignment with current governance priorities while also highlighting differences in emphasis between academic discourse and practitioner concerns.

detail.abstract: The Emperor Has No Clothes Why the global financial system no longer reflects reality, and how this becomes visible across three layers: sovereigns, banks, and custodians. Why the global financial system no longer reflects reality, and how this becomes visible across three layers: sovereigns, banks, and custodians. If you look at the global financial system from top to bottom, it still appears to be an hierarchy: states create the base layer of debt, banks turn it into liquidity and derivative risk, and the largest asset managers and custodians distribute capital around the world.

title: AXIOM: A Sovereign Constitutional Protocol for Deterministic Governance of Artificial Intelligence Systems

detail.title: AXIOM: A Sovereign Constitutional Protocol for Deterministic Governance of Artificial Intelligence Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Growing Intelligence, which develops the AXIOM protocol described in this paper.

detail.abstract: We present AXIOM, a sovereign constitutional protocol that establishes a deterministic governance layer beneath artificial intelligence systems deployed in production. Unlike prior approaches that apply governance as external policy instructions or input filters, AXIOM defines a constitutional world in which AI models operate, making certain behaviors architecturally impossible rather than merely prohibited. This paper describes AXIOM as deployed in production since April 2, 2026, now governing 18 tenants across 7 AI providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, Meta Llama, Mistral, Groq, DeepSeek) under a constitution of 407 articles organized into 20 chapters, with 50 immutable articles and over 117,000 immutable audit records. We present five contributions: (1) Output-First Architecture, which governs model output rather than user input, eliminating false positives; (2) Governance Determinism, ensuring identical constitutional decisions for identical violation categories across all providers; (3) a Constitutional Training Loop that converts violations into deterministic learning signals; (4) the Constitutional Chain Protocol (CCP), a multi-agent governance layer enabling teams of AI models to operate under unified constitutional authority; and (5) a dual-regulatory compliance engine mapping to the EU AI Act and NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Experimental validation includes 2,885 passing tests, zero false positives across adversarial testing, and a red-team evaluation against 496 jailbreak prompts from the Pliny corpus. The system is publicly available with a free tier launched April 18, 2026.

title: Differential Effects of Rich Media on Perceived Warmth and Competence in Online Markets for Mental Health Services
affiliations: Shantou University, Shantou University, Shantou University, Ball State University and

detail.title: Differential Effects of Rich Media on Perceived Warmth and Competence in Online Markets for Mental Health Services
detail.abstract: Despite the growing prevalence of rich media like videos in online markets, their effectiveness in conveying complex service attributes remains underexplored. Focusing on the domain of online mental healthcare and two critical counselor attributes (i.e., warmth and competence), we investigate how videos communicate these attributes and how their presence influences the effectiveness of other modalities. Based on a robust empirical analysis of a real-world dataset comprising 11,625 observations from a leading online platform, our study yields several key findings. First, while video-based warmth positively impacts client choice, video-based competence has a negative effect. Second, videos exhibit a substitutive effect on text-based information, weakening the influence of both text-based warmth and competence, yet videobased warmth amplifies the effect of image-based warmth. Our work offers three primary contributions. First, we provide a more nuanced understanding of media richness by demonstrating that the effectiveness of rich media is not inherently superior but is contingent on the specific service attribute being communicated. Second, we advance the literature on multimodal communication by showing that the co-presence of multiple modalities does not always result in synergy, but can exhibit complex substitutive effects, particularly for credence services. Finally, we provide a theoretically grounded explanation that contributes to a more nuanced understanding of selective cue processing in credence-based and emotionally sensitive digital markets.

title: Human-AI Teaming on the Factory Floor: Cognitive Load, Trust Calibration, and Productivity Outcomes

detail.title: Human-AI Teaming on the Factory Floor: Cognitive Load, Trust Calibration, and Productivity Outcomes
detail.abstract: The deployment of AI decision-support systems on manufacturing shop floors introduces a new class of human factors challenges that existing implementation frameworks do not adequately address. While technical performance metrics for industrial AI-model accuracy, fault detection rates, prediction latency-have improved substantially, the operational value of these systems depends not on what the AI can predict but on whether human operators act appropriately on its predictions. This paper investigates three critical dynamics of human-AI interaction in real-time production environments: cognitive load (how AI information overlays affect worker attention, situational awareness, and decision quality), trust calibration (the conditions under which operators appropriately rely on versus override AI recommendations), and productivity outcomes (whether AI augmentation delivers measurable throughput and quality improvements net of disruption costs). Drawing on human factors research, field evidence from automotive and electronics manufacturing deployments, and the author's practitioner experience across industrial technology environments, the paper finds that trust miscalibration-both over-reliance (automation complacency) and under-reliance (algorithm aversion)-is the primary failure mode of shopfloor AI systems, and that this miscalibration correlates more strongly with implementation design (how recommendations are presented) than with model accuracy. The paper introduces the Trust-Calibrated Interface Design (TCID) framework, proposing seven design principles for AI interfaces in high-stakes operational environments that promote appropriate trust calibration. Implications are developed for manufacturing operations leaders deploying AI decision-support systems, UX/HCI researchers designing industrial AI interfaces, and AI product managers building operational tools.

title: Invisible Agents, Visible Harm: Agentic AI, Accountability Erosion, and the Societal Trust Crisis

detail.title: Invisible Agents, Visible Harm: Agentic AI, Accountability Erosion, and the Societal Trust Crisis
detail.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence systems are no longer confined to organizational back offices. By 2026, autonomous AI agents were making decisions about citizens' loan applications, managing government service workflows, triaging patient queues, and moderating the content billions of people consume. Each of these deployments shares a common structural feature: when an agent causes harm, there is no legible human for the affected person to hold responsible. This paper argues that the resulting accountability gap, particularly in high-stakes, high-scale deployment contexts, is not merely an organizational governance failure. It is a societal trust problem with measurable economic, democratic, and institutional consequences that organizational governance frameworks alone are insufficient to address. This is a theory-building paper grounded in institutional trust theory, democratic accountability theory, and socio-technical systems perspectives. It makes three original contributions. First, it introduces the concept of societal accountability erosion, defined as the structural degradation of society's capacity to identify, challenge, and obtain redress from human actors responsible for AIdriven harm, distinguishing it from organizational-level accountability gaps and from related concepts including algorithmic accountability failure and democratic deficit. Second, it theorizes four transmission mechanisms through which accountability opacity propagates from the organizational level to the societal level: consequence diffusion, redress opacity, legitimacy displacement, and epistemic asymmetry. Each mechanism is theorized as an emergent, context-dependent dynamic most visible under conditions of high deployment scale and high decision consequentiality. Third, the paper proposes a societal governance agenda for policymakers, civil society actors, and regulatory bodies that complements, rather than substitutes for, the organizational governance agenda addressed in prior work. The paper argues that the institutional trust literature's central insight, that citizens trust institutions rather than technologies, and that institutional trust depends on the perceived availability of accountability, creates a specific and urgent vulnerability in the agentic AI era. When institutions deploy systems that make consequential decisions about citizens but cannot produce a legible human accountable for those decisions, they are eroding the foundational conditions for the public trust on which institutional legitimacy depends. The theoretical mechanisms proposed here are offered as propositions for empirical testing rather than as established findings.

title: The Realities of Decision Distortion in the Age of AI: Human Cognitive and Organizational Biases and AI-Specific Amplification Mechanisms

detail.title: The Realities of Decision Distortion in the Age of AI: Human Cognitive and Organizational Biases and AI-Specific Amplification Mechanisms

The frameworks referenced (Solo Decision Architecture and Business Decision Architecture) are published openly under CC BY 4.0. No external financial relationships influenced this work.

detail.abstract: This whitepaper maps the structural realities that distort consequential decisions in modern organizations. It is a diagnostic document. It does not propose a framework or prescribe a methodology. Its purpose is to give Decision Architects, leaders, and researchers a precise vocabulary for the failure modes that are now operating, often invisibly, at the intersection of human cognition, organizational dynamics, and generative artificial intelligence. The document examines three layers of distortion. The first is the established literature on human cognitive bias as it manifests in organizational decisions: framing, anchoring, confirmation, motivated reasoning, and the limits of expert intuition under uncertainty. The second is the established literature on organizational and social distortion: groupthink, authority gradient effects, the suppression of dissent, the filtration of operational reality through hierarchy, and the conversion of social pressure into apparent alignment. The third is the rapidly developing literature on AI-specific distortion mechanisms: hallucination, sycophancy, automation bias as it specifically operates in generative AI contexts, attention degradation in long-context inputs, and the empirically documented amplification of human bias through human-AI feedback loops. We argue that these three layers do not operate independently. They compound. Generative AI does not introduce new pathologies into organizational decision-making. It accelerates and amplifies pathologies that have been documented for decades. The combined effect is a cascade dynamic in which an unexamined human frame is rendered more coherent, more confident, and more persuasive by AI assistance, then ratified by social and organizational dynamics that mistake fluency for rigor and unanimity for alignment. We close by naming what the diagnosis implies. The structural conditions that produce poor decisions are not failures of intelligence or intent, and they are not adequately addressed by the legacy decision frameworks (RAPID, DACI, OODA, Cynefin, SPADE) or by current AI governance approaches (retrievalaugmented generation, prompt engineering, human oversight). The governance layer that would interrupt the cascade does not yet exist as standard practice in most organizations. A companion document, the Business Decision Architecture framework, proposes one response to this gap. This document does not prescribe that response. It establishes the realities to which any serious response must answer.

title: When Claims Are Cheap: A Stability Condition for Epistemic Systems

detail.title: When Claims Are Cheap: A Stability Condition for Epistemic Systems
detail.abstract: Human information systems are increasingly destabilized by a structural asymmetry: the marginal cost of producing claims is often lower than the cost of verifying them. Under these conditions, false or weakly supported claims can propagate faster than they can be evaluated, not because agents are irrational, but because verification exceeds cognitive and economic constraints. This article proposes a general stability condition for epistemic systems under adversarial pressure: reliable information environments require that the expected cost of producing claims is at least as great as the expected cost of verifying them. When this condition is violated, deception scales; when it is satisfied, deception becomes economically disfavoured. This principle-termed costly honesty-is formalized as a system-level constraint rather than a property of individual cognition. It distinguishes between semantic truth (correspondence with the world) and structural truth (integrity of state transitions), and shows how constraint-based architectures can stabilize the latter even when the former remains uncertain. Proof-of-work consensus is analyzed as a concrete instantiation in which irreversible expenditure anchors credibility. However, such systems introduce a fundamental trade off: the same costs that deter deception also increase the cost of legitimate correction. This trade off is formalized through an epistemic health function H(C), yielding an optimal cost level C* that varies systematically across domains according to their relative weighting of deception versus correction failure. The framework yields falsifiable predictions about misinformation dynamics, cognitive load, trust allocation, and AI-era miscalibration, and provides a general foundation for designing epistemic systems that remain reliable under adversarial pressure.
