title: Individual-Anchored Narrative Analytics: Testing RHIS Transferability Through The Godfather

detail.title: Individual-Anchored Narrative Analytics: Testing RHIS Transferability Through The Godfather
detail.abstract: This paper tests the transferability of RHIS (Refine Humanistic Intelligence System) from its earlier political and organizational applications to narrative film through an individual-anchored methodology. Rather than beginning with abstract system properties, RHIS starts from observable individual behavior, establishes baseline configurations (Path1) from repeated lowpressure scenes, and compares them with activated states (Path2) under high-pressure conditions. Structural deviation, represented by θ, is treated here as the effective structural deviation of the activated state from the baseline configuration under field pressure. θ is defined by its ontological role rather than by any single fixed mathematical implementation.

title: The Human Data Collective: A Standard for Open, Sustainable, and Equitable Artificial Intelligence With Transparency and Compensation Optionality for Large Language Model Inference

detail.title: The Human Data Collective: A Standard for Open, Sustainable, and Equitable Artificial Intelligence With Transparency and Compensation Optionality for Large Language Model Inference

keywords: The Artificial Intelligence Inference Standards Protocol

detail.abstract: Several of the biggest challenges plaguing the development and utilization of large language models in 2026, notably bias, the difficulty of monitoring undesirable and illegal content, the psychological safety risks associated with human-led alignment, and severe environmental impact, can be partially or completely mitigated through the careful curation of high-quality human-generated content paired with fair incentives. This paper offers an alternative to the existing paradigm of extraction and privatization by proposing a decentralized network of human-generated content created, curated, and labeled specifically for the purpose of training large language models. By introducing a new inference standard rooted in cryptographically verifiable tokens tied to environmental impact, those who do the creating, curating, and labeling can be fairly compensated, the carbon and water footprint of large language models can be addressed at compute time, and the artificial intelligence industry can be returned to its original mission of open access and equality for all while preserving productive free-market competition.

title: From Local Practices to a Minimum Common Standard: A Modular, Phased Framework for Supplier Evaluation Harmonization

detail.title: From Local Practices to a Minimum Common Standard: A Modular, Phased Framework for Supplier Evaluation Harmonization

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants or personal data and therefore does not require ethical approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Supplier evaluation is often approached as a scoring problem, while many deployments fail due to lack of harmonization across sites, entities and evolving external constraints. This paper proposes a framework to harmonize supplier evaluation through a minimum common standard and modular extensions. Design/methodology/approach-Conceptual synthesis of recurring implementation challenges in multisite and turbulent contexts. The framework defines a Minimum Common Standard (process, data, evidence, rules, governance), a modular architecture to absorb local variability and new external requirements, and a five-phase rollout model. Three structured vignettes (Create/Extend/Transform) illustrate applicability. Meta-performance indicators and failure modes are proposed. Findings-The framework specifies what must be standardized to ensure comparability, auditability and actionability (and what should remain configurable). It separates internal harmonization (cross-entity comparability) from external harmonization (integration of new standards/regulations/constraints via modules), and provides a phased rollout logic to reduce adoption risk. Originality-The paper reframes supplier evaluation from "how to score suppliers" to "how to harmonize an evaluation system under organizational and external turbulence", introducing a Minimum Common Standard and modular governance as a deployable blueprint.

This paper is also available on Zenodo (DOI): https://zenodo.org/doi/10.5281/zenodo.18850155

title: A Bargaining Theory of the Leverage-Profitability Relationship

detail.title: A Bargaining Theory of the Leverage-Profitability Relationship

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper shows that a static trade-off model generates a negative cross-sectional relationship between leverage and profitability once ex ante Nash bargaining over the perpetual debt coupon is introduced. The central mechanism works as follows: higher shareholder bargaining power lowers the negotiated coupon, which reduces leverage — the ratio of debt to equity — and shrinks the interest tax shield, thereby lowering firm value for fixed earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) and raising the earnings yield. Heterogeneity in bargaining power across firms thus produces a negative co-movement between leverage and valuation-based profitability in the cross-section. A key implication concerns how this mechanism maps into accounting data. Under historical-cost measurement (GAAP), book assets do not respond to the bargaining environment, so the mechanism is attenuated in reported return on assets (ROA). Under fair-value-oriented measurement (IFRS), book assets track enterprise value more closely, making the negative relationship more visible in the data. This asymmetry has particular relevance for multinational groups operating across jurisdictions with heterogeneous accounting standards, where within-group comparisons of leverage and profitability may be systematically distorted by the coexistence of the two regimes.

title: When Warnings Become Advertising: How Government Announcements Disrupt AI-Mediated Content Gatekeeping on TikTok
affiliations: , University of North Texas and University of North Texas

detail.title: When Warnings Become Advertising: How Government Announcements Disrupt AI-Mediated Content Gatekeeping on TikTok
detail.abstract: AI recommendation algorithms learn from viewer engagement to distribute content, but the Persuasion Knowledge Model predicts that viewers engage less with content they recognize as commercial. The result is an emergent commercial content view gap: videos containing callsto-action receive systematically fewer algorithmic impressions than non-commercial content. We document this view gap across four tax seasons on TikTok and show that a single exogenous shock-the IRS naming TikTok in its 2025 Dirty Dozen warning-temporarily closed it (p = 0.021). Two placebos confirm specificity: neither the 2024 nor 2026 Dirty Dozen (which did not name TikTok) produced any closure. Also, the effect concentrates in tax hack content; the specific tax the IRS named. These findings reveal that the automated systems platforms use to limit commercial content reach can be inadvertently disabled by the government warnings meant to protect consumers.

title: Traceability of Automated Decisions in Digital Forensic Investigations: A Methodological Framework and Smart Building Case Study

detail.title: Traceability of Automated Decisions in Digital Forensic Investigations: A Methodological Framework and Smart Building Case Study
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a methodological framework for the traceability of automated decisions in digital forensic investigations, addressing the increasing complexity of distributed and IoT-based environments. While prior work has examined logging, evidence acquisition, and system-level analysis, the reconstruction of decision pathways in automated systems remains insufficiently structured. The proposed framework introduces a traceability-oriented approach that integrates technical logging, decision reconstruction, and evidentiary integrity into a unified analytical model. Unlike purely system-centric methodologies, this framework explicitly targets the forensic reconstruction of automated decision processes, enabling a more robust attribution of actions and responsibilities. A smart building case study is used to illustrate the applicability of the model, demonstrating how automated control systems generate traceable decision chains that can be systematically reconstructed for forensic purposes. The paper contributes to the development of more rigorous methodologies for handling automated decision-making systems in digital forensic contexts, with implications for accountability, evidentiary reliability, and the analysis of complex cyber-physical environments.

reference: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series Paper No. 26-05
title: Unlocking Opportunity: The Remarkable Success of the Baltimore Regional Housing Partnership
affiliations: ENS de Lyon and Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: Unlocking Opportunity: The Remarkable Success of the Baltimore Regional Housing Partnership

keywords: rental housing demand JEL Classification Codes: I38

publicationDetails.detailsText: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series Paper No. 26-05
publicationDetails.journalName: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Existing research shows that the neighborhood where a child grows up has a causal effect on their later economic prospects. Yet in many cities, low-income nonwhite families with children often live in the lowest opportunity neighborhoods. Over the past few decades, a number of housing mobility programs using vouchers to assist families in making moves to higher-resourced communities have shown considerable success toward increasing neighborhood opportunity, garnering significant policy support. As public housing policy is increasingly influenced by Housing Mobility Programs (HMPs), we study the HMP that has generated the largest improvements in neighborhood characteristics. Participants in the Baltimore Regional Housing Partnership (BRHP) reside in neighborhoods with schools performing 40 percentile points higher on state tests than poor Black residents of Baltimore City-ten times the difference between experimental and control groups in Moving to Opportunity. Oaxaca-Blinder decompositions attribute the majority of the BRHP's success to its regional design, which allows participants to access all opportunity neighborhoods in metropolitan Baltimore. The BRHP breaks strong neighborhood sorting by income and race. BRHP households live in neighborhoods with socioeconomic status comparable to the highest income Black households and live in more racially-integrated neighborhoods than Black households at any income level. BRHP improvements in neighborhood characteristics are durable.

title: Fiscal Policy and Labor Market Outcomes in Europe

detail.title: Fiscal Policy and Labor Market Outcomes in Europe

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The macroeconomic effects of fiscal policy are central to both research and policymaking, yet relatively little is known about how fiscal shocks impact men and women differently across diverse labor market and institutional contexts. This paper provides the first comparative analysis of gender-specific responses to exogenous fiscal shocks in the Balkans relative to the rest of Europe. Using a cross-country panel dataset and the local projection method, we trace the dynamic effects of fiscal expansions and contractions on labor force participation, employment, and wage outcomes. The results reveal substantial regional variation and pronounced gender asymmetries. Expansionary fiscal shocks lead to modest and delayed improvements in female labor market outcomes in the Balkans, whereas effects in other European countries are stronger and more immediate. Conversely, contractionary shocks disproportionately reduce female employment, especially during downturns, with greater volatility observed in Balkan economies. These patterns reflect differences in sectoral employment composition, care infrastructure, and public service provision. Overall, the findings suggest that fiscal policy operates within structurally gendered labor markets, highlighting important implications for macroeconomic stabilization and labor market resilience in transitional economies.

reference: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series Paper No. 26-07
title: Time Use and the Pursuit of Happiness
affiliations: ENS de Lyon and University of Houston

detail.title: Time Use and the Pursuit of Happiness

publicationDetails.detailsText: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series Paper No. 26-07
publicationDetails.journalName: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We develop a new economic framework to study the relationship between how we spend our time and our well-being. Our key insight is that while we may pursue enjoyable activities, they do not all equally contribute to happiness. Moreover, even if we understand what we enjoy, we may not fully understand what makes us happy; we learn this over time. We incorporate these ideas into the standard model of time allocation and introduce the notion of psychic capital, a mental stock that facilitates happiness and is augmented by constructive uses of time. This allows us to connect basic tools from price theory to recent empirical findings in the study of well-being and centuries old ideas in moral philosophy. We under-invest in salubrious activities because we do not fully understand how we derive happiness. The relative prices of heterogeneous activities determine the extent of this under-investment and the speed of our learning. Our model explains several puzzles in the economics of happiness such as the Easterlin paradox and the lifecycle trajectory of subjective well being. We use data from the American Time Use Survey to present a variety of evidence in support of this claim and to show that work is most responsible for increases in well-being in older ages.

title: Wrist Watch Law: A Behavioural Science Framework on Time Perception, Cognitive Regulation, and Task Productivity

detail.title: Wrist Watch Law: A Behavioural Science Framework on Time Perception, Cognitive Regulation, and Task Productivity
detail.abstract: This paper develops a comprehensive behavioural science framework termed the "Wrist Watch Law," which examines the relationship between wristwatch usage, subconscious time perception, cognitive regulation, and task productivity. The central premise is that human productivity is influenced more by perceived time availability than by objective time itself. The presence of a wristwatch functions as a continuous external cognitive cue that alters time awareness, perceived control over time, urgency perception, and psychomotor performance. The theory proposes a dual-pathway mechanism in which increased time awareness may either enhance discipline and structured behaviour or reduce urgency due to psychological time cushioning effects. The paper integrates psychological foundations, proposes a theoretical model, presents an illustrative behavioural scenario, and outlines empirical testability and applications in organizational and educational contexts. The framework contributes to behavioural science by linking time perception with performance outcomes in a structured and testable model.

title: Decomposing the Earnings Response Coefficient under Partial Information

detail.title: Decomposing the Earnings Response Coefficient under Partial Information
detail.abstract:
We develop a continuous-time model of earnings response under partial information, in which investors infer latent firm fundamentals from noisy accounting signals through stochastic filtering. In this setting, observed earnings response coefficients arise as finite-horizon integrals of an underlying instantaneous response process.
The framework provides a unified account of both the magnitude and timing of price responses to earnings. Differences in earnings responses across firms reflect both economic fundamentals, such as growth and persistence, and features of the information environment, such as signal precision. At the same time, price adjustment is gradual even under optimal filtering, so that post-earnings-announcement drift arises as the continuation of the same process that generates contemporaneous price reactions.
A key implication is that observed earnings response coefficients do not identify the underlying valuation impact of earnings surprises, but instead conflate valuation effects with the speed of information absorption. Similarly, the detectability of post-earnings-announcement drift depends on the speed of information absorption, with faster learning concentrating price adjustment within the event window and leaving little scope for subsequent drift.
Under a tractable linear-Gaussian benchmark, the framework yields a set of empirically testable restrictions and provides a structural interpretation of return dynamics around earnings announcements.

title: Estimating Tax-Dependent Compliance: Theory and Evidence from Trade Wars
affiliations: University of Nevada, Las Vegas, , University of Mannheim and University of Nevada, Las Vegas

detail.title: Estimating Tax-Dependent Compliance: Theory and Evidence from Trade Wars

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Statutory tariff rates may overstate the tariffs actually paid due to evasion and avoidance. We develop a novel method to estimate tariff compliance and apply it to the 2018 trade war, when several countries imposed retaliatory tariffs on U.S. exports. Estimated compliance falls by 25 percentage points after tariff increases; a one percentage point tariff increase reduces compliance by 1 to 2 percentage points. Compliance is lower for intermediate goods, which often qualify for duty-free treatment, and for differentiated products, whose valuation is more difficult to verify. The decline accounted for approximately $3.5 billion in foregone tariff revenue in 2019.

title: Redefining Financial Data Governance in the Digital Money Era: Central Banks, Platforms, and Users
affiliations: University of Calgary - Haskayne School of Business and University College London

detail.title: Redefining Financial Data Governance in the Digital Money Era: Central Banks, Platforms, and Users

declarations.funderStatement: Funding acknowledgement. Redefining Financial Data Governance in the Digital Money Era: Central Banks, Platforms, and Users is co-funded by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and UK Research and Innovation Arts and Humanities Research Council and Economic and Social Research Council.

detail.abstract: Digital money is no longer only a faster way to make payments. Stablecoins, digital wallets, platform-based payment systems, and potential central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) also create, verify, and transmit transaction-level records and user-level financial information. This information can improve screening, settlement, fraud detection, and access to financial services. At the same time, it raises new governance questions: who controls users’ financial histories, who can access or verify them, how portable they are, and how public and private authorities should be constrained. This report synthesizes research on these questions through a Governance Triangle connecting three actors: central banks, digital platforms, and users. The framework helps organize fragmented literatures on monetary policy, central bank digital currency (CBDC) design, stablecoins, financial intermediation, platform economics, privacy, and data governance.

title: Public Administration Digitalisation and Microenterprise Productivity in India

detail.title: Public Administration Digitalisation and Microenterprise Productivity in India

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We find that public administration digitalisation, carried out state-by-state in India between 2010 and 2015, led to an improvement in micro-enterprise productivities, based on the Unincorporated Non-Agricultural Enterprises Surveys. We categorise the digitalisation of public administration into six groups: tax filing and payments, construction permits, environment and labour regulations, inspections, commercial disputes, and single-window systems. States are ranked according to the subsets of digitalisation carried out by them. Using the difference-in-difference estimations with propensity score matching, we find that the average firm-level productivities have risen in the states carrying out more digitalisation. There, also, dispersions in productivities have become narrower.

title: Infrapopulism: A Concept Note on Infrastructure Narratives as a Political Technology

detail.title: Infrapopulism: A Concept Note on Infrastructure Narratives as a Political Technology
detail.abstract: This concept note introduces Infrapopulism-a phenomenon whereby the media, political, and diplomatic intensity surrounding an infrastructure project systematically and substantially exceeds its actual economic and logistical effect. Infrapopulism is analysed as a political technology of expectation management characteristic of immature institutional systems and transitional geopolitical configurations. The concept is developed within the author's IPG (Infrastructure Projection of Geopolitics) framework (SSRN 6564659) and complements it with a dysfunctional dimension. The primary empirical case is the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway (CKU): a project with nearly thirty years of declarations and zero kilometres of track laid by the time of writing. The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR / Middle Corridor) serves as a comparative case. The note has the character of a working hypothesis open to subsequent verification.

title: Revenue Sharing Meets Civil Rights: Title IX's Collision with College Athletics' New Economy
affiliations: University of Colorado School of Law and Florida State University

detail.title: Revenue Sharing Meets Civil Rights: Title IX's Collision with College Athletics' New Economy
detail.abstract:
This article discusses how the rapid transformation of college athletics, driven by the Supreme Court's NCAA v. Alston decision and the House v. NCAA settlement, has made universities direct payors to student athletes.  This, in turn, creates substantial new legal obligations under Title IX that institutions have yet to fully reckon with. 

As schools allocate revenue-sharing funds and build NIL support infrastructure, those decisions constitute institutional conduct that most observers believe is within Title IX's prohibition on sex discrimination.  This renders the familiar "revenue generation" justification for favoring football and men's basketball programs legally vulnerable. 

The Office for Civil Rights and plaintiffs' counsel are already positioned to use emerging compensation data for enforcement.  The article concludes that institutions that proactively audit their NIL support structures and revenue-sharing methodologies through a Title IX lens, rather than waiting for an official safe harbor, will be far better positioned when litigation and regulatory scrutiny arrive.

title: Preventive Care Disparities and AI Fairness Considerations in U.S. Women

detail.title: Preventive Care Disparities and AI Fairness Considerations in U.S. Women

publicationDetails.detailsText: Submitted to SAGE Digital Health (under review). Accepted for peer review at the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI (IASEAI) 2026 Conference, UNESCO, Paris.

detail.abstract: Preventive screenings such as mammograms reduce mortality, but access remains a challenge for many women. This study examines women above the age of 40, and how insurance coverage, education, and relationship status relate to whether mammograms are received. Unpartnered women, including those who were widowed, divorced, or never married, had lower screening rates than married women, even after accounting for age and insurance. Women without insurance were much less likely to be screened than those with private coverage. Those with public insurance also showed lower use. These results highlight that access to preventive care is influenced not only by personal choice, but also by broader societal systems. Strengthening workplace and insurance protections, along with building tools and policies that recognize social barriers, can help make preventive care more equitable and within reach for all women.

title: Can Algorithmic Stablecoins Be Stable? *
affiliations: University of Toronto and University of Witten/Herdecke

detail.title: Can Algorithmic Stablecoins Be Stable? *
detail.abstract: The objective of an algorithmic stablecoin is to create a dollar-denominated claim backed entirely by assets internal to the blockchain network that issues it, without external reserves or a trusted intermediary. This paper separates three objects that are often conflated: the accounting mechanics of burn-mint convertibility, secondary-market arbitrage, and the endogenous value of the backing token. When network value is exogenous, convertibility is neutral as in Modigliani-Miller. A secondary-market de-peg attracts arbitrage but the ensuing conversions themselves do not destabilize the peg, nor the native token. Instability originates in the native token's pricing as money on its network. We formalize the problem using a cash-in-advance microfoundation, where the token's aggregate value equals the dollar volume of transaction demand, which does not increase when new tokens are minted. When users respond to expected inflation, a nonlinear feedback loop emerges. The redemption elasticity of native-token value is near zero for small shocks but diverges as cumulative redemptions approach a critical threshold, so that repeated small de-pegs can lead to sudden collapse. Equilibrium multiplicity exacerbates the fragility. Calibrated to hourly UST and LUNA data, the model locates the Terra-Luna point of no return to be within hours of the actual collapse occurring.

reference: 79 Stanford Law Review Online, Special Collection on Technology, AI, and the Future of Civil Rights (2026)
title: Disparate (Algorithmic) Advantage
affiliations: Hofstra University - Maurice A. Deane School of Law and Florida State University College of Law

detail.title: Disparate (Algorithmic) Advantage

publicationDetails.detailsText: 79 Stanford Law Review Online, Special Collection on Technology, AI, and the Future of Civil Rights (2026)

detail.abstract:
When a hiring manager’s decisions produce a disparity, the causes are opaque, the data are noisy, and isolating the source of the disparity from “holistic judgment” is nearly impossible. When an algorithm produces a disparity, practices are specified, outputs are reproducible, and biases can be measured under controlled conditions. Yet scholars argue that algorithms make civil rights enforcement harder.

This consensus has it backwards. Disparate impact law is better suited to algorithms than to the humans it was designed to police. Algorithms are consistent: they apply the same criteria to every input, producing the cleanest statistical evidence the law has ever seen. They are replicable, making the business necessity defense specific, the less-exclusionary-alternative analysis tractable, and the algorithm identifiable as the particular practice that has eluded the doctrine since Wal-Mart v. Dukes. Algorithms are flat: a single process, not a web of cognition, culture, and bias, making the source of disparity easier to isolate. 

Society should not fear algorithms. It should welcome them—not because they are fair, but because they make disparities easier to expose. If this advantage has not produced successful litigation, it is because the law is starved of information. Plaintiffs cannot challenge what they cannot see. The civil rights community has misdiagnosed information asymmetry as legal inadequacy, proposing new law when we really need new infrastructure—algorithmic testing, outcome reporting, and audit rights—to let the law see what it was built to expose.

title: The Scarcity of Oil Resources in Azerbaijan and the Rising Costs of Oil Production: An Economic Assessment
affiliations: University of London, Royal Holloway College

detail.title: The Scarcity of Oil Resources in Azerbaijan and the Rising Costs of Oil Production: An Economic Assessment
detail.abstract: Azerbaijan's hydrocarbon sector, long the engine of national prosperity, is approaching a critical threshold. Crude oil production peaked in 2010 at almost 1.0 million barrels per day and has since contracted by approximately 40 per cent, while proven reserves stand at only 7 billion barrels (EIA, 2025). The Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli (ACG) complex, which still generates around 60 per cent of national output, has been in irreversible natural decline since 2010 (Astrasheuskaya, 2025). Maintaining production now requires capital-intensive interventions, including the $6 billion Azeri Central East platform and a $370 million seismic programme, that have raised the effective cost of an incremental barrel well above the historical $20 reported by SOCAR (Intellinews, 2016; Astrasheuskaya, 2025). This article examines the structural drivers of resource scarcity in Azerbaijan, evaluates the rising marginal and fiscal break-even costs of production, and assesses the macroeconomic consequences for a still-rentier economy. It concludes that without accelerated diversification, the gap between extraction costs and resource value will widen, threatening fiscal sustainability.

detail.abstract: Customs duty and tariff constitute the primary fiscal and regulatory instruments governing cross-border trade in goods. This paper presents a comprehensive examination of customs duty and tariff structures in international trade, with particular focus on the Indian framework governed by the Customs Act 1962, the Customs Tariff Act 1975, and the Foreign Trade Policy 2023-28. The study analyzes the types of customs duties-including Basic Customs Duty (BCD), IGST on imports, Anti-Dumping Duty, and Safeguard Dutythe Harmonized System (HS) of tariff classification, step-by-step duty calculation methodology, and India's tariff policy in the context of Free Trade Agreements. Critically, the paper examines the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence in customs administration-spanning automated HS classification using Natural Language Processing, AI-powered risk profiling, customs valuation verification, trade compliance automation, and predictive tariff impact assessment. The paper draws on regulatory frameworks, WTO guidelines, and practical industry examples to provide actionable insights for exporters, importers, and policy professionals.

title: The Demographic Regulatory Doom Loop: When Safe Asset Rules Meet Aging Fiscal Reality

detail.title: The Demographic Regulatory Doom Loop: When Safe Asset Rules Meet Aging Fiscal Reality
detail.abstract: We document a self-reinforcing loop between population aging, pension obligations, fiscal deterioration, and sovereign risk-and show that prudential regulation amplifies rather than mitigates the resulting fragility. Using a panel of 31 sovereign-rated issuers (1990-2024), we show that: (1) old-age dependency drives government expenditure faster than revenue, with the asymmetry varying by institutional context (3:1 for OECD countries below 30% OADR, narrowing to near-parity above 30%, but acute for non-OECD issuers); (2) pension spending interacts with demographics to accelerate debt accumulation (interaction p=0.04); (3) the expenditure-revenue gap compounds debt dynamics (interaction p<0.001); and (4) the debt-demographics interaction predicts sovereign rating deterioration (p=0.07). Japan, France, Italy, Finland, and Belgium rank highest on our composite doom loop index. The regulatory overlay is critical: Basel III assigns 0% risk weights to sovereign debt rated AA-or above, Solvency II exempts EEA sovereign bonds from capital charges entirely, and pension fund mandates concentrate holdings in domestic sovereigns. The March 2026 US Basel III Endgame reproposal retained this 0% treatment, and the Basel Committee's 2017 discussion paper on reforming sovereign risk weights (BCBS d425) has produced no regulatory action in nearly a decade. The mechanism is recursive and the regulatory lock-in is politically entrenched: institutional investors are compelled to hold precisely the sovereigns whose fiscal backing is eroding, with market discipline suppressed until a rating cliff forces abrupt repricing.

title: The Applicability of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights in Purely National Pension Disputes: A Critical Reassessment in Light of Recent CJEU Jurisprudence

detail.title: The Applicability of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights in Purely National Pension Disputes: A Critical Reassessment in Light of Recent CJEU Jurisprudence
detail.abstract: The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (‘Charter’ or ‘CFR’) was conceived as a safeguard for fundamental rights within the EU’s legal order. In the Netherlands, where judicial review of primary legislation against the national Constitution is precluded and the Pensions Act offers no independent avenue of legal protection, EU law—including the Charter—constitutes the sole effective legal safeguard in disputes between pension beneficiaries and mandatory industry-wide pension funds. A restrictive approach to the Charter’s field of application, which confines its relevance to situations in which Member States are directly implementing Union law, stands in tension with the Charter’s protective purpose. This view has been rendered obsolete by three recent developments at the Court of Justice.

title: When Law Creates Wasting Assets: The Terminal Value Crisis in Leasehold REITs in India

detail.title: When Law Creates Wasting Assets: The Terminal Value Crisis in Leasehold REITs in India
detail.abstract:
As the Indian Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) market matures toward inclusion in global equity indices, a structural legal contradiction threatens its long-term viability: the "Terminal Value Crisis." Unlike their counterparts in the United States or Singapore, which predominantly hold freehold land, Indian REITs are heavily concentrated in leasehold assets—particularly in regulatory environments like Noida and Lucknow. Under the SEBI (Real Estate Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014, these entities are structured as perpetual trusts, yet they are underpinned by finite 99-year leasehold interests that mathematically "waste" toward zero.
This paper identifies a critical divergence between the legal assumption of perpetual value and the financial reality of leasehold decay. It analyzes the risk of "Sponsor-Dumping," where promoters may offload wasting assets onto retail investors at inflated prices, leveraging the absence of mandatory "Terminal Value Decay" scrutiny in current valuation standards. Drawing on the jurisprudence of Kailash Nath Associates v. DDA to address administrative reasonableness in leasehold forfeiture, the research proposes a two-fold regulatory reform:
1. The Lease Renewal Reserve (LRR): A mandatory sinking fund mechanism to preserve principal capital against lease expiry.
2. Active Oversight Certificates: Empowering Trustees with veto powers over Related Party Transactions (RPTs) that fail to account for capital decay.
By bridging the gap between property law and financial regulation, this article provides a blueprint for safeguarding retail capital in the burgeoning Indian

title: Two Contracts, Not Two Firms: The Manager-Priced SME Credit Contract in a Middle-Income Economy

detail.title: Two Contracts, Not Two Firms: The Manager-Priced SME Credit Contract in a Middle-Income Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: No human subjects
declarations.funderStatement: Funded by Banco Estado, Chile.

detail.abstract: Why does the bank charge more when the numbers look better? Chilean small and medium-sized firms borrow less than large firms-a 39 percent debt-to-assets ratio against 55, and a 46 percent short-term-debt-to-sales ratio against 83-and present managers who are slightly older and more experienced than their large-firm counterparts (53.5 years against 51.1; 23 years of experience against 20). They pay, on the same data, an effective lending rate of approximately 6.2 percent against 4.4 percent for large firms-a 1.8-percentage-point premium that survives every direct balance-sheet control. The premium is the puzzle. We answer it by recognising that SME credit and large-firm credit are not points on a single size-of-firm curve: they are two distinct contractual regimes. The SME contract is a person-priced signature contract-a loan executed with a personal guarantee and underwritten on the owner's biography (age, education, experience, ownership share, family history). The large-firm contract is a balance-sheet-priced contract executed without a personal guarantee. Working with the Tercera Encuesta Longitudinal de Empresas (ELE-3)-approximately 2,174 SMEs and 3,299 large firms across twelve sectorswe estimate, side by side, the same five outcome equations on each subsample: total debt, short-term debt, long-term debt, the debt-to-assets ratio, and default. Manager characteristics enter the SME equations with magnitudes an order of magnitude larger than they enter the large-firm equations, and a Wald χ² Chow test rejects pooling decisively at every conventional level (manager block: χ²(8) = 164.7, p ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻³¹; full coefficient vector: χ²(18) = 350.8, p ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻⁶³). Our theoretical contribution is the explicit reframing of SME credit as a person-priced signature contract identifiable in cross-sectional data through the differential significance of owner-level variables. Our empirical contribution is the first joint quantification, on a single representative middle-income dataset, of the manager-priced regime across five outcomes-including a maturitysubstitution mechanism that links pledged fixed assets to lower default risk via the lengthening of debt maturity. The policy implication is direct: state-owned development banks and credit-guarantee programmes-FOGAPE in Chile, the Credit Guarantee Corporation in Malaysia, CGTMSE in India, KUR in Indonesia, the Chinese provincial guarantee networksshould condition eligibility on owner-level information rather than on firm-size thresholds alone.

title: A Rebuttable Inference Framework for Section 2 Causation
affiliations: University of California, Davis - School of Law

detail.title: A Rebuttable Inference Framework for Section 2 Causation
detail.abstract:
Causation is central to monopolization law under Section 2 of the Sherman Act. Plaintiffs must demonstrate that the challenged conduct was sufficiently connected to the defendant’s maintenance or acquisition of its monopoly power. Despite its importance, the causation requirement remains among the least developed aspects of Section 2 doctrine. The few cases that have addressed the issue diverge on how rigorous the plaintiff’s showing of causation must be.

This uncertainty has resurfaced in the district court’s liability decision in United States v. Google. The case highlights a longstanding tension in D.C. Circuit precedent between United States v. Microsoft and Rambus v. FTC. Microsoft allows courts to infer causation from exclusionary conduct that is reasonably capable of contributing to monopoly power, while Rambus applied the more rigorous requirement that the Section 2 plaintiff demonstrate but-for causation, i.e., show that the defendant would not have had its monopoly power had it not engaged in the challenged conduct. The choice between these approaches has significant implications for the scope of Section 2 liability and the evidentiary burden on plaintiffs.

This Article argues that Section 2 causation should be governed by a rebuttable inference framework. Under this approach, Microsoft supplies the initial inference: plaintiffs may obtain an inference of causation by demonstrating that the defendant’s conduct was reasonably capable of contributing to the defendant’s monopoly power. The inference, however, ought to be rebuttable. If the defendant produces sufficient evidence to support a finding that its monopoly power is attributable to other factors, the inference is overcome. The plaintiff must then establish but-for causation by a preponderance of the evidence.

This approach reconciles Microsoft's focus on the evidentiary limits of counterfactual proof with Rambus’ demand for causal rigor. By striking this balance, the proposed framework seeks to reduce both false positives and false negatives in Section 2 cases and to provide a clearer and more structured approach for courts to follow in assessing causation.

title: Beyond Wages: Trade Exposure, Job-Finding, and the Gender Gap

detail.title: Beyond Wages: Trade Exposure, Job-Finding, and the Gender Gap
detail.abstract: This paper documents that trade exposure reshapes gender labor-market inequality through a margin distinct from wages: the rate at which displaced women return to formal employment. Using twenty years of Argentine administrative panel data covering 511,000 formally employed workers and a Bartik shift-share design at the province × industry × year cell, I estimate the differential effect of export exposure on log real wages and on log non-employment-spell duration. The wage interaction is null across all specifications. The spell interaction is large, negative, and robust: women's non-employment spells in highly exposed cells are roughly 10 log points shorter than in unexposed cells, closing about half of the 22-log-point baseline gender gap. Argentina's 2002-2015 export expansion concentrated in male-intensive commodity sectors, leaving too few women in directly exposed cells for the pro-competitive mechanism that drives wage convergence in the OECD and Mexican-NAFTA literature to operate. What does operate is a quantity-margin channel that mirrors the wage non-result: the same scarcity that leaves women too few in goods-tradables to drive within-firm wage compression makes them disproportionately valuable at the hiring margin when those cells become labor-tight. The wage null and the spell-shortening are two manifestations of the same structural feature. The effect concentrates in the prime-fertility 25-34 age bracket and amplifies under the 2010-2015 capital-controls regime. In commodity-exporting economies where the canonical wage-narrowing mechanism cannot operate, trade reshapes gender inequality through reemployment dynamics, not wage-setting.

title: Demographics and Financial Crises: Age Structure as an Early Warning Signal

detail.title: Demographics and Financial Crises: Age Structure as an Early Warning Signal
detail.abstract: I test whether demographic structure improves financial crisis prediction and current account reversal forecasting using a 174-country panel spanning 1950-2024 merged with the Laeven-Valencia systemic crisis database. Baseline controls use log GDP per capita and a Z₁ × log GDP/cap interaction to condition demographic effects on income level; the Chinn-Ito KAOPEN index is excluded from the baseline and tested separately as a hypothesis-specific variable. Old-age dependency is protective for CA reversals (logit MFX =-0.420**, original 3pp definition;-0.600*** for persistent reversals); youth dependency effects are not robustly significant in the income-conditioned specification. Demographics add approximately 49% incremental pseudo-R² to standard early warning models for banking crises (logit: 0.044 → 0.066) and 46% for CA reversals (0.041 → 0.059), though absolute prediction gains are modest given the rarity of crisis events (~0.8% of country-years). Out-of-sample testing on the 2007-2012 crisis wave confirms that demographics substantially improve CA reversal prediction (recall from 0.06 to 0.27) but fail for banking crisis onset. Decomposing current accounts into predictable and idiosyncratic components reveals that financial openness does not systematically widen CA volatility (Levene p = 0.14), but the interaction of demographic stage and openness is critical: early-stage open economies exhibit residual standard deviations nearly double the sample average and Value-at-Risk of-22.6 percentage points of GDP. At the system level, global capital flows are concentrated in an effective number of just 2.9 countries (HHI = 3,504), with the US and China accounting for 83% of variance; the countries that are individually safest create the greatest systemic concentration risk.

title: A Method for Measuring Wealth Disparity Using a Consumer Coefficient

detail.title: A Method for Measuring Wealth Disparity Using a Consumer Coefficient
detail.abstract: Since the dawn of recorded history, humanity has contemplated the disparities in wealth and poverty present in daily life. However, the development of systematic methods to quantify these disparities is a phenomenon that emerged only with the rise of modern social sciences. For a long time, the primary metrics used to quantify wealth disparity have been based predominantly on income-most notably, the Gini coefficient. Yet, this approach arguably runs counter to our true-lived understanding of wealth disparity. In our daily lives, such disparities are often manifested most visibly through consumption patterns. Consequently, this paper proposes a novel method for measuring wealth disparity based on a "consumer coefficient" derived from consumption data.

title: Explaining the K‑Shaped Economy: What’s Behind the Divide?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Federal Reserve Bank of New York

detail.title: Explaining the K‑Shaped Economy: What’s Behind the Divide?

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
In our companion post, we used a new module of our Economic Heterogeneity Indicators (EHIs) to shed light on how recent retail spending growth has been driven by high-income households. This fact is consistent with the popular press’s idea of a “K-shaped economy” in which higher-income households experience faster growth in spending than lower-income households. In this post, we dive deeper into the reasons behind this divergence by analyzing for which goods this trend holds true and ask whether it can be explained by changes in wages, inflation, or wealth. We find that, since 2023, wealth has increased the most for high-income households, while inflation has risen the most for low-income households, with both factors helping explain the fact that real retail spending rose the most for high-income households. In contrast, earnings display a more mixed pattern, though earnings of the highest earners have grown more rapidly than earnings of the lowest earners.

To view post: https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2026/05/explaining-the-k-shaped-economy-whats-behind-the-divide/

title: The Petrodollar Under Pressure Iran, OPEC Fragmentation, Gulf Realignment, and Canada's Strategic Interests in a Changing Energy Order

detail.title: The Petrodollar Under Pressure Iran, OPEC Fragmentation, Gulf Realignment, and Canada's Strategic Interests in a Changing Energy Order
detail.abstract:
The post-1973 petrodollar system became a foundational pillar of the modern international financial order. Built upon U.S.–Saudi strategic coordination, dollar-denominated oil trade, and American protection of global maritime energy routes, the system reinforced U.S. reserve currency dominance, Treasury market liquidity, and geopolitical influence over global commerce and finance.

Over the past two decades, however, structural pressures have increasingly challenged the durability of this arrangement. The rise of China as the world’s largest energy importer, the expansion of BRICS financial coordination, repeated sanctions regimes, alternative settlement systems, and broader geopolitical fragmentation have accelerated debates surrounding “de-dollarization” and the long-term resilience of the petrodollar order.

A regional conflict involving Iran could become one of the most significant accelerants of this transition. Iran occupies a uniquely strategic position adjacent to the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of globally traded petroleum flows each day. Sustained military disruption in the Gulf would likely trigger immediate consequences for oil prices, shipping routes, insurance markets, inflation, sovereign borrowing costs, and broader financial stability. At the same time, increasing divergence within OPEC and OPEC+—including growing production autonomy among Gulf producers such as the United Arab Emirates (“UAE”)—raises questions regarding the long-term cohesion of the cartel architecture that historically reinforced dollar-based hydrocarbon pricing.

This report examines the origins of the petrodollar system, the strategic implications of a potential Iran conflict, evolving Gulf energy politics, and the broader implications for the emerging international order. Particular emphasis is placed on Canada’s strategic position as a stable democratic energy exporter, LNG supplier, G7 middle power, and potential beneficiary of capital and supply-chain realignment amid geopolitical fragmentation.

The report argues that the petrodollar system is unlikely to collapse abruptly. Instead, the international system is gradually evolving toward a more multipolar and transactional energy-financial architecture characterized by diversified settlement mechanisms, regional hedging strategies, and reduced automatic alignment with U.S. geopolitical preferences. The central threat to the existing order is therefore not a single catastrophic event, but the cumulative erosion of institutional trust, energy-security assumptions, and monetary concentration that underpinned the post-Cold War era.

In such an environment, states possessing political stability, strategic natural resources, reliable legal institutions, and secure export capacity—including Canada—may emerge as disproportionately important actors within an increasingly fragmented geopolitical landscape.

title: Same Shock, Different Roads? A K‑Shaped Pattern at the Pump
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Federal Reserve Bank of New York

detail.title: Same Shock, Different Roads? A K‑Shaped Pattern at the Pump

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
In March 2026, energy prices surged to a four-year high, driven by the Iranian closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. In this Liberty Street Economics post, we use the new consumer spending module of the Economic Heterogeneity Indicators to analyze recent changes in nominal and real gas consumption across different income groups. We find that households had very different experiences with gasoline spending: in March, high-income households increased nominal spending the most and kept real consumption essentially unchanged, while low-income households decreased real consumption of gasoline but still saw sharply increased nominal spending because of the rise in gas prices. Therefore, with the sharp increases in gasoline prices in March, a K-shaped pattern in gasoline consumption emerged—showing faster consumption growth for high-income households relative to low-income households. These gasoline consumption patterns qualitatively match those following the increase in energy prices at the beginning of the Russia-Ukraine war in spring 2022, even though the gap in consumption trends during the current episode is quantitatively larger.

To view post: https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2026/05/same-shock-different-roads-a-k-shaped-pattern-at-the-pump/

title: Clientelism and Local Governance: Evidence from Brazil
affiliations: New York University Abu Dhabi and Université Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne - Centre d'Economie de la Sorbonne (CES)

detail.title: Clientelism and Local Governance: Evidence from Brazil
detail.abstract: We estimate the causal effect of electing a clientelistic party on local governance in Brazilian municipalities over more than two decades. Using a regression-discontinuity design in close mixed-type mayoral races and ex-ante party classifications from three independent expert surveys, we find that clientelistic victories raise temporary public hiring by about 20 percent, increase audit irregularities by about 9 cases, and raise school dropout by 0.2 percentage points, while aggregate expenditure and revenue are unchanged. These results suggest that party organization shapes governance through the discretionary execution of a given budget, not through its size.

title: THE MAKING OF THE COPYRIGHT ACT OF 1976: PART I-TECHNOCRACY AND COMPROMISE

detail.title: THE MAKING OF THE COPYRIGHT ACT OF 1976: PART I-TECHNOCRACY AND COMPROMISE
detail.abstract:
After multiple aborted attempts to reform the 1909 Copyright Act, Congress in 1955 embarked on an unprecedented “experiment in legislative technique,” tasking the Copyright Office with researching, drafting, and vetting what it hoped would become the next general revision of the Copyright Act. In recognition of the difficulties and long delay in reforming the 1909 Act and amidst ongoing advances in communications technologies, the drafters of what would become the 1976 Act were especially concerned that copyright reform be resilient to technological change. They wrote in 1965 that “[o]bviously no one can foresee accurately and in detail the evolving patterns in the ways author’s works will reach the public 10, 20, or 50 years from now. Lacking that kind of foresight, the bill should, we believe, adopt a general approach aimed at providing compensation to the author for future as well as present uses of [the] work that materially affect the value of [the] copyright.” It would take another decade for omnibus copyright reform to reach fruition.
     As we mark the 50th anniversary of the 1976 Act, it is useful to trace and reflect upon the origins and ramifications of this momentous legislative achievement. This article reconstructs the drafting and legislative process as the foundation for understanding the meaning and interpretation of the 1976 Act. Although the 1976 Act has been criticized as merely the product of interest group politics of its time, viewing the Act through a wide-angle lens reveals a much richer story. Contrary to accounts emphasizing industry capture or unprincipled compromise, the 1976 Act exemplifies a deeply engaged, transparent, and inclusive drafting and legislative process in which an expert agency carefully studied the issues and focused on society’s broader interests, while stakeholders and legislators jointly navigated the tradeoffs in crafting forward-looking and balanced statutory regime based on what was known and knowable and amidst the political landscape. 
     This article traces the personnel, key debates, drafting process, hearings, and reports that led to the final bill. This exploration reveals that the making of the Act unfolded over two distinct phases: the first leading to the core principles, architecture, and provisions by the mid-1960s, and the second, unfolding in fits and starts over the next decade, addressing both particular disruptions caused by rapid technological advances and lingering tensions over unresolved issues. 
     Part II of this project explores the political economy of this experiment in technocratic legislative drafting, investigates the ramifications of the phased legislative history for the interpretation of the 1976 Act, and examines the actual practice of interpreting the 1976 Act, revealing an uneven and at times internally inconsistent jurisprudential record.

title: In What Ways Has U.S. Trade with China Changed?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York

detail.title: In What Ways Has U.S. Trade with China Changed?

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Over the past year, U.S. trade policy with China has undergone enormous changes, but with surprisingly little effect on overall trade balances. In fact, the U.S.’s twelve-month trade deficit, while highly volatile due to import front-running early in the year, ended 2025 at $1.2 trillion, almost unchanged from 2024. At the same time, China’s trade surplus with the world actually increased from $1 trillion to $1.2 trillion. However, when looking at changes between individual countries, one sees large shifts in bilateral balances. In this post, we will focus on changing trade flows between the U.S., China, and southeast Asia.

To view post: https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2026/05/in-what-ways-has-u-s-trade-with-china-changed/

title: Author Empowerment in the Copyright Act of 1976: Work Made for Hire and Termination of Transfers
affiliations: UC Berkeley School of Law and Irell & Manella LLP

detail.title: Author Empowerment in the Copyright Act of 1976: Work Made for Hire and Termination of Transfers

declarations.declarationOfInterest: David Nimmer has represented parties in termination of transfer litigation.

detail.abstract:
From its genesis in the wake of the printing press, copyright law has mediated the division of autonomy and remuneration between publishers (and, later, other intermediaries) and authors. For much of copyright’s history, publishers held tremendous sway due to organizational strength and the high cost of mechanically reproducing and distributing books. 
     The Copyright Office drafters of what would become the Copyright Act of 1976 sought to shift the balance toward author control and remuneration. In that context, they sought to break free from the Supreme Court’s 1943 decision validating advance assignment of copyright renewal terms, which constituted a significant setback to author control and remuneration. Moreover, the desire to move U.S. copyright law to the international unitary duration norm complicated affording a right to reclaim copyright protection.
     Part I traces the development of an inalienable termination of transfer right in conjunction with the work made for hire definition the 1976 Act. Part II examines how courts have interpreted—and at times destabilized—that integrated ownership architecture.

title: Genetic Experiential Perceptual Model

detail.title: Genetic Experiential Perceptual Model
detail.abstract: Genetic Experiential Perceptual (GEP) Model The Genetic-Experiential-Perceptual (GEP) Model is a proposed linear framework for understanding human behaviour, developed to address the need for a structured, non-circular approach to psychological theory. This model suggests that behaviour is formed through a sequential interaction of three distinct stages: genetic predispositions, experiential factors (including sociocultural and environmental contexts), and perceptual interpretation. By rejecting the common feedback-loop approach in behavioural psychology, the GEP Model asserts that each layer shapes the next, but does not retroactively alter the previous. Genes provide the neurological foundation; experience molds psychological patterns; perception filters meaning and together they culminate in behaviour. The model identifies perception as the only modifiable component, offering a practical focal point for psychological interventions. This theory is intended to complement existing cognitive and developmental models by offering a clearer structure for analysing individual behavioural outcomes across diverse cultural contexts. The GEP Model encourages a re-evaluation of how we define "normal" or "abnormal" behaviour, advocating instead for a lens rooted in structured causality and cultural realism.

title: A PATH-DEPENDENT UTAUT MODEL APPLIED TO ROBO-ADVISOR ADOPTION

detail.title: A PATH-DEPENDENT UTAUT MODEL APPLIED TO ROBO-ADVISOR ADOPTION

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

keywords: unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT)

detail.abstract: The adoption of a new technology often depends on individuals' prior decisions to use certain upstream technologies. We fill a research gap by introducing path dependence into UTAUT models, deriving a general path dependence augmented UTAUT (PDA-UTAUT) model to analyze such two-step technology adoption decisions and define conditions in which it is applicable. The model is applied to the demand for robo-advisory services in the United States using survey data. Partial least squares estimation results confirm the PDA-UTAUT model. The empirical findings significantly improve the understanding of private financial investor decision making and have implications for the robo-advisor industry.

title: The Cognition-Technology-Institution Triple-Layer Framework of Socio-Technical Systems: An Analytical Narrative Based on Asian Local Bottom-Up Development Practices

detail.title: The Cognition-Technology-Institution Triple-Layer Framework of Socio-Technical Systems: An Analytical Narrative Based on Asian Local Bottom-Up Development Practices

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests, financial conflicts, or personal relationships that could have influenced this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or identifiable personal data. It is based on publicly available materials, policy documents, and case-process information. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was conducted independently and received no external funding or institutional support.

detail.abstract: When digital technology enters local societies, why are some socio-technical systems able to form new development capabilities, while others weaken local knowledge, community subjectivity, and institutional correction capacity during the process of expansion? Addressing this question, this paper constructs a Cognition-Technology-Institution triple-layer analytical framework based on the hypotheses of triple-layer coupling, cumulative cross-layer friction, and contextualized rebalancing. Taking bottom-up development practices in Asian localities as the empirical field, it examines how local cognitive and action signals generated from community action, local knowledge, and organizational learning are transformed into local development capabilities through technological bearing and institutional absorption. This paper argues that the evolution of socio-technical systems is not a simple process of unidirectional technological diffusion, but a continuous process of matching, misalignment, and rebalancing among cognitive externalization, technological bearing, and institutional adaptation. The research finds two types of triple-layer isomorphic paths in the selected Asian local fields: a Culture-Community path, characterized by the matching between local beliefs, ecological ethics, community identity, digital communication, and community institutions; and a Production-Market path, characterized by the matching between local production knowledge, market cognition, platform systems, logistics quality control, and local governance. Despite differences in industrial forms and technological carriers, both paths indicate that bottom-up local practices are more likely to become sustainable development capabilities when they are effectively borne by technology and appropriately absorbed by institutions while preserving local subjectivity. Furthermore, the formation of a new steady state does not necessarily equate to a robust steady state. It must be examined whether local knowledge, community subjectivity, autonomous space, and institutional correction capacity are preserved after local mechanisms enter larger-scale market, platform, and governance systems. The practical implication is that local digital governance should not be understood as unidirectional technological importation or model replication, but as support for continuous matching between local signal generation, technological bearing, and institutional adaptation.

title: Capital Trigger Topology: Public-Rule Activation Surfaces, Replay Reproducibility, and Honest Falsification for Installed Capital

detail.title: Capital Trigger Topology: Public-Rule Activation Surfaces, Replay Reproducibility, and Honest Falsification for Installed Capital

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial, personal, or professional interests that could have influenced the research, analysis, interpretation, or conclusions of this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, patients, animals, clinical data, surveys, interviews, or personally identifiable private information. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: We introduce Capital Trigger Topology (CTT), a deterministic public-rule activation surface instrument that measures where installed capital becomes mechanically compelled to act, given only public holdings disclosures, codified mandate documents, benchmark definitions, and an information cutoff. The first-domain primitive is the closed-form daily-reset automaton ΔE = β • A • (β-1) • r for leveraged and inverse exchange-traded funds (Cheng and Madhavan 2009; Avellaneda and Zhang 2010), applied to an append-only registry of 18 certified ProShares products with SHA-256-hashed prospectus and Schedule of Investments evidence. From the automaton we derive sign and materiality boundary surfaces at four pre-registered ADV thresholds, crossing detection, visibility scoring, five integrity gates, and a per-cohort one-page memo with ACCEPT, REROUTE, KILL, or UNIDENTIFIED states. We replay two stress windows, the August 14, 2015 and February 2, 2018 information cutoffs, against ProShares Trust II SEC EDGAR Schedule of Investments XBRL filings (CIK 0001415311). At quarter-end anchors, realized signed VIX-futures position deltas across SVXY, UVXY, VIXM, and VIXY match the CTT-predicted episode-level direction in 8 of 8 ticker-episode pairs. On the daily-resolution diagnostic proxy stack, however, CTT ties the strongest close-cousin daily-reset baseline in both replays and the August 2015 ablation suite emits a hard-kill failure artifact. We commit to honest reporting of the failure: the preregistered flagship gate of 20 or more Tier 1/Tier 2 daily-crossing-aligned events with baseline beat is uncrossed, and the next valid path is daily official action evidence, not proxy relaxation. All artifacts, run identifiers, and failure states are persisted with parent-hashed registry manifests; 43 tests reproduce both replays byte-for-byte.

title: “Chrétien and the World: Canadian Foreign Policy from 1993 to 2003” — Book Review

detail.title: “Chrétien and the World: Canadian Foreign Policy from 1993 to 2003” — Book Review
detail.abstract: This review examines Chrétien and the World: Canadian Foreign Policy from 1993 to 2003, edited by Jack Cunningham and John Meehan. It argues that the volume offers a persuasive corrective to the view of Jean Chrétien as a domestically focused prime minister with little foreign-policy ambition. Instead, the book presents the Chrétien decade as a period of pragmatic, austerity-constrained liberal internationalism, shaped by trade diplomacy, multilateral coalition-building, human security initiatives, Canada–U.S. relations, domestic unity politics, and selective military engagement. The review highlights the volume’s value as a structured account of Canada’s post–Cold War foreign-policy transition.

title: Ontology of the Complex System of Money

detail.title: Ontology of the Complex System of Money

keywords: An Economic Framework Based on Dissipative Structure Theory
and the Coordination Cost Symmetry Principle complex science-specifically
and Shannon-Brillouin Information Theory-and extends it to a coexistence

detail.abstract: This paper reconstructs the ontological foundation of money from the perspective of complex science—specifically, Prigogine’s Dissipative Structure Theory, Haken’s Synergetics, and Shannon-Brillouin Information Theory—and extends it to a coexistence framework for the era of volitional artificial intelligence (AI).

title: Managing the Energy and Environmental Costs of AI
affiliations: Vanderbilt University - Law School,  and Vanderbilt University - Law School

detail.title: Managing the Energy and Environmental Costs of AI

publicationDetails.journalName: Vanderbilt University Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to yield not only major economic and social benefits, but also major energy and environmental costs. Recent research and policy have focused on how governments can increase the supply of energy, but many of these options risk increasing the energy and environmental costs of AI as well. This Article takes a different approach by focusing on private actors, not governments, and by focusing on demand-side, not supply-side, responses. Drawing on the extensive interdisciplinary private ordering literature, the Article argues that the motivations of corporate and retail AI users, AI providers, data centers, and utilities provide an opportunity to reduce AI-driven data center energy demand and its financial and environmental costs. The options for this demand-side management range from standard disclosure metrics for corporate and retail AI users, to changes in carbon accounting standards, to supply chain contracting initiatives, to development of a comprehensive standards, certification, and labeling system. The private governance approaches explored in the Article are not a complete response to the energy and environmental challenges of AI, but they are non-intrusive, viable instruments that can be adopted quickly even in a deregulatory era and can address the risks arising from AI-driven electricity demand growth. By shifting the focus from government to private actors and from energy supply to energy demand, the Article offers a new perspective on the vigorous debate about how to manage the effects of AI and demonstrates how insights from the growing private ordering literature can fill gaps in public governance.

title: Migration Policies and the Informal Economy: A Systematic Review of the literature

detail.title: Migration Policies and the Informal Economy: A Systematic Review of the literature
detail.abstract: Economic informality remains a persistent challenge within the European Union and is increasingly related to the governance of labour migration. This systematic literature review examines how migration policies-ranging from restrictive entry regimes to inclusive integration measures-influence migrants' economic incorporation and the dynamics of the informal economy. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic search of Scopus and Web of Science identified 38 peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2024. The evidence was synthesised using a qualitative thematic approach. The review identifies a consistent "regulatory paradox": restrictive migration policies, including limited entry quotas and residence permits tied to specific employers, are associated with higher levels of informal economic activity by increasing administrative precarity and excluding migrants from formal labour market protection. In contrast, regulation and inclusive integration measures-such as access to employment rights, collective bargaining, and vocational support-are shown to reduce participation in the shadow economy. However, these effects are highly context-dependent and mediated by enforcement capacity, institutional quality, and sector-specific labour demand, particularly in agriculture, construction, and domestic care. The findings suggest that exclusive migration governance often contributes to informality rather than its reduction. While the evidence base is heterogeneous and largely observational, the review highlights the structural role of migration policy design in shaping informal labour markets. The study concludes that reducing informality in the EU requires a shift from restrictive control-oriented regimes toward rights-based regulatory frameworks, including the decoupling of residence permits from single employers and the expansion of accessible legal migration pathways.

title: Cooperation in Knowledge Sharing and R&D Investment

detail.title: Cooperation in Knowledge Sharing and R&D Investment
detail.abstract: This paper reports a laboratory experiment that provides insights on cooperation in R&D investment when knowledge sharing decisions are endogenous. Specifically, there are two types of treatments: one in which participants decide on whether to share knowledge before they make their investment decisions and one where the knowledge sharing constellation is exogenously given, both with and without non-binding communication. The results show that there are behavioural spillovers between the decisions on knowledge sharing and investment. When exogenously set, the degree of knowledge sharing does not affect cooperation. Communication increases cooperation more when participants can decide on knowledge sharing.

title: Initial Evidence on Earnings Conference Call Mention Contracts for Investor Relations Officers
affiliations: Duke University - Fuqua School of Business and

detail.title: Initial Evidence on Earnings Conference Call Mention Contracts for Investor Relations Officers
detail.abstract: Prediction markets now offer contracts on whether managers will mention specific words during earnings conference calls. While prior research shows that prediction market prices can identify outcomes, it is unclear whether prices provide incremental predictive power relative to existing firm disclosures. Using 1,437 earnings call mention contracts from the Kalshi platform during its first nine months, we find that prices strongly predict contract outcomes, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.893. Although well above chance, this AUC is only slightly higher than the AUC of 0.891 based on disclosures alone. Prices remain incrementally predictive when combined with disclosures, but the improvement is economically modest. The association between prices and outcomes is stronger in the presentation portion than in the Q&A, consistent with managers responding to perceived information demand. Overall, while price effects are inconsistent with gambling-driven noise, prices add limited new information beyond existing disclosures.

title: Economic growth in countries depended on natural resource (by emphasizing on oil resources)
affiliations: Tarbiat Modares University, University of Mazandaran (UMZ) and

detail.title: Economic growth in countries depended on natural resource (by emphasizing on oil resources)
detail.abstract: This paper, by focusing on oil resources, tries to investigate the relationship between natural resources abundance and ECONOMIC GROWTH in 8 OPEC selected countries during 1970-2008. We used Dynamic Panel Data and Static Panel Data Model for this purpose and estimated the relations by Generalized Method of Moments, Fixed Effects and Random Effects Estimator. The results represented that there is a negative relationship between oil resources abundance and ECONOMIC GROWTH in above mentioned countries.

title: Responses to Income Tax Changes in Low-Friction Labor Markets: Evidence from the Removal of Tax on Tips

detail.title: Responses to Income Tax Changes in Low-Friction Labor Markets: Evidence from the Removal of Tax on Tips
detail.abstract: I study how workers respond to income tax changes in a low-friction labor market by exploiting the recent removal of federal taxes on tipped income in the United States. Tipped occupations are unique compared to the broader labor market in that there is generally more scope to adjust labor supply and wages. Using monthly, individual-level U.S. Current Population Survey data from 2024 and 2025, I compare workers in tippedincome occupations to a set of highly comparable occupations with low exposure to tipping. I find evidence suggesting that pre-tip hourly wages decreased, driven by states with more stringent labor regulations. I find no convincing evidence of a large, broad labor market response for hours worked or multiple job holding. There is, however, weak evidence that hours worked increased in states with less stringent labor market regulations. The findings suggest that while employers may have captured a proportion of the policy incidence, I find no evidence of meaningful behavioral responses among workers to the removal of tax on tips.

title: Multi-Asset A/A+ Momentum Fair Value Gap Strategy

detail.title: Multi-Asset A/A+ Momentum Fair Value Gap Strategy
detail.abstract: This paper presents a rigorous quantitative analysis of the Multi-Asset A/A+ Momentum Fair Value Gap (FVG) Trading Strategy, backtested across Gold (XAUUSD), Euro (EURUSD), British Pound (GBPUSD), and Japanese Yen (USDJPY) over the calendar year 2025, using one-minute OHLC data from HistData. The strategy employs strict multi-confluence filtering: momentum leg detection on the 5-minute timeframe, Fair Value Gap identification within a 2-hour forward window, and Higher Timeframe (1H) structural confluence via EMA-20, EMA-50, and a 30-period Point of Control. Setups are classified as A-grade or A+-grade based on body ratio thresholds and HTF alignment quality. Over 473 qualifying trades, the strategy produced +265.0 R in cumulative profit-equivalent to a $66,250 net gain on a $50,000 account risking $250 per trade-representing a 132.5% annual return. The overall win rate was 78.0%, with A+-grade setups achieving 86.7%. Maximum drawdown was contained to-$1,000 (-2.0%), demonstrating exceptional capital preservation alongside strong absolute performance.

title: How technological progressions at various stages of the digital age impact household income: Transmission Mechanisms and the Chinese Paradox

detail.title: How technological progressions at various stages of the digital age impact household income: Transmission Mechanisms and the Chinese Paradox
