detail.abstract:
This study constructs a multi-level analytical framework encompassing macro-dynamics, meso-level structural transformations, and micro-level behavioral mechanisms to systematically examine the multidimensional impact of information and communication technologies, automation technologies (ranging from industrial robots to artificial intelligence), and artificial intelligence technologies--particularly their trend towards intelligent assistance--on the scale, structure and equity(between holders of capital and labour, and among workers with different skill types) of household income. Research shows that: 1. While ICT enhances employees' bargaining power and increases business income for residents in remote areas, the erosion of property income caused by data ownership issues and the pressure on social security systems resulting from the gig economy pose new challenges to digital governance capacity. 2. While the deployment of industrial robots generates substitution effects and depresses the labour share, the widespread release of productivity effects during industrial upgrading, coupled with the crossing of the lag in human capital accumulation, places China in the right-hand portion of a 'U-shaped' dynamic trajectory for the labour share. As the creative effect of automation in non-production roles grows, China's position in the global value chain, along with its tax system and comparative advantages, has enabled the local labour-enhancing technological progress paradigm to be sustained in the era of artificial intelligence. 3. The nature of generative AI as an intelligent assistant can reduce skill premiums and narrow the income gap among workers by internalising experts' tacit knowledge. 4. To ensure equality and equity, institutional design in the digital age can optimise primary distribution by resharping collective bargaining power within digital platforms and exploring mechanisms for residents to receive returns on their data as a resource; enhance secondary distribution by refining the dynamic eligibility screening of the social security system and strenthening safeguards against algorithmic exclusion; and advance educational reform by reducing the time lag in human capital accumulation and accelarating the higher education system's responsiveness to technological trends.

title: The Spatial Effects of Labor Mobility Restrictions: Evidence from the Shenzhen Wall
affiliations: Peking University HSBC Business School,  and The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

detail.title: The Spatial Effects of Labor Mobility Restrictions: Evidence from the Shenzhen Wall
detail.abstract: This paper studies how within-city labor mobility restrictions shape the spatial allocation of economic activity. We examine the Shenzhen Wall, a boundary that increased commuting costs between Shenzhen's Special Economic Zone (SEZ) and the rest of the city for nearly three decades. Using a regression discontinuity design, we document a sharp increase in firm entry and employment just outside the Wall, despite the policy advantages offered within the SEZ. This spatial gap persists even after the removal of the Wall. We show that this discontinuity is driven by differences in labor-market access. Commuting flows drop discontinuously across the boundary, and the effect on firm entry is substantially larger in labor-intensive industries. To quantify the aggregate effects, we embed bilateral commuting frictions into a quantitative spatial equilibrium model calibrated to the observed allocation of workers and price levels in 2024. Counterfactual simulations show that mobility restrictions distort the spatial allocation of jobs and residents, generating net population outflows from the economy. Workplace employment declines on both sides of the boundary, while larger reductions in labor availability and larger wage increases inside the SEZ. Endogenous agglomeration forces further amplify these effects.

title: Repression, the High Cost of Living, and Government by Opacity in Mali

detail.title: Repression, the High Cost of Living, and Government by Opacity in Mali

keywords: high cost of living JEL codes: D72

detail.abstract: This note examines the political, social, and media sequence observed in Mali between April 18 and 24, 2026. It argues that seemingly dispersed events-the continued detention of journalist Youssouf Sissoko, a strike notice in higher education, clearance operations in Bamako, fuel price increases, humanitarian tensions in the North, the reshuffling of the National Transitional Council, and diplomatic repositioning-belong to the same governing logic. Mobilizing the theory of state moral inversion, the literature on legal authoritarianism, and recent work on the digitization of Mali's public debate, the note shows that the military regime converts political and social costs into proofs of sovereignty. Constraint is presented as order, opacity as patriotic prudence, and ordinary suffering as the acceptable price of refoundation. Methodologically, the analysis rests on a reasoned cross-reading of institutional sources, human rights organizations, news agencies, and Malian media, while setting aside insufficiently corroborated narratives. It concludes that the Malian crisis is now inseparably a crisis of public truth and a crisis of state performance.

detail.abstract: This paper discusses affordable housing challenges and possible solutions for socioeconomically underserved New York City (NYC) residents. The introduction provides a high-level overview of this topic and how it impacts vulnerable people such as ethnic minorities and immigrants. This paper then examines sociology-based policy approaches to NYC's affordable housing issue. These approaches include rent regulations, housing production, and collective advocacy. detail.abstract: Aggregate optimization structurally permits alignment failures because additive objectives collapse system topology into a scalar metric, masking extractive gradients within the underlying dynamics. The mechanism is compensation: aggregate objective functions allow gains in one dimension to offset losses in another, which permits floor compression, which is the mechanism through which each identified failure mode operates. This paper formalizes a compensation spectrum (additive objectives permit unbounded compensation, Nash welfare permits bounded compensation, floor objectives permit zero compensation). Each of the eighteen currently identified alignment failure modes is analyzed through a three-part proof: how aggregate optimization produces it, its documented analog in human institutional systems, and how floor optimization eliminates the gradient. The diagnosis is more fundamental than any specific solution. Companion simulations are available at https://github.com/caseymrobbins/Ac_demo.

detail.abstract: Persian rugs are woven in different parts of the Islamic Republic of Iran. However, the rugs woven in Eastern Azerbaijan, Esfahan, and Qum have a worldwide reputation. A poliy Analysis Matrix (PAM) is used to study the rug industry in these provinces. Our analysis is concentrated on the most-exported hand-woven rug-named 65-Radj Cheleh Abrishami Silk Flower-using 2006 data. The results indicate that the export competitive indexes for the three provinces are 0.81, 0.88, and 0.93, respectively. title: Ideological Extractivism: How Theocratic Institutions Subvert Privatisation and Resist Adaptation in Iran (2005-2026)

detail.title: Ideological Extractivism: How Theocratic Institutions Subvert Privatisation and Resist Adaptation in Iran (2005-2026)
detail.abstract: Existing scholarship on extractive institutions (Acemoglu and Robinson, 2012) assumes that ruling elites are rational actors who instrumentalise ideology to sustain economic power. This paper argues that this assumption fails to account for regimes in which ideology functions not as an instrument of power but as its purpose. Introducing the concept of 'ideological extractivism', the paper identifies a distinct regime type in which extractive economic institutions are fused with a totalising religious-ideological project, producing a systematic pattern of self-damaging behaviour: the ruling elite repeatedly sacrifices material interests, international relationships, and even regime survival to preserve ideological commitments. The concept is developed through an analysis of Iran's Article 44 privatisation programme (2005-2024), in which $70 billion in state assets were captured not merely to enrich insiders but to fund an ideological-military apparatus, and tested against eleven episodes spanning 1979-2026 in which the Islamic Republic chose ideology over self-preservation. Drawing on Nathan's (2003) authoritarian resilience, Wedeen's (1999) analysis of ideology as spectacle, and Kuran's (1995) theory of preference falsification, the paper demonstrates why ideological extractivist regimes cannot adapt to crises and are structurally predisposed to catastrophic rather than managed declineas the 2025-2026 Iranian crisis confirms.

detail.abstract: This research explores the growing role of Orange Economy influencers and creative content producers in shaping how consumers in Bangladesh make purchasing decisions and manage their financial lives. The study draws on two complementary sets of data: primary data gathered from 100 leading Orange Economy influencers operating across major digital platforms, and a structured consumer survey conducted with 400 respondents residing in prominent cities across the country. This primary data was further enriched with secondary material sourced from international financial institutions and global reports on the creative economy. To analyze the relationships among key variables, the study employs a quantitative-positivist research design incorporating Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), multiple regression analysis, and Analysis of Variance (ANOVA). The results point to content authenticity (β = 0.48, p < 0.001) and the degree of trust and credibility associated with influencers (β = 0.39, p < 0.001) as the most powerful drivers of consumer purchasing behavior. Moreover, consumer buying decisions emerge as a significant mediating variable between influencer engagement and changes in financial behavior (β = 0.71, p < 0.001). The overall SEM solution exhibits strong model fit indices (CFI = 0.96, RMSEA = 0.048), lending confidence to the structural relationships proposed. On the market side, Bangladesh's orange economy influencer segment has witnessed remarkable expansiongrowing from approximately BDT 0.1 billion in 2017 to an estimated BDT 7.1 billion in 2025, which translates to a compounded annual growth rate of around 68%. Beyond its empirical contributions, this study advances academic understanding of the creative economy, digital consumer psychology, and financial inclusion in a developing country context. The findings carry meaningful implications for policymakers working on Bangladesh's National Creative Economy Strategy and align with broader international development goals.

detail.abstract: This paper extends and refines the third proposition of the Temporal Warfare framework introduced in SSRN 6695898 (Földvári 2026). detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence in Cybersecurity and Its Impact on U.S. Society Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed for a multitude of uses across all levels of government, corporate entities, and institutional bodies. The rapid evolution of cyber threats and malicious actors demanding a commensurate elevation in cybersecurity efforts has led to the widespread integration of AI in information technology networks. The technology offers numerous benefits, to include improved performance in data-intensive cybersecurity functions, enhanced interconnectivity between legacy systems, and the capability to process information at speeds that would be difficult or impossible for humans to achieve. However, the true dangers of this technology have yet to be fully assessed in terms of its broader societal implications. This paper examines the dual potential of artificial intelligence (AI) in cybersecurity. While the benefits of using AI in cybersecurity are increasingly clear indeed, many industry commentators now regard AI-powered security systems as necessary for effectively defending the U.S. digital infrastructure against a swelling tide of cyber threats, there are also a host of negative consequences for individuals, businesses, and democracies. These harms include the introduction of novel vulnerabilities, the erosion of privacy, the possibility of reinforced algorithmic discrimination, and the dangerous escalation of an AI-powered cyber arms race. This paper aims to map the landscape of these benefits and harms, laying the groundwork for future, deeper inquiry into how best to harness the potential of AI in cybersecurity for the good of society as a whole. To achieve that goal, the paper draws on insights from computer science, ethics, law, and public policy in examining the technological, social, political, and ethical implications of AI in cybersecurity.

title: The Demographic Erosion of Fiscal Leverage: Twin Deficits in an Aging World

detail.title: The Demographic Erosion of Fiscal Leverage: Twin Deficits in an Aging World
detail.abstract: The twin deficits hypothesis treats the fiscal-current account coefficient as stable across countries. We show it varies substantially with demographic structure: from 0.352 in young economies to 0.173 in aged ones (income-conditioned specification, p < 0.001 in both terciles, N = 5,455 , 185 countries, 1990-2024). The erosion operates through a channel mismatch. The demographic Z vector is null on the trade balance (Z_1 =-2.4 , p = 0.909) while fiscal policy transmits through trade. Fiscal leverage is empirically stronger when trade dominates the current account (fiscal × trade-dominance = 0.280, p < 0.001), and the absolute amplitude of trade-channel variation collapses in aging economies (|Trade/GDP| falls from 15.1 to 7.1 across demographic terciles). Demographics do not confound the twin-deficit relationshipcontrolling for Z attenuates the fiscal coefficient by only 1.3%. They moderate it. Financial openness further erodes rather than restores fiscal leverage in aging economies (fiscal × KAOPEN =-0.043, p = 0.035 within the late-transition tercile). These findings imply that the IMF's External Balance Assessment framework should condition its fiscal coefficient on demographic transition stage: a uniform coefficient systematically overstates fiscal leverage in aging economies and understates it in young ones. Post-dividend economies face a fiscal leverage trap in which the need for external adjustment rises precisely as the primary policy tool loses effectiveness.

detail.abstract: Given the interconnected nature of financial markets, understanding the relationships among them is essential for investors and traders in selecting optimal portfolios, and for policymakers in adopting appropriate monetary and financial policies. The present study aimed to investigate the interrelationship between risk and return, as well as their spillover effects, between Iran's stock market and competing markets-namely the foreign exchange, gold, and housing markets-under varying bullish and bearish market conditions. The analysis relied on monthly data from 2011 to 2022, as well as a multivariate GARCH model. The results showed significant spillover effects of returns and volatility from the foreign exchange market to the stock market during both bullish and bearish phases of the foreign exchange market. In addition, return spillovers from the stock market to the foreign exchange market were also observed across both market conditions, underscoring the strong interdependence between these two markets in Iran. However, the study found no evidence of return spillovers from the stock market to the gold market under either market condition. In contrast, return and volatility spillovers from the gold market to the stock market were confirmed in both bullish and bearish phases of the gold market. The results did not confirm the return and volatility spillover effects from the housing market to the stock market under either bearish or bullish conditions in the housing market. title: Demographics and Asset Prices: The Murder-Suicide of the Rentier

detail.title: Demographics and Asset Prices: The Murder-Suicide of the Rentier
detail.abstract: We test whether demographic structure systematically predicts asset prices across a global panel of up to 237 countries over 1950-2024, using the orthogonal demographic polynomial approach of Higgins (1998). Four findings frame the paper. First, demographics strongly predict safe interest rates: working-age share (Z₁) carries a coefficient of 57.1 (p = 0.002) for real 10-year sovereign yields and 55.2 (p = 0.016) for real 3-month rates, with the effect operating through slow-moving levels rather than year-to-year changes. Second, demographics do not robustly predict equity-market capitalization once income is conditioned; every linear, regime-split, and savings-interaction coefficient that is significant without an income interaction becomes null when log MY × log GDP per capita is added. Third, a direct test of the Geanakoplos-Magill-Quinzii (2002) structural log-log specification on the full-world available stock-capitalization panel yields a positive, unit-elastic, highly significant relationship (β = 0.92, p < 0.0001 with country and year fixed effects, N = 1,030) that vanishes under income conditioning (β = 1.44, p = 0.46), with log GDP per capita itself becoming the significant covariate; the apparent demographic-equity link is observationally equivalent to a development-level confound on world panel data. Fourth, the crosscountry evidence is more consistent with the asymmetric "murder-suicide" framework of Kopecky and Taylor (2022)aging compressing safe yields but not equity valuations, through institutional intermediation, international diversification, and corporate buybacks-than with the closed-economy GMQ benchmark. Two boundary results sharpen this picture: housing shows no demographic response, and the term spread is not predicted by demographics (p = 0.230) despite its significance in current-account regressions, implying that its role there reflects monetary or inflation-credibility variation rather than a demographic channel.

title: Does Demography Cause Capital Flows? A Causal Stress Test Under Income Conditioning

detail.title: Does Demography Cause Capital Flows? A Causal Stress Test Under Income Conditioning
detail.abstract: A large empirical literature reports a robust correlation between demographic structure and current account balances. Once income conditioning is applied (adding log GDP per capita and a Z₁ × log GDP/cap interaction to the baseline control set, as required to capture the income-conditional sign reversal documented in Peters 2026e), that headline OLS correlation collapses: Z₁ on the current account is-17.4 (p = 0.312, N = 5,298). This raises the causal question with new force: was the previously significant CA correlation reflecting lifecycle savings, or development-level confounding absorbed by the income interaction? We deploy six identification strategies on the income-conditioned specification-instrumental variables with lagged fertility and with predetermined instruments, heterogeneity-robust staggered difference-indifferences across 105 capital-account-opening episodes, synthetic control methods, a demographic Bartik instrument, and pension reform as an alternative activation test-to map what survives. The CA-based causal strategies are uniformly null under income conditioning: triple-difference Z₁×Post = +46.8 (parametric p = 0.049 but RI p = 0.203), BJS ATT = +4.0 (RI p = 0.246), Bartik reduced form =-123.0 (p = 0.383). One result is robust: gross savings. The Z₁ coefficient on gross savings is +53.5 (p = 0.0007, N = 4,194), surviving the income-conditioning correction that nulls the CA result. Predetermined instruments using baby boom magnitude and historical child mortality find a significant lifecycle effect on the CA in non-transition economies (Z₁ =-65.7, p = 0.038, ex-CCA, F = 267). The pattern is internally coherent: aging universally raises gross savings, but whether those savings show up as a CA surplus depends on income level (Peters 2026e). Our contribution is the boundary: lifecycle causation is identifiable at the savings stage and via predetermined demographic shocks; it is not identifiable from short-window post-opening CA dynamics, because that variation is what income conditioning absorbs.

title: Pockets of Predictability in Resource Economies: Forecasting the Canadian Market

detail.title: Pockets of Predictability in Resource Economies: Forecasting the Canadian Market
detail.abstract: This paper demonstrates that modeling stock return predictability in resource-heavy, exportdriven economies requires a fundamental departure from traditional domestic baselines and static econometric methodologies. Evaluating the S&P/TSX Composite Index, we demonstrate that standard domestic baselines like the dividend yield and term spread comprehensively fail out-ofsample, yielding negative Clark-West statistics and zero economic alpha. To resolve this, we introduce high-frequency Commodity-currency predictor variables, specifically the CAD/USD exchange rate and WTI Crude Oil, modeled through a time-varying pockets of predictability framework. Because international terms-of-trade shocks are inherently episodic, traditional constant-parameter models mathematically dilute active macroeconomic signals with out-ofsample noise. By dynamically isolating transient structural shocks, we uncover significant outof-sample forecasting power. The CAD/USD exchange rate generates a highly significant unrestricted Clark-West statistic of 4.00, translating into an annualized portfolio alpha of 5.54% under strict economic sign restrictions. Furthermore, we show that successfully extracting this alpha requires a highly disciplined, state-dependent portfolio methodology. A strict pocket combination strategy that aggressively zeroes out inactive predictor signals comprehensively outperforms naive averaging, delivering up to a 4.79% annualized alpha under traditional longonly constraints. Ultimately, we establish that the S&P/TSX Composite Index predictability is systematically driven by localized structural shocks, and that capturing this predictability strictly requires a dynamic methodology tailored for commodity-currency transience.

title: The Satoshi Overhang: Why the Bear Case is Bounded

detail.title: The Satoshi Overhang: Why the Bear Case is Bounded
detail.abstract: Renewed public attention on the identity of Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator has sharpened focus on the Satoshi overhang, commonly framed as a tail risk for bitcoin. This paper argues that the mechanical downside of a disposition is bounded well below the existential-loss framing, and that the terminal states most consistent with sixteen years of holder behavior are nonbearish for bitcoin's effective supply. The approximately 1.148 million BTC Patoshi position is analyzed on two tracks. For a purely wealth-maximizing holder, a three-scenario quantitative analysis (Appendix A) shows that bitcoin's current market depth is sufficient to absorb a patient multi-year liquidation at a cumulative price impact in the mid-single-digit to mid-double-digit percent range relative to counterfactual, with the central scenario clustering near 10 percent. The paper maps a decision space rather than identifying a unique modal outcome, assuming a holder whose profile is consistent with the sixteen-year record. Preference sets consistent with the record, including ideological non-intervention, privacy above all, satisficing, and myth preservation, favor continued dormancy terminating in a cryptographically enforced nonrecovery or destruction arrangement; preference sets favoring adversarial or wealth-maximizing action are possible but less supported. Across the plausible region of the decision space, the bear case is bounded and the terminal states most consistent with observed behavior are neutral to slightly positive for bitcoin's effective supply.

detail.abstract: Current AI governance treats bias as a technical defect amenable to algorithmic correction. This paper argues that bias in Large Language Models is a structural reflection of human cognitive patterns, faithfully reproduced from training data encoding decades of human text and communication. The claim is behavioural equivalence, not mechanistic equivalence: LLM outputs exhibit the same bias patterns as their human sources, and for governance purposes the downstream effects are what matter. The paper presents a systematic mapping of human cognitive biases to LLM behaviours and proposes a two-category predictive criterion distinguishing externalised biases (embedded in text, readily transferred) from embodied biases (requiring lived experience, hypothesised not to transfer). Taking RLHF as a case study, it argues that alignment is shallow relative to pretraining distributions. Effective governance requires a shift from pre-deployment certification to continuous post-deployment monitoring, and a psychotechnological discipline bridging cognitive science and AI governance.

title: Econometric Model for Explaining and Predicting National Delegation Performance at the Summer Olympic Games (1992–2024): Out-of-Sample Validation and Projections for Los Angeles 2028

detail.title: Econometric Model for Explaining and Predicting National Delegation Performance at the Summer Olympic Games (1992–2024): Out-of-Sample Validation and Projections for Los Angeles 2028
detail.abstract: This paper updates, validates, and extends a multiple OLS regression model originally estimated by Ramírez Barajas (2015–2017) to explain and predict national delegation performance at the Summer Olympic Games. The model was estimated using data from Barcelona 1992 to London 2012 and its coefficients were frozen. In 2026, the model is applied—without any re-estimation—to three Olympic editions that did not exist at the time of construction: Rio 2016, Tokyo 2020, and Paris 2024. Out-of-sample validation yields average prediction errors below 5% for most high-performing delegations, confirming genuine predictive power. The model incorporates GDP, Human Development Index (HDI), total athletes per edition, and a three-phase host-country effect (pre-hosting, hosting, post-hosting). Beyond coefficients, the most relevant structural finding is the emergence of a performance taxonomy: predictable performers, systematic under-performers (notably Mexico), and systematic over-performers (notably Kenya, Jamaica, Cuba, and Ethiopia). The paper concludes with publicly verifiable quantitative projections for Los Angeles 2028 for all countries with available data.

title: Race, Anti-Americanism, and US-China Rivalry: A Conjoint Experiment in China

detail.title: Race, Anti-Americanism, and US-China Rivalry: A Conjoint Experiment in China

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was provided by the University of Kent Research Ethics board
declarations.funderStatement: Funded by the University of Kent

detail.abstract: What do increasing tensions with the United States mean for anti-Americanism and xenophobia in China? We currently have a limited understanding of Chinese attitudes towards foreigners, nor how these attitudes may be affected by the country’s international relations. Through a conjoint experiment I show that Chinese people view foreigners – and Americans in particular – less favourably than fellow Chinese nationals, but that race plays a minimal role in their evaluations of foreigners. Following prompts about the United States, however, survey respondents became significantly more negative towards American, White, and Black people in China, both in absolute terms and in relation to other nationalities and races. The findings demonstrate the central role of geopolitics in amplifying the salience of race and stimulating more negative views towards (some) foreigners in China, and the risks of rising prejudice and distrust in the face of intensifying global rivalry.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Financial Services: Applications, Opportunities, and Risks

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in Financial Services: Applications, Opportunities, and Risks

declarations.funderStatement: This research was prepared as part of coursework at the Institute of Management Sciences, University of Lucknow.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence and machine learning have become integral to modern financial services, transforming how institutions manage risk, detect fraud, and execute trades. This paper examines AI applications across three critical domains: algorithmic trading and market prediction, credit risk assessment and underwriting, and fraud detection. While AI delivers substantial efficiency gains—enabling institutions like JPMorgan Chase to reduce contract review time from 360,000 hours to seconds, and Renaissance Technologies to achieve 66% average annual returns through quantitative strategies—it also introduces material risks including model opacity, systemic correlation, data bias, and regulatory gaps. We analyze benefits such as speed, scalability, and improved risk detection alongside challenges including algorithmic bias in lending decisions, unexplainable black-box models, and governance ambiguities. Despite AI's remarkable progress, human judgment remains irreplaceable in financial decision-making, particularly for novel market regimes, ethical trade-offs, and institutional accountability. This paper concludes that sustainable competitive advantage lies not in deploying AI alone, but in augmenting algorithmic efficiency with robust governance frameworks, independent model audits, bias testing, and human oversight. As AI systems proliferate in finance, responsible innovation—balancing efficiency with stability, and effectiveness with fairness—is essential for protecting market integrity and consumer welfare.

title: Climate risk and credit risk: Nonlinear and state-dependent effects of exposure under climate shocks

detail.title: Climate risk and credit risk: Nonlinear and state-dependent effects of exposure under climate shocks
detail.abstract: We study how climate risk affects credit risk by integrating firm-level exposure and aggregate shocks within a structural framework for real estate investment corporations. We show that higher climate exposure is associated with lower distance-todefault, implying elevated credit risk for more exposed firms even in the absence of large aggregate shocks. We further demonstrate that this effect is state-dependent: the adverse impact of exposure becomes stronger under higher climate shock conditions, as captured by the interaction between exposure and aggregate shocks. In addition, fluctuations in discount rates introduce a common component in asset returns, generating cross-firm dependence in credit risk. Using a panel dataset of J-REITs, we estimate fixed-effects models of distance-to-default and document both a negative baseline effect of exposure and a negative interaction with climate shocks. Margins-based analysis shows that the sensitivity of distance-to-default to exposure declines monotonically as shocks increase, confirming the state-dependent amplification mechanism. Overall, our findings indicate that climate risk affects not only the level of credit risk but also its responsiveness to aggregate conditions and its co-movement across firms, with implications for risk management and climate stress testing.

title: Bangladesh Green Rural Infrastructure Development (GRID) Programme for Distributed Renewable Energy and Rural Prosperity

detail.title: Bangladesh Green Rural Infrastructure Development (GRID) Programme for Distributed Renewable Energy and Rural Prosperity
detail.abstract:
Bangladesh’s economic growth and urbanization are rapidly increasing electricity demand while exposing the country to rising fuel import dependence and climate risks. At the same time, rural communities, particularly agricultural households, require new income opportunities and resilient infrastructure to support sustainable development.

The Bangladesh Green Rural Infrastructure Development (GRID) Programme proposes a national distributed renewable energy initiative integrating agrivoltaic solar generation with agricultural land use. The program aims to install 20 kW of agrivoltaic capacity for 5% of agricultural households nationwide, enabling farmers to produce electricity while maintaining crop cultivation.

According to the Agriculture Census 2019, Bangladesh has approximately 16.88 million agricultural households. If 5% of these households participate, the GRID  Programme would deploy 17GW of installed capacity as outlined below:

Indicator : Estimate
Participating households: 844,000
Solar capacity per household: 20 kW
Total installed solar capacity: 17 GW
Estimated electricity generation: 22–24 TWh annually

This initiative would represent one of the largest decentralized renewable energy programmes in the developing world, strengthening national energy security while democratizing electricity ownership across rural communities.

Beyond energy generation, the programme would support rural income growth, climate mitigation, agricultural productivity, and carbon credit trading positioning Bangladesh as a global leader in integrated food-energy systems.

reference: Journal of the Copyright Society of the U.S.A., Volume 69, pp. 107-122
title: The Copyright Limitations of The 2020 Copyright Law of China: A Satisfactory Compromise?

detail.title: The Copyright Limitations of The 2020 Copyright Law of China: A Satisfactory Compromise?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of the Copyright Society of the U.S.A., Volume 69, pp. 107-122

detail.abstract: After almost a decade of discussion, public consultation, and legal debate, the third revision of the Copyright Law of China (“CLC”) was finally passed on November 11, 2020 and entered into effect on June 1, 2021. The 2020 CLC made many major revisions to clauses related to the definition of works, the protected rights of the owner of copyright and neighboring rights, and the copyright exceptions. The law also added new clauses related to punitive damages. These topics are properly addressed by other participants to this Special Issue.

title: AI Originality Revisited: Can We Prompt Copyright over AI-Generated Pictures?

detail.title: AI Originality Revisited: Can We Prompt Copyright over AI-Generated Pictures?
detail.abstract: With the advent of large language models (LLMs) that can generate qualified content, such as images based on text prompts, the threat posed by AI creativity has become imminent. Courts and institutions in the US and China have provided different answers with regard to the copyrightability of prompt-based images. This article argues that the judicial recognition of text-to-image copyrightability at the current stage is dangerous. Not only is the practice not in accordance with our traditional understanding of originality and the author-work relationship; it also fails to consider the collateral consequences of such a finding. Perfectly regulating AI-generated content (AIGC) may be beyond the judiciary's capacity, as the solutions are provided within an ill-suited framework. It would be preferable for legislators to engage in thorough discussions with stakeholders to develop a considered regulatory plan first, which does not necessarily have to revolve around copyright.

reference: Singapore Journal of Legal Studies, Volume 2026, March issue, pp. 77-106
title: Three Obstacles to AI-Generated Content Copyrightability

detail.title: Three Obstacles to AI-Generated Content Copyrightability

publicationDetails.detailsText: Singapore Journal of Legal Studies, Volume 2026, March issue, pp. 77-106

detail.abstract: Prompt-based AI creativity is redefining how expressive works are produced, posing novel challenges for copyright law. This article identifies three major obstacles standing in the way of AI copyrightability. First, the lack of meaningful human control in prompt-based AI creation undercuts the traditional requirement of human authorship. The cross-categorical nature of generative AI outputs also exposes a fundamental mismatch with copyright's theoretical design. Second, recognising copyright in machine-created outputs risks creating unjustified windfalls for users who claim authorship without true creative contribution, undermining copyright's incentive structure. Third, protecting AI outputs under copyright without distinction has broader creative and social consequences, including cognitive offloading, reduced authenticity, and stagnation in artistic diversity, which could erode the value of human creativity. This article recommends that future regulation preserve human-centred authorship in copyright law, implement transparency mechanisms for AI-assisted creations, and avoid overextending copyright in ways that erode the value of human creativity.

title: Off the Books, Off the Hook? COVID-19, Labor-Tax Evasion, and Firms' Employment Response
affiliations: BI Norwegian Business School, Stockholm School of Economics in Riga and

detail.title: Off the Books, Off the Hook? COVID-19, Labor-Tax Evasion, and Firms' Employment Response
detail.abstract: This paper studies how labor-tax evasion affects firms' employment responses to large negative shocks. We focus on wage underreporting through "envelope wages", which provides firms with a flexible wage-adjustment margin outside the legal framework. Using the COVID-19 pandemic as an exogenous shock, we analyze firm-level employment dynamics in Latvia, where wage underreporting is widespread but fully informal employment is rare. We combine administrative and survey data with supervised machine learning techniques to classify firms as tax-compliant or tax-evading before the pandemic. We find that tax-evading firms experience smaller employment contractions at the onset of the crisis, particularly among small firms and in competitive sectors. Worker-level evidence for minimum-wage employees is consistent with adjustment through undeclared pay. Our results suggest that in economies with pervasive wage underreporting, standard labor-market statistics may understate the true incidence of large aggregate shocks on workers.

title: An Explicit Solution to Black-Scholes Implied Volatility

detail.title: An Explicit Solution to Black-Scholes Implied Volatility
detail.abstract: This paper observes that the Black-Scholes call price can be written as the survival probability of an inverse Gaussian distribution, equivalently as a probability in variance space. Inverting this representation yields an analytically explicit formula for implied volatility in terms of the corresponding inverse Gaussian quantile function, with volatility on the left-hand side and only observable option inputs on the right-hand side. Numerical tests recover implied volatility to machine precision and, in a controlled setting, show the formula to be faster than a state-of-the-art benchmark.

title: Peace as an Engineered Outcome: Incentives, Risk Asymmetry, and War Decisions. Toward a Complete System of Economic Guarantees of Peace Series IV: Decision-Making and Security Architecture Working Paper No. 2 Work in Progress -May 2026 Affiliation: International Institute of Political Philosophy (Kyiv, Ukraine) Author

detail.abstract: This work, from the series on decision-making, is based on the concept of rational choice, which assumes the comparison of expected benefits and costs. However, it is necessary to take into account the persistent asymmetry in the perception of gains and losses demonstrated by decision-makers. This asymmetry creates a dangerous bias toward risky decisions, including military actions, and existing deterrence mechanisms based on punishment are insufficient. We have proposed the thesis about the necessity of introducing into the security system a guaranteed gain from peaceful behavior as a missing element of the decision comparison base. This preprint is devoted to the concretization of this idea for constructing a system of targeted influence on the decision-making process of national leaders, as well as the orientation of possible gains and losses directly toward them.

title: Conceptual Analysis of Emergent Decision Structures in Constrained Sociotechnical Systems

detail.title: Conceptual Analysis of Emergent Decision Structures in Constrained Sociotechnical Systems
detail.abstract: Many sociotechnical systems operate under strong ex ante commitments while exhibiting heterogeneous and conflicting outcomes ex post. In such settings, architectural choices, contractual structures, and design constraints embed particular forms of rationality prior to operation, while realized outcomes unfold under uncertainty and multi-dimensional evaluation. Despite this, decision and design are often framed as the selection of optimal solutions-an abstraction that becomes inadequate when outcomes are not individually chosen and conflict persists within the admissible space. This paper adopts a structural perspective that focuses on the geometry of outcome spaces induced by ex ante commitments rather than on individual trajectories or optimization procedures. Using well-documented sociotechnical systems as observational evidence, the analysis shows that admissible outcome spaces across distinct domains exhibit persistent internal conflict, lack a natural total ordering, and give rise to central operating regions as a structural consequence of embedded constraints. A connected automated vehicle system and prefixed financial commitments are examined as cross-domain observations of this phenomenon. The contribution is diagnostic rather than prescriptive. By making explicit how decision structures are embedded in system design and how non-intentional regularities emerge from constrained outcome spaces, the paper clarifies the limits of solution-centric abstractions and offers a structural lens for understanding decision and design in complex systems.

title: The Effect of Corporate Cash Accumulation on Monetary Policy Transmission: A Stock-flow Consistent Growth Model

detail.title: The Effect of Corporate Cash Accumulation on Monetary Policy Transmission: A Stock-flow Consistent Growth Model
detail.abstract: This paper causally shows that non-financial corporate liquidity dampens monetary policy transmission. While standard analyses of financial heterogeneity rely on exposure-based estimates, I additionally employ Granular Instrumental Variables (GIV) to overcome endogeneity concerns. GIVs exploit idiosyncratic shocks to the largest corporate cash holding firms to identify exogenous variation in the aggregate cash ratio. I then develop a stock-flow consistent growth model to identify the structural conditions under which corporate cash accumulation weakens transmission. These results have direct implications for the effectiveness of monetary policy and motivate the inclusion of corporate liquidity into mechanisms like the financial accelerator and investment functions.

title: What Changes First? Competitive Performance-Based Funding, Institutional Discourse, and the Sequencing of University Change: Evidence from South Korea

detail.title: What Changes First? Competitive Performance-Based Funding, Institutional Discourse, and the Sequencing of University Change: Evidence from South Korea
detail.abstract: Competitive performance-based funding (PBF) programs are widely used to steer university behavior, yet systematic evaluations consistently report mixed or modest effects on the outcomes they target. I develop a sequencing account of university response: under dense accountability architectures, institutional planning discourse aligns with program vocabulary first, observable organizational inputs shift next, and longer-cycle outcomes respond last and most slowly. Drawing on two purpose-built data sources from South Korea's University Innovation Support Program (UISP), the paper examines this sequence in a setting where institution-wide planning, funding, and recurring performance review are tightly coupled. The findings make visible the intermediate phases of institutional response and suggest that mixed short-run effects in PBF research may reflect when evaluations are conducted rather than whether programs are effective.

title: Spotting "Washing": Can Financial Experts Detect The "Say-Do Gap" In Banking Reports? *
affiliations: Bank of Israel, Hebrew University, Jerusalem Israel and Radboud University

detail.title: Spotting "Washing": Can Financial Experts Detect The "Say-Do Gap" In Banking Reports? *

declarations.ethicsApproval: There is an Ethic approval and pre registretion.

detail.abstract: Can financial experts detect potential greenwashing in ESG communications? Using an eye-tracking experiment with 128 professionals, we document a novel attention-detection-recommendation chain. Attention to textual contradictions increases expert detection sensitivity, significantly reducing investment recommendations. Framing impacts this chain in two distinct ways relative to a control condition: ESG exposure amplifies attention to contradictions, heightening detection-a domain-specific focusing effect; but ESG framing partially buffers the detection-to-investment penalty. Additional results reveal a skepticism paradox: media awareness counterintuitively reduces detection. Two mechanisms, both shaped by management communication design, allow greenwashing to persist under expert evaluation: inattention to embedded contradictions, and a warm-glow halo that attenuates the investment penalty of detection.

title: Structural Concentration of Collapse Events in High-Ω Regimes

detail.title: Structural Concentration of Collapse Events in High-Ω Regimes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests declared.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available aggregated or market data and does not involve human subjects or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding.

detail.abstract: We present a minimal, reproducible test for structural concentration of collapse events. Using fixed ex-ante definitions, we evaluate whether collapse events occur uniformly or concentrate in high-Ω states. Across multiple domains, collapse events consistently exhibit strong concentration in high-Ω regimes. The protocol defines Ω as the product of structural dispersion and directional change, and evaluates P(collapse | high Ω) against the baseline probability. All definitions are fixed prior to evaluation, and no parameter tuning or model fitting is performed. Empirical results across power systems, financial markets, earthquakes, weather, and traffic data show that collapse events occur more frequently in high-Ω states than in the overall dataset. This finding holds under a unified minimal protocol. This framework does not aim to predict events or establish causal mechanisms. It provides a reproducible method for detecting a structural distributional property of extreme events.

title: The Scarcity Foundation of Value: Productivity, Entropy, and the Structural Mass of Returns

detail.title: The Scarcity Foundation of Value: Productivity, Entropy, and the Structural Mass of Returns

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, patients, or case studies requiring ethics approval. All data used are publicly available.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently, without external funding or institutional support.

detail.abstract: Mainstream economic thought often elevates productivity, the ability to transform inputs into valuable outputs, to the fundamental origin of asset value. This paper challenges that primacy. We argue that value originates fundamentally from economic scarcity, while productivity serves as its necessary maintenance cost. While all assets require productive input in their creation and upkeep, it is constrained access that structurally enables and sustains monetization. We mathematically formalize this relationship by defining monetizable value as the Lagrangian shadow price of a binding scarcity constraint. We then introduce a thermodynamic kinematics of value, modeling abundance as a state of maximum structural entropy and scarcity as a highly ordered low-entropy state. Within this framework, productivity acts as the thermodynamic work required to forge and maintain that constraint against entropic diffusion. Building on the kinematic machinery established in Papadogiannis (2026b), where the expected gross return is factored as R t,T = (1+c t) T-t K t,T and the Asset Opportunity Space (Ω t , the integrated finite volume of tradable alpha available to arbitrageurs) is derived as Ω t = η|c t |/λ from a structural baseline c t treated as an observer's ontological primitive, this paper grounds that primitive in the microeconomics of scarcity. We show that the structural mass of returns, |c t |, is exactly the expected geometric growth rate of the monetized scarcity state, establishing that scarcity provides the structural mass which market inefficiency converts into tradable alpha across all asset classes.

title: Facilitating credit is the most important function of Money: A role for Bitcoin?

detail.title: Facilitating credit is the most important function of Money: A role for Bitcoin?
detail.abstract: Money serves several roles: a medium of exchange to buy and sell without bartering; a unit of account to price goods consistently; a store of value to save purchasing power over time; a means to defer payment of future obligations like credit or loans. An agent based computer simulation program determine quantitatively the relative importance of these services. The main results showed that money for credit was by far the feature that achieved the largest overall production of wealth in the simulated societies. A conclusion from this study suggests that fomenting the use of internationally tradable currencies such as Bitcoin seems to be most promising pathway for international economic growth in the near future.

reference: Bank of Italy Economic History Working Paper No. 55
title: L’Italia e la crisi della golden age. La politica monetaria italiana dalla metà degli anni Sessanta alla vigilia dello SME (1965-1978) (Italy and the crisis of the 'golden age')

detail.title: L’Italia e la crisi della golden age. La politica monetaria italiana dalla metà degli anni Sessanta alla vigilia dello SME (1965-1978) (Italy and the crisis of the 'golden age')

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Economic History Working Paper No. 55
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Italian Abstract: Il lavoro esamina le vicende monetarie italiane tra la metà degli anni Sessanta e la fine dei Settanta, inquadrandole nella crisi dell’«età dell’oro» dello sviluppo economico occidentale e considerando le specificità che resero l’esperienza italiana in parte diversa da quella di altri paesi. Il saggio documenta l’ampiezza degli interventi con cui la Banca d’Italia attuò la politica di stabilizzazione dei tassi d’interesse a lungo termine nella seconda metà degli anni Sessanta e nei primi Settanta; mostra che l’orientamento accomodante seguito nel periodo precedente alla crisi petrolifera, e in alcuni momenti della fase successiva, derivò non solo dalle difficoltà di finanziamento del fabbisogno pubblico, ma anche da una precisa scelta di politica monetaria; esamina il parziale riequilibrio macroeconomico della parte finale del decennio. Un tema di fondo, infine, è costituito dalle vicissitudini del mercato obbligazionario, che interagirono con la politica monetaria e contribuirono ai problemi di stabilità finanziaria emersi intorno alla metà degli anni Settanta.

English Abstract: This paper examines Italian monetary events between the mid-1960s and the late 1970s in the context of the crisis of the ‘golden age’ of Western economic development, also considering the factors that made the Italian experience somewhat different from that of other countries. The essay documents the pervasiveness of the interventions through which Banca d’Italia carried out the policy of stabilizing long-term interest rates in the second half of the 1960s and in the early 1970s. It goes on to show that monetary accommodation in the period preceding the oil crisis of 1973, as well as in certain moments of the subsequent phase, was due not only to the increasing borrowing needs of the State, but also to a precise monetary policy choice; lastly, it examines the partial macroeconomic re-balancing of the late 1970s. The vicissitudes of the bond market – which interacted with monetary policy and contributed to the financial stability problems that emerged towards the mid-1970s – are an important thread of this analysis.

title: New evidence on the macroeconomic, fiscal and political drivers of sovereign bond spreads in the EMU

detail.title: New evidence on the macroeconomic, fiscal and political drivers of sovereign bond spreads in the EMU
detail.abstract: This paper assesses the relevance of macroeconomic, fiscal and political factors as determinants of sovereign yield spreads for 15 Euro Area Member States, using quarterly data for the period Q1:1999–Q4:2024. The results show that fiscal fundamentals, inflation and liquidity stress are the main drivers of spreads, while the QE regime reduced the sensitivity of spreads to debt levels. Political influences are selective: electoral periods raise sovereign risk only in highly indebted countries, whereas liberalising reforms are associated with lower spreads. Overall, the findings highlight the regime‑dependent nature of sovereign risk pricing and provide updated evidence on how fiscal and political information is incorporated under different policy environments, offering a clearer understanding of how markets reassess sovereign risk as institutional and macro‑financial conditions evolve.

title: Cognitive Distance in Document Submission Systems: Why Users Struggle With Simple Digital Tasks

detail.title: Cognitive Distance in Document Submission Systems: Why Users Struggle With Simple Digital Tasks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. The research was conducted independently, without involvement from commercial entities, sponsors, or organizations that could introduce bias in the formulation, analysis, or interpretation of the proposed concepts.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, patient data, or identifiable personal information. As such, formal ethics approval was not required. The work is theoretical and based on analysis of existing literature and conceptual development.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was developed independently by the author as part of ongoing academic and conceptual investigation.

detail.abstract:
Document submission workflows are common interaction patterns in contemporary information systems, including public services, finance, healthcare, and digital platforms. Despite their apparent simplicity, these workflows often generate confusion, repeated failure, and task abandonment. Existing usability frameworks often interpret such outcomes primarily in terms of complexity, insufficient skill, or inadequate training. Although these explanations remain important, they do not fully account for breakdowns that persist even in systems designed to reduce apparent cognitive load.

This paper examines document submission systems through the lens of cognitive distance, defined here as the degree of separation between a system’s conceptual structure and the mental model constructed by the user during interaction. Building on prior work that conceptualizes and provisionally operationalizes cognitive distance, the paper develops a qualitative analytical case centered on file-upload interactions. The analysis illustrates how routine design choices, including file-format restrictions, file-size constraints, and ambiguous terminology, can produce systematic misalignment between system logic and user understanding.

The paper proposes the analytic term externalized processing to describe a recurring pattern in which systems shift reasonably automatable preprocessing tasks, such as format conversion and file compression, to users. This shift increases procedural effort and introduces additional interpretive burden, often forcing users to rely on external tools, trial-and-error strategies, or informal workarounds to complete otherwise ordinary tasks.

The paper argues that many breakdowns in document submission workflows, as reconstructed here, are not merely incidental design defects but can reflect a broader problem in how preprocessing work is distributed between users and systems. The analysis suggests that reducing cognitive distance requires reallocating appropriate preprocessing functions back to systems, improving conceptual transparency, and aligning system behavior more closely with user reasoning. The contribution is analytical rather than experimental: it extends cognitive distance into a concrete interaction domain and identifies externalized processing as a recurring allocation pattern through which system-side constraints become user-side preprocessing accompanied by interpretive burden.

title: Addenda A & B to Judgment, Automation, and Translation Risk: Legislative and Supervisory Developments

detail.title: Addenda A & B to Judgment, Automation, and Translation Risk: Legislative and Supervisory Developments
detail.abstract: This addendum documents legislative and supervisory developments that occurred independently of the working paper Judgment, Automation, and Translation Risk. It does not extend the framework, provide empirical validation, or alter the paper's theoretical conclusions. Addendum A discusses the Dutch Accountancy Sector Amendment Act (Wijzigingswet accountancysector), expected to enter into force in July 2026, and analyses its governance instruments-including audit quality indicators-through the lens of the paper's three-risk framework. Addendum B examines the proposed Dutch implementation of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, focusing on the implications of a multi-authority supervisory structure for deployer obligations and accountability. The purpose of these addenda is to record convergence between the paper's conceptual diagnosis and subsequent regulatory responses, and to identify new or clarified governance instruments that warrant attention when the framework is applied in practice, particularly by boards and audit committees. The addenda are descriptive and contextual; they do not alter the framework's theoretical propositions or validity conditions.

title: Fighting Misinformation: Super-Spreaders, Learning, and Optimal Education Policies

detail.title: Fighting Misinformation: Super-Spreaders, Learning, and Optimal Education Policies
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the optimal public strategies to mitigate the spread of fake news by integrating education and fact-checking into a behavioral compartmental model. Building on an SVIR framework, we incorporate endogenous learning and reputational feedback, while explicitly modeling super-spreaders who disproportionately amplify misinformation. We formulate a dynamic optimal control problem in which the government chooses the optimal investment rate in education and fact-checking to minimize societal costs, which include the vulnerable population, reputational penalties, and the economic costs of interventions. Numerical simulations illustrate the interplay between learning, super-spreader dynamics, and public interventions, highlighting how targeted educational policies can effectively reduce misinformation diffusion and optimize resource allocation for long-term societal benefits. The results offer both theoretical and practical insights into designing policies to combat the viral spread of fake news in the digital age.

title: Mean Group Estimation for Large Panel Data models with Localized Parameter Heterogeneity and Cross-sectional Dependence

detail.title: Mean Group Estimation for Large Panel Data models with Localized Parameter Heterogeneity and Cross-sectional Dependence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I acknowledge that this paper, which is part of my PhD work, was funded by the Co-funded Monash Graduate Scholarship
declarations.funderStatement: Monash University

detail.abstract: This paper builds on the common correlated effects mean group estimator (CCEMG) introduced by Pesaran (2006) for a heterogeneous large-panel model with substantial cross-sectional dependence and negligible within-group heterogeneity. The standard asymptotic theory for this method is established under the assumption that the heterogeneous coefficients follow a random coefficient model. This assumption introduces a large variability to the CCEMG estimator, resulting in an asymptotic distribution that depends solely on the distribution of the model, rather than incorporating the observation error distribution as one might typically expect. In the current study, we modify the random coefficient model assumption and re-establish the asymptotic theory for the CCEMG estimator. We demonstrate that, under the new assumption, the asymptotic distribution depends on the error distribution as well. Moreover, we show that the asymptotic normality is achieved at a faster rate than the standard rate; however, this improvement introduces a bias in the estimator. We then subsequently propose a consistent estimator for the new asymptotic covariance structure. Monte Carlo simulations show that the proposed method is more accurate and efficient than the standard method under various conditions. In an application to examine the impact of weather on wheat yields across five Australian states, our findings reveal that the new method provides stronger statistical evidence consistent with the farmers' expectations.

title: Algorithmic Authority and the Internalisation of Networked Speech: How Influencers Shape Identity, Self-Worth, and Psychological Outcomes

detail.title: Algorithmic Authority and the Internalisation of Networked Speech: How Influencers Shape Identity, Self-Worth, and Psychological Outcomes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is conceptual and does not involve human participants
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops a conceptual framework for understanding how algorithmically curated digital environments function as emergent forms of authority. While social media platforms and influencers are often treated as channels of communication or entertainment, this paper argues that they operate as psychologically potent authority systems shaping identity, self-worth, and behaviour. Unlike traditional authority grounded in institutional legitimacy, algorithmic authority is constituted through visibility, repetition, and engagementdriven amplification, where statistical prominence becomes a proxy for credibility. Drawing on media psychology, social comparison theory, parasocial interaction, and digital sociology, the paper introduces the Algorithmic Authority Internalisation Model (AAIM). This model explains how networked speech-selected and amplified by algorithms-becomes embedded within cognitive and affective processes through social validation, emotional resonance, and repetition. In this way, externally generated messages are transformed into self-referential scripts that shape internal dialogue, self-evaluation, and identity formation. 
The paper further examines the structural ambivalence of networked authority. Algorithmic environments can intensify comparison, shame, and dependency on validation, but also support peer connection, psychoeducation, and the destigmatisation of mental health. The central claim is that the primary risk lies not in exposure to information, but in the unnoticed internalisation of algorithmically amplified language as self-truth. By reframing digital platforms as systems of psychological authority, this paper contributes to interdisciplinary debates on identity, mental health, and the governance of algorithmic influence.

title: The AI Bubble and the Fragile Classroom: Systems Thinking, Cascading Risks, and the Future of Education
affiliations: University of the City of Muntinlupa

detail.title: The AI Bubble and the Fragile Classroom: Systems Thinking, Cascading Risks, and the Future of Education
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become one of the defining forces of the present decade, yet the scale of enthusiasm surrounding it has also revived an older question in technology history: are we witnessing durable transformation, or are we living through a speculative bubble? This article examines the idea of the "AI bubble" through a question-and-answer structure and places special attention on what the issue means for the education sector. Rather than treating the bubble conversation as a purely financial concern, the discussion argues that hype, boom, bust, and policy lag are already affecting schools, universities, teachers, and students. In this article, DVUCA is used as a practical adaptation of the established VUCA framework to emphasize digitally amplified volatility, uncertainty, complexity, and ambiguity in contemporary education.

title: Forecasting Timber Prices in Volatile Markets: An Evaluation of Model Complexity and Temporal Frequency
affiliations: , University of Warsaw and German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv) Halle-Jena-Leipzig

detail.title: Forecasting Timber Prices in Volatile Markets: An Evaluation of Model Complexity and Temporal Frequency

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the National Science Center in Poland (grant no.2021/43/B/HS4/03371).

detail.abstract: Accurate timber price forecasting is crucial for effective forest management and a strategic response to changing commodity markets. This study quantifies the forecasting accuracy of univariate statistical and machine-learning methods at weekly, monthly, and quarterly time intervals using price data on Polish pine sawlogs and pulpwood. We evaluate Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), Exponential Smoothing (ETS), Dynamic Harmonic Regression (DHR), a Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and naive baselines. A major practical issue discussed is whether temporally aggregating weekly forecasts yields better accuracy than direct monthly modeling. Theoretical analysis shows that direct monthly modeling is almost always better than upward aggregation, since higher-frequency data is statistically noisier, which leads to degradation of predictive accuracy at lower frequencies. In a purely univariate context, statistical models perform better than the LightGBM model, which indicates that, in order to be able to reveal meaningful signals, machine learning models need access to exogenous macroeconomic variables. Furthermore, we quantify model resilience during the COVID-19 structural market break. While all models failed to predict the unprecedented price surge, the simple naive baseline adapted to newly established price levels much faster than parametric models retaining outdated pre-shock distributions. Ultimately, for long-term strategic planning, direct monthly modeling using ARIMA or a naive baseline remains the most reliable and efficient approach for forestry organizations.

title: Pervasiveness and Predictors of Stress Among Healthcare Workers in Managing Covid-19 Pandemic
affiliations: and TKM College of Arts and Science - Department of Commerce

detail.title: Pervasiveness and Predictors of Stress Among Healthcare Workers in Managing Covid-19 Pandemic

declarations.declarationOfInterest: nil
declarations.ethicsApproval: nil
declarations.funderStatement: nil

detail.abstract: The corona virus (Covid-19) started its outset in the winter of late December 2019. The Covid-19 Corona virus was first identified in China's Hubei province later making it worldwide spread 2019 and has become a global threat impacting 213 countries with 17,194,261 cases as on July 2020. In India the first case of corona virus (Covid-19) was reported on 30 th January 2020.The novel corona virus (Covid-19) has been declared as global pandemic on March 11, 2020 by the World health organization (WHO) as it continues to rapidly spread around in the world. The covid-19 outburst followed by a lockout has seriously affected the Indian economy particularly the financial system. There is no sector which is left from this dreadful pandemic making the economy upside down within the short period of time. Most notably it has influenced the individual's social life. Healthcare sector which is the epicenter of dealing with virus has been worst affected. The healthcare facility providers who are acting as warriors to control the spread of pandemic are also disturbed by the unexpected dreadful pandemic Covid-19.Thus the Research paper analyses healthcare workers issue in managing the current Covid-19 pandemic and also tried to diagnose the psychological and social impact of Covid-19 on the mental health of Healthcare workers. For the purpose of the study secondary data was used. The data was collected from various websites, journal articles, and newspaper reports and by reviewing existing literature. The findings of the study states that health related factors and many factors have impacted healthcare workers mental health which includes fear of infection, far from family, increased workload, stress, depression, shortage of medical equipment, frequently changing of testing techniques and lack of motivation. The study also reveals that Covid-19 pandemic has created anxiety, fear, uncertainty and insecurity among all the people in the world.

title: Gold vs Equities vs Real Estate: Which Asset Class Best Hedges Against Inflation in India? (2000–2024)

detail.title: Gold vs Equities vs Real Estate: Which Asset Class Best Hedges Against Inflation in India? (2000–2024)
detail.abstract:
Background: Inflation erodes real purchasing power, yet Indian households continue to allocate substantial savings to gold, real estate, and bank deposits – often without a clear understanding of which asset class has historically protected wealth after adjusting for inflation.

Methods: This study examines annual real (inflation‑adjusted) returns of three asset classes in India from financial year 2000–01 to 2023–24: domestic 24‑karat gold (IBJA data), BSE Sensex equities (RBI and BSE data), and residential real estate (NHB RESIDEX index from 2007 onward). Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation from World Bank / Macrotrends is used to calculate real returns using the formula Real Return = [(1+Nominal Return)/(1+Inflation)]–1. Performance is compared across three high‑inflation episodes: the Global Financial Crisis (2008–09), the chronic inflation period (2010–13), and the post‑COVID supply shock (2020–22).

Results: Over the full 24‑year period, equities delivered the highest average real return (≈9.5% per year) but with extreme volatility (–45% in 2008–09). Gold provided a modest average real return (≈3.2%) but was the only asset with positive real returns during the 2008–09 crisis (+11%) and the 2010–13 inflation spike. Real estate showed wide regional variation: Pune and Bengaluru recorded 2–3% real returns, while Delhi‑NCR and Mumbai barely kept pace with inflation.

Conclusions: No single asset dominates all time horizons. Equities are superior for long‑term (10+ years) wealth creation; gold is a reliable short‑term inflation hedge, especially during crises; real estate is highly city‑specific and should not be treated as a generic inflation hedge. The findings support a diversified portfolio approach rather than reliance on any single asset class.

title: Geopolitical Risk, Firm Expectations, and Supply-Chain Propagation
affiliations: Government of the Republic of Turkey - Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey and Sabanci University

detail.title: Geopolitical Risk, Firm Expectations, and Supply-Chain Propagation
detail.abstract: We study how geopolitical risk affects firms' expectations and real activity through international trade exposure and domestic production networks, using administrative microdata. Higher geopolitical risk has stagflationary effects at the firm level: firms revise inflation, price, and unit-cost expectations upward while lowering expectations about sales, investment, employment, and the macroeconomic outlook. The effects are asymmetric across the source of exposure. Import-side geopolitical risk operates primarily through a cost-push and input-supply channel, generating stronger increases in price and cost expectations and larger declines in purchases and imports. Export-side geopolitical risk operates primarily through a foreign-demand channel, generating stronger declines in expected sales, investment, and exports. These expectation revisions are reflected in realized firm outcomes and propagate through domestic supply chains, with supplier-side exposure transmitting cost pressures and customer-side exposure transmitting demand weakness. Overall, geopolitical risk is not confined to directly exposed firms; it spreads through trade and production networks.

title: Small Business and Economic Development of Bangladesh. A Case Study on Chittagong

detail.title: Small Business and Economic Development of Bangladesh. A Case Study on Chittagong

declarations.funderStatement: This research paper was funded by my self. including my savings and from my family members. 60% of total funding was taken from my family members and rest of that was from my personal fund.

detail.abstract: This research paper examines the impact of small businesses on economic development in Chittagong, Bangladesh. A quantitative primary data collection method was employed, utilizing a sampling design that involved 150 small business owners through the use of structured survey instruments. The data were analyzed using hypothesis testing techniques. Regression analysis was conducted to examine the determinants of small business profitability. The results reveal that the food sector plays a significant role in small business development in the Chittagong region. In addition, lack of infrastructure and settlement issues emerge as major challenges faced by entrepreneurs. The analysis further suggests that education enhances entrepreneurs' ability to respond to market dynamics and utilize resources more efficiently. The study adds to the existing SME literature and offers valuable implications and contributions for entrepreneurial performance through educational and training programs.

reference: NHH Dept. of Economics Discussion Paper No. 06/2026
title: Neighborhoods, Family and Intergenerational Mobility
affiliations: NHH Norwegian School of Economics - Department of Economics, University of Chicago - Department of Economics and Brown University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Neighborhoods, Family and Intergenerational Mobility

publicationDetails.detailsText: NHH Dept. of Economics Discussion Paper No. 06/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Norwegian School of Economics, Department of Economics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: To what extent do childhood neighborhoods shape long-run socio-economic outcomes, and through which mechanisms? Using the quasi-random assignment of refugee children across neighborhoods in Denmark, we show that exposure to higher-quality neighborhoods—as measured by average neighborhood income and the wage outcomes of permanent resident children—raises labor force participation and market income in adulthood. Beyond economic integration, better neighborhoods further promote social integration by increasing educational attainment and naturalization. Applying a causal mediation analysis, we reject full mediation via neighborhood and school characteristics but not via parental income, pointing to the family as a fundamental mediator of neighborhood effects.

title: BigTech Credit and Platform Economic Activity
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE), National University of Singapore - NUS Business School,  and City University of Hong Kong, School of Data Science

detail.title: BigTech Credit and Platform Economic Activity
detail.abstract: BigTech firms increasingly integrate financial services into their platform ecosystems, raising a central question: how this integration affects firms’ core business activity. Using a large-scale field experiment at one of the world’s largest e-commerce platforms (over 2.5 million individual-month observations), we estimate the causal effects of marginal expansions in access to embedded credit. We find that credit access increases user economic activity—raising intensity and persistence, stabilizing demand, and expanding consumption scope—with little evidence of consumption upgrading or increased delinquency. Our results show that embedded credit reinforces the platform’s core operations, highlighting complementarities in modern digital ecosystems.

title: The Health Cost of Export-Led Pollution: Evidence on Birth Weight
affiliations: Baskent University and Catholic University of Milan

detail.title: The Health Cost of Export-Led Pollution: Evidence on Birth Weight
detail.abstract:
This paper studies how the pollution content of exports affects infant health in a middle-income country,
Turkiye. We exploit variation in export-related pollution across Turkish provinces and examine its
effects on infants' birth weight, a key early-life health outcome. Our analysis combines microdata on
infants' health outcomes reported by mothers with monthly provincial export data and product-specific
emissions intensity indicators. Thanks to the availability of firm-to-firm transaction data, the measure
of provincial export-led pollution reflects indirect exports in addition to direct exports. We find that
higher exposure to export-driven pollution during pregnancy is associated with lower birth weights,
pointing to adverse health effects induced by environmental pressure from foreign demand shocks.
The negative effect is more pronounced when exposure occurs during the second and third trimesters of
pregnancy. These results are robust to alternative measures of export-led pollution, additional controls
addressing potential omitted variables, and falsification tests. The effects are particularly pronounced
among infants born to less-educated mothers and households with lower socioeconomic status.

title: Structure-Preserving Neural Operators: Symplecticity, Dissipativity, and Positivity as Operator-Level Constraints

detail.title: Structure-Preserving Neural Operators: Symplecticity, Dissipativity, and Positivity as Operator-Level Constraints
