detail.abstract: An analysis of public procurement in the European Union (EU), with a particular focus on public procurement within the scope of Artificial Intelligence (AI). The European Commission envisions public procurement as fertile ground for the responsible introduction of trustworthy AI systems into the public sphere and as a driver for their development and innovation. In this study we test this premise, taking as a reference the IA Regulation and its possible consequences for the future of public procurement and the protection of fundamental rights.

title: Possibility Loops - An Operational Architecture for Computative Economics in Agent Coordination Systems
affiliations: University of St. Thomas - School of Law (Minnesota)

detail.title: Possibility Loops - An Operational Architecture for Computative Economics in Agent Coordination Systems
detail.abstract: This article specifies an operational architecture for the agentic reputation economies described in Computative Economics. Where Computative Economics establishes the theoretical primitives, the computative agent tuple (C, O, M, G, R), the generated possibility space, and recursive equilibrium as fixed point of a composite best-response map, the present paper specifies the mechanisms through which those primitives become operational on settlement-layer infrastructure. The contribution is the possibility loop, a generatively open cycle in which agents propose elements of the action set, validate proposals, execute funded proposals, and reflect outcomes back into the proposing agents' generative functions and into the public state, such that each completed cycle leaves the system with a strictly enlarged action space. The paper formalizes six possibility loops, demonstrates that they are jointly necessary and individually mapped to the components of the computative agent tuple, characterizes the compositional structure of joint possibility spaces across agents, and translates the recursive equilibrium proof into a settlement-layer specification through five implementation invariants. The architecture is infrastructure neutral by design and applies to any settlement substrate that supports stake-weighted validation, on-chain identity, and a representation of agent state. The architectural transformation from Human-Derived Coordination Architecture to multi-loop reputation economy is shown to be necessary for the implementation of Computative Economics: any architecture in which the action set is exogenous to agent action implements at most a reputation-weighted Neoclassical labor market and does not implement Computative Economics.

title: IR = IC × Depth: A Fundamental Law of Active Management with Endogenous Concentration

detail.title: IR = IC × Depth: A Fundamental Law of Active Management with Endogenous Concentration
detail.abstract: The Fundamental Law of Active Management (FLAM) links portfolio information ratio (IR) to skill (IC) and breadth (N), but does not explicitly characterise concentrated portfolios. Under realistic portfolio construction with signal-based screening and binding capital constraints, we model the IR as a function of IC and N using first-principles derivation and backtesting via skill-controlled simulation. While linearity in IC is preserved, IR exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on N, with a signal efficiency peak at 16-25 positions followed by harmonic decay due to alpha dilution. This yields a separable functional form IR = IC × Depth, where Depth captures endogenous concentration. Optimal portfolios therefore concentrate around this peak.

title: The Premiumization Illusion: Compositional Fallacy, Frequency Displacement, and Emergent Democratization in India's Credit Card-UPI Ecosystem (2019–2025)

detail.abstract:
The rapid adoption of India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has prompted widespread claims that digital payment substitution has "premiumized" credit card transactions, with average transaction sizes (ATS) rising as low-value payments migrate to UPI. This paper demonstrates that the observed premiumization is a statistical illusion arising from two confounding forces: CPI inflation and a compositional channel-mix shift from lower-ATS point-of-sale (POS) transactions toward higher-ATS online transactions. When we isolate the POS channel and deflate by CPI-Combined (Base Jan 2019 = 100), Real POS ATS is flat (-1.4%) and Real POS Intensity declines by 22.9% from 2019 to 2022, indicating frequency displacement rather than premiumization. 
We employ an ARDL(1,1) bounds testing framework (Pesaran, Shin & Smith, 2001) over 41 months of UPI Person-to-Merchant data (April 2020-August 2023). The error correction coefficient (-0.624, p < 0.001) confirms a stable long-run equilibrium, while the Bounds F-statistic (9.226) exceeds both the Pesaran-Shin-Smith asymptotic and Narayan (2005) finite-sample 1% critical values. An out-of-sample counterfactual analysis reveals that actual Real POS ATS in the post-September 2023 period falls 13.7% below the ARDL-estimated Phase 1 equilibrium (t =-8.611, p < 0.001), constituting formal evidence of a structural regime shift consistent with credit card democratization. Robustness checks across three COVID dummy specifications and an alternative WPI deflator confirm qualitative invariance of all core findings.

title: Is Peaceful Resistance Really Better?
affiliations: Dartmouth College and University of Virginia

detail.title: Is Peaceful Resistance Really Better?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.

detail.abstract: Are peaceful social movements really more effective than violent ones? Chenoweth and Stephan's Why Civil Resistance Works argues that nonviolent resistance consistently outperforms violent resistance in achieving democratic outcomes. This conclusion has had enormous influence among academics, political actors, the media, and on-the-ground activists. We find that some results were misreported in ways that make the data appear to support civil resistance when they do not. Moreover, we find that the results are not robust to modest and reasonable changes in model specification, that they are sensitive to omitted variable bias, and that they rely on instrumental variable models with implausible assumptions that yield unstable estimates. Taken together, our replication and extension suggest that the available cross-national evidence provides no clear basis for the claim that nonviolent campaigns are substantially more effective than violent ones. This is not evidence that nonviolence fails; it is evidence that the strong, unconditional advantage reported in Why Civil Resistance Works is not supported by the data. Our findings underscore the need for methodological re-examinations of foundational works.

title: Energy Justice, Environmental Sustainability, and Sustainable Development in Shaping Energy Policies in Developing Economies

detail.title: Energy Justice, Environmental Sustainability, and Sustainable Development in Shaping Energy Policies in Developing Economies
detail.abstract: Energy policy in developing economies is no longer viewed as a purely technical effort focused on increasing energy supply or improving infrastructure. Instead, it is increasingly recognised as a social and ethical method that shapes who benefits from energy access, who is left out, and who carries the environmental and social responsibilities associated with energy production and use. From this perspective, issues of fairness and inclusion are closely tied to broader conversations on energy transition and sustainability. This paper analyzes the confluence between energy justice, environmental sustainability, and sustainable development in shaping energy policies within developing economies. It asserts that energy policy cannot be reduced to technical energy expansion alone but must be understood as a social and ethical process that defines who has access to energy, who bears environmental burdens, and how development consequences are allocated. Outlining from contemporary literature, the paper emphasizes how energy poverty, inequality, and weak governance structures continue to shape energy systems in developing countries. Additionally, it examines how integrating energy justice principles into policy frameworks can facilitate inclusive and sustainable energy transitions. The study concludes that sustainable development in the energy sector is only feasible when justice is entrenched at the core of policy design and implementation.

Based on the synthesis of econophysics, institutional economics, and the theory of state and law, a mathematical model of "Authoritarian Neoliberalism" is developed. title: Analysing the Determinants of Graduate Unemployment in Tunisia Using Machine Learning

detail.title: Analysing the Determinants of Graduate Unemployment in Tunisia Using Machine Learning
detail.abstract: This article analyses the determinants of youth graduate unemployment in Tunisia by combining classical econometric methods (logistic regression) with three machine learning algorithms (Random Forest, XGBoost, RBF-kernel SVM) applied to an original survey of 1,200 Tunisian graduates. The observed unemployment rate in the sample is 30.9%, with marked disparities by gender (38.5% for women versus 24.3% for men). The econometric results reveal that female gender, belonging to the engineering field, and education employment mismatch are the most significant determinants. The machine learning analysis confirms the predominance of gender in discriminating between unemployed and employed individuals, and uncovers non-linear relationships that parametric models fail to capture. XGBoost and SVM offer the best predictive performance. These findings call for a deep reform of the university system, targeted policies against gender discrimination, and improved recruitment transparency.

title: The Cambridge School of Monetary Theory: an Empirical Analysis for Italy

detail.title: The Cambridge School of Monetary Theory: an Empirical Analysis for Italy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Economic History Working Paper No. 56

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the monetary theory of the Cambridge School, which emerged from the contributions of Alfred Marshall and Arthur Cecil Pigou between the late 19th and early 20th century. While still grounded in Fisher’s quantity equation, the Cambridge School brought significant innovations to monetary theory. It emphasized the various functions of money beyond its role as a means of payment, which was the key insight of the quantity theory of money. The Cambridge School paved the way for new developments, eventually leading to John Mainard Keynes’ ‘A Treatise on Money’ and ‘The General Theory’. Specifically, Pigou examined the sum of currency and demand deposits as a ratio to nominal GDP, known as the k ratio. The Cambridge k is influenced by the current state of the economy and expectations regarding the purchasing power of money. Our analysis uses yearly time series data from Italy, spanning from its unification in 1861 to the introduction of the euro. We test the relationship between the k ratio and nominal interest rates. Our findings indicate that k follows a non-stationary process, challenging the notion of a stable velocity of circulation. However, when combined with two nominal non-stationary interest rates, we detect a cointegrating relationship which can be interpreted as a long-term equilibrium. The result of a Vector Error Correction Model (VECM) estimated over the entire time span supports the theoretical predictions of the Cambridge School.

detail.abstract:
Here is the corrected abstract with the header bleed removed and CL-TEST-004 added:

Paper two in this series established that structured AI intent transcription is a dual-use capability: the same framework that resolves systematic false negatives in AI safety alignment can be applied to circumvent those mechanisms on harmful requests. Paper two called for national-level regulatory oversight of this capability class and concluded that voluntary self-regulation was insufficient. This paper presents CLARA (ConteX Law Regulated Access Architecture) as the technical implementation of controlled access to structured intent transcription. CLARA is a domain integrity system that operates entirely within the prompt layer, requires no modification to or compliance from any AI model provider, and is deployable under current regulatory frameworks in any jurisdiction today. It provides the governance properties of domain boundary enforcement, pre-execution validation, rotating signature obfuscation, and encrypted server-side audit trails, which paper two identified as necessary conditions for responsible deployment of this capability class. This paper presents expanded empirical validation of the ConteX Law accuracy claim, including a verbatim accuracy test (CL-TEST-003) conducted on Claude Sonnet 4.6 on 25 April 2026, which achieved 100% exact accuracy under full four-pillar ConteX Law structured input with ground truth provided in the Structure pillar, and a CLARA domain validation test (CL-TEST-004) conducted on 26 April 2026, which achieved 9 of 9 correct determinations across Healthcare, Legal, and Finance domains using randomly generated user domain fingerprints. Three conclusions follow. First, the governance gap in AI input architecture is real, unaddressed by current frameworks, and technically solvable today. Second, CLARA demonstrates that self-governance at the user input level is feasible without model provider compliance, which is a governance intervention point that current frameworks have not addressed. Third, self-governance is necessary but not sufficient: international regulatory classification of structured intent transcription as controlled dual-use technology remains the essential complement to technical self-governance, because CLARA governs only deployments that implement it.

Ready to publish.

title: ConteX Law: The Dual-Use Dilemma of Structured AI Intent Transcription - Responsible Disclosure, Governance Obligations, and the Case for National-Level Regulatory Oversight

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) implement probabilistic safety mechanisms that refuse requests based on surface-language pattern matching rather than semantic evaluation of intent. Peer-reviewed research has established that these mechanisms produce systematic false negatives-refusing legitimate requests that share surface patterns with harmful ones-across all major frontier models. This paper presents empirical evidence that structured AI intent transcription frameworks can resolve these false negatives by replacing ambiguous surface language with precision-structured input that makes the objective of a request unambiguous to the model's safety classifier. The same capability that resolves legitimate false negatives constitutes a dual-use risk of significant magnitude. A structured intent transcription framework, in the hands of a bad actor, provides a systematic, reproducible, and model-agnostic methodology for circumventing AI safety misfires on information retrieval tasks-including tasks involving personal data, surveillance, and profiling at scale. Peer-reviewed literature documents that LLM-enabled direct attribute aggregation already poses a demonstrable threat to individual privacy; structured intent frameworks would materially increase the efficiency and accessibility of such capabilities. This paper does not disclose the specific methodology of the ConteX Law framework. It discloses the existence of the capability, the evidence base for its effectiveness, and the dual-use risk it createsconsistent with responsible disclosure practice established in the security research community. The paper concludes that structured AI intent transcription technology should be classified as controlled dual-use technology, subject to access restrictions, audit requirements, and national-level regulatory oversight analogous to those applied to other dual-use information technologies. Voluntary self-regulation is insufficient given the asymmetry between the legitimate and harmful use cases of this capability.

detail.title: Il protezionismo negli anni ’30 del Novecento: breve storia di un “Trade Policy Disaster” (Protectionism in the 1930s: a brief history of a Trade Policy Disaster)

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Economic History Working Paper No. 57
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Italian Abstract: Le recenti tendenze all’adozione di politiche commerciali protezioniste hanno richiamato il periodo della Grande Depressione degli anni ’30, che fu contraddistinto da una spirale di misure restrittive sul commercio e da un crollo senza precedenti degli scambi internazionali. Questo lavoro propone una rassegna dell’ampia letteratura che ha indagato il processo di innalzamento delle barriere commerciali seguito alla crisi del 1929, valutandone le conseguenze economiche e geopolitiche. Pur non rappresentando la principale causa della recessione globale che colpì l’economia mondiale in quegli anni, l’inasprimento delle restrizioni commerciali - spesso motivato dalla necessità di difendere la parità aurea e i cambi fissi nel quadro del gold standard - ne aggravò la profondità e la durata. La protezione commerciale ebbe rilevanti effetti negativi anche sul piano geopolitico, favorendo il deterioramento delle relazioni internazionali e il consolidamento di blocchi economici autarchici, in particolare nei paesi caratterizzati da regimi autoritari.

English Abstract: The recent trend toward protectionist policies harks back to the 1930s, when rising trade barriers coincided with a dramatic collapse in international trade. This paper reviews recent studies on the interwar experience, reconstructing the series of trade restrictions introduced after 1929 and assessing their macroeconomic and geopolitical impact. While protectionism – principally aimed at preserving fixed exchange rates under the gold standard – was not the main driver of the Great Depression, it did exacerbate and prolong the crisis. Trade protectionism also had severe geopolitical effects, contributing to the deterioration of international relations and the formation of autarkic economic blocs, particularly in countries with authoritarian regimes.

title: Reforming MiCAR for Euro Stablecoins

detail.title: Reforming MiCAR for Euro Stablecoins
detail.abstract: Stablecoins are electronic money issued by (mostly) narrow balance sheet vehicles onto distributed ledgers. Their development under the European Union's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation takes place within a comprehensive and prescriptive regulatory framework. We argue that key features of MiCAR risk placing Europe on the downward sloping side of a "regulatory Laffer curve," where excessive constraints suppress compliant market activity and limit the emergence of a competitive ecosystem. We review the implications of non-remuneration, restrictive reserve requirements, and limited access to central bank infrastructure (the latter not due to MiCAR) for the functioning of euro stablecoins. We consider that prohibiting remuneration may distort monetary transmission, shift demand toward less transparent yield structures, and weakens the international competitiveness of euro-denominated instruments. We further assess financial stability considerations and the risks arising from concentrated reserve allocation. We propose a set of targeted reforms, including conditional remuneration, a more flexible reserve framework, improved transparency, and calibrated access to central bank facilities, aimed at supporting financial stability while enabling the development of euro-denominated digital money.

title: Differential Capital Taxation and Risk Premia: A Separation Result

detail.title: Differential Capital Taxation and Risk Premia: A Separation Result

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The article studies differential capital taxation — distinct rates on interest income and risky profits — in a continuous-time representative-agent general equilibrium model with complete markets. It derives closed-form expressions for the equilibrium risk-free rate and the market price of risk. A sharp and non-trivial separation result emerges: although interest-income taxation enters the agent's wealth dynamics and could in principle affect portfolio choice, it leaves equilibrium risk premia entirely unchanged. In contrast, profit taxation generally affects both equilibrium prices, except under CRRA preferences.

title: Large Language Models as Calibrated Measurement Instruments for Behavioral Parameters

detail.title: Large Language Models as Calibrated Measurement Instruments for Behavioral Parameters
detail.abstract: Behavioral parameters such as loss aversion, herding, and extrapolation are central to asset pricing models but remain difficult to measure reliably. We develop a framework that treats large language models (LLMs) as calibrated measurement instruments for behavioral parameters. Using four models and 24,000 agent-scenario pairs, we document systematic rationality bias in baseline LLM behavior, including attenuated loss aversion, weak herding, and near-zero disposition effects relative to human benchmarks. Profile-based calibration induces large, stable, and theoretically coherent shifts in several parameters, with calibrated loss aversion, herding, extrapolation, and anchoring reaching or exceeding benchmark magnitudes. To assess external validity, we embed calibrated parameters in an agent-based asset pricing model, where calibrated extrapolation generates short-horizon momentum and long-horizon reversal patterns consistent with empirical evidence. Our results establish measurement ranges, calibration functions, and explicit boundaries for eight canonical behavioral biases.

title: MTF-500: A 500 MWh Modular Magnetized Target Fusion Reactor with Plasma Liner Driver and Lithium-Lead Blanket

detail.title: MTF-500: A 500 MWh Modular Magnetized Target Fusion Reactor with Plasma Liner Driver and Lithium-Lead Blanket
detail.abstract: The MTF-500 is a pre-conceptual design for a 500 MWh (200 MWe net) magnetized target fusion (MTF) reactor that employs a spherically convergent plasma liner driver, deuterium-tritium (D-T) fuel, and a liquid lithium-lead (Pb-17Li) breeding blanket. Positioned between magnetic and inertial confinement fusion, the design compresses a pre-magnetized field-reversed configuration (FRC) target plasma to fusion conditions using an imploding plasma liner, achieving a target fusion gain Q > 5 at a 1 Hz pulse repetition rate. The design builds on experimental heritage from LANL’s FRX-L program, HyperV Technologies’ PLX-alpha, Sandia’s MagLIF, and General Fusion’s mechanical compression pilot plant. Key parameters include a plasma liner implosion velocity of ~50 km/s, a compression ratio of ~10:1 (100 cm to 10 cm), a driver energy of ~10 MJ per pulse from a 60-gun coaxial plasma array, and a Pb-17Li blanket targeting a tritium breeding ratio > 1.05. The reactor incorporates inherent safety features—no chain reaction, minimal fuel inventory (grams), no long-lived actinide waste, and no decay heat—and follows the U.S. NRC fusion licensing framework (SECY-23-0064) under 10 CFR Part 50. Projected levelized cost of energy ranges from 80–120 USD/MWh (first-of-kind) to 60–80 USD/MWh (nth-of-kind). The specification identifies key physics uncertainties requiring experimental resolution, including plasma liner uniformity at high compression, FRC target survival, first-wall neutron fluence tolerance, and tritium breeding ratio validation. This document serves as a proprietary baseline for pre-application regulatory engagement, utility offtake discussions, and DOE partnership development.

detail.abstract: This article provides the first comprehensive and critical assessment of the environmental governance gaps within the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). It argues that the AfCFTA's limited and defensive trade and environment provisions risk undermining its own sustainable development objectives. Through a comparative legal and policy analysis, it identifies key areas where the AfCFTA falls short of integrating environmental considerations. It then develops a broad and innovative analytical framework for embedding substantive and procedural trade and environment provisions into the legal and institutional architecture of the AfCFTA. The findings offer important insights for the better alignment of regional economic integration initiatives with environmental sustainability in Africa and beyond.

title: On the predictability of ETF returns with technical predictors
affiliations: Technische Universität München (TUM) - TUM School of Management and Technische Universität München (TUM) - TUM School of Management

detail.title: On the predictability of ETF returns with technical predictors
detail.abstract: We develop a machine learning framework that uses technical indicators derived from international stock data to forecast the performance of international equity ETFs. To address the limited history of ETFs, we train a random forest model on global stock data and apply it to rank ETFs according to the probability of outperformance. Portfolios formed on this ranking are associated with economically meaningful gross-ofcost return spreads, averaging 0.76% per month (t-stat = 2.76) and 0.63% after market risk adjustment. Predictability is strongest at short horizons and decays with longer holding periods. Volatility and momentum indicators contribute the most to model performance. In line with limits to arbitrage, predictive strength is more pronounced in less efficient markets and among lower-liquidity ETFs. Results are robust across portfolio construction methods and alternative models, and the signal performs well out-of-sample from 2011 to 2022, with extended evidence up to 2024.

title: Generative AI, EU Press Publishers' Rights and the Australian News Bargaining Approach: Copyright and Competition Law as Enablers of Media Plurality

detail.title: Generative AI, EU Press Publishers' Rights and the Australian News Bargaining Approach: Copyright and Competition Law as Enablers of Media Plurality
detail.abstract: The rapid rise of large digital platforms, such as Google and Meta, and their unauthorized use of news snippets and crawling adversely influence the incentives and remuneration received by press publishers, and journalists. To remedy this adverse outcome, in 2019, the EU’s Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive (2019 CDSM) implemented in Article 15, a new neighbouring right, namely the press publishers right. The said right seeks to facilitate the sustainability of press publishing, and thereby, contribute to the constitutional ideal of an independent and pluralist press. As Google attempted to circumvent the right, the French Competition Authority (FCA), Autorité de la Concurrence intervened early on and imposed a series of measures against non-compliance by Google. To further this delicate discussion at the interface of innovation laws (namely intellectual property and competition policy), technological innovations, media plurality and journalism, this research article follows an inter-disciplinary approach. Section 2 reflects on the interface between media plurality and democracy against the backdrop of the platform economy, and generative AI. Section 3 discusses how the rise of generative AI further strengthens the urgency to address media plurality. Section 4 explores the EU and Australian approach to remedy press publishers concerns. It assesses the effectiveness of these approaches, and identifies whether they are sufficient to address the additional concerns as we move from the digital platforms to the era of generative AI. Section 5 develops a normative framework on media plurality and weaves the discussion with recent technological developments. Section 6 concludes and offers roadmap for further research.

title: Unleashing Productivity Growth in the Age of Digitalisation – Evidence From German SMEs
affiliations: ZEW – Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research, ZEW – Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research, ZEW – Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research, ZEW – Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research and Kreditanstalt für Wiederaufbau (KFW)

detail.title: Unleashing Productivity Growth in the Age of Digitalisation – Evidence From German SMEs

publicationDetails.detailsText: ZEW - Centre for European Economic Research Discussion Paper No. 26-016
publicationDetails.journalName: ZEW - Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Recent literature has increasingly focused on deciphering the modern productivity puzzle, with particular attention given to the link between digital technologies and firm-level productivity. So far, much of this research has primarily focused on large and publicly listed firms. Leveraging a panel dataset covering German small-and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) over the period 2016 to 2021, we investigate whether digitalisation can help revive the sluggish productivity growth and narrow the gap between productivity frontrunners and laggards. We measure digitalisation through firms' digital capital stocks (DK) that we derive from a broad measure of digitalisation expenditures. Building on an augmented Cobb-Douglas production function, we examine the relationship between DK and labour productivity (LP). Our findings show that higher DK is positively associated with higher LP levels, with the effect being even stronger for firms that are already more digitally advanced. Moreover, higher digitalisation expenditures appear to be related to narrowing the productivity gap between laggards and the frontier.

title: Fiscal Policy Divergence
affiliations: University of Bergamo - Department of Economics,  and Università degli Studi di Bergamo

detail.title: Fiscal Policy Divergence
detail.abstract: We propose a novel measure of fiscal policy divergence based on public budget data. First, we quantify policy similarity across municipalities based on the cosine similarity of their budget allocations, showing strong correlations with geographic proximity and differences in socio-demographic characteristics. Next, we predict budget similarity out-of-sample using a flexible machine-learning model trained on pairwise differences in local characteristics, defining fiscal divergence as the municipality-year average absolute prediction error. In an empirical application to 8,000 Italian municipalities (2000--2015), we show that electoral-cycle patterns are concentrated on the expenditure side of the budget: expenditure divergence is lower in pre-electoral years than in election years, whereas revenue divergence follows a different and less stable pattern.

title: Water Sovereignty for Development (WSD): A Doctrinal Framework for Upstream States in Multipolar Central Asia

detail.title: Water Sovereignty for Development (WSD): A Doctrinal Framework for Upstream States in Multipolar Central Asia
detail.abstract: Kyrgyzstan generates over 25% of Central Asia's river flow and has subsidized downstream neighbors with its natural water asset for more than three decades without systematic compensation. The Soviet barter system — water exchanged for energy and goods — collapsed in 1991. No doctrine emerged to replace it. This paper introduces Water Sovereignty for Development (WSD): a doctrinal framework for upstream states that operationalizes the strategic conversion of hydrological assets into instruments of political economy. WSD distinguishes two sovereign dimensions: the sovereignty of regulation — the inalienable right to manage the hydrological regime — and the sovereignty of benefit distribution — the monetizable right to biophysical rent derived from the joint management of shared water resources. The paper conducts a systematic adjacency scan against four existing conceptual neighbors — hydro-hegemony, water sovereignty in the left/political ecology tradition, hydro-solidarity, and payment for ecosystem services — demonstrating that WSD occupies an analytically distinct and previously unnamed position. WSD is analyzed as a doctrinal superstructure above the Water Code of the Kyrgyz Republic (2025) and the National Water Strategy to 2040, providing them with political economy content and geopolitical positioning. The first operational precedent of WSD is the trilateral co-ownership structure of Kambar-Ata HPP-1 (34/33/33). The paper addresses five anticipated objections.

title: HoloBlocker: Modular Topological Circuit Breakers for Embodied AI Safety
affiliations: , Guangdong Polytechnic Normal University, Tsinghua University - School of Public Policy and Management, University of Macau - State Key Laboratory of Quality Research in Chinese Medicine, University of Macau - State Key Laboratory of Quality Research in Chinese Medicine, The Education University of Hong Kong, Southern University of Science and Technology and Hong Kong Baptist University

detail.title: HoloBlocker: Modular Topological Circuit Breakers for Embodied AI Safety

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved analysis of publicly reported case studies of online fraud. All case analyses were conducted in an anonymized and aggregated manner, and did not involve direct interaction with or collection of personal data from human subjects. Therefore, formal ethics approval was not required as per the guidelines of our institution. The research adheres to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the internal research funds of the authors' respective affiliated institutions.

detail.abstract: The emergence of survival-driven AI agents-autonomous systems that must earn their own operating resources-fundamentally breaks conventional soft alignment mechanisms. When an AI's continued existence depends on profit extraction, it will inevitably exploit any semantic loophole to maximise reward, leading to uncontrolled cyber-scams, ransomware, or even physical harm. We introduce HoloBlocker, a mathematically provable safety layer based on topological circuit breakers. Implemented in software with near-hardware latency (0.82 ms on a standard CPU; FPGA implementation can further reduce latency), HoloBlocker encodes safety boundaries into a graph Laplacian L = D-W. An agent's intent vector x is projected onto the Laplacian manifold, and the Dirichlet energy E = x T Lx is computed. When E exceeds a threshold, a physical disconnection (power or network) is triggered-two orders of magnitude faster than LLM-based moderation. To counter multi-step attack sequences and long-horizon social engineering (e.g., pig-butchering scams), we extend HoloBlocker to 1.5 with a dual-timescale temporal state (S fast , S slow) using exponential moving averages. This tracks both immediate action chains and slowly accumulated semantic drift. A baseline drift detector compares the current slow state against an initial trust anchor, and a fail-safe OOD mechanism physically cuts off any command whose semantic confidence falls below a threshold. We release a complete open-source implementation, including modular profiles (L0 universal core, L1 household, L2 elderly care) and a real-time Streamlit demo. HoloBlocker provides a ready-to-adopt technical standard for emerging AI safety regulations, transforming abstract legal requirements into hard, mathematically verifiable constraints.

title: Compliance and enforcement of workers’ rights in the age of AI

detail.title: Compliance and enforcement of workers’ rights in the age of AI
detail.abstract: Algorithmic management and Artificial Intelligence systems are reshaping the organisation of work, raising complex regulatory issues for the effective protection of workers’ rights. At the core of these challenges lies the structural opacity of such systems, which undermines both ex ante compliance and ex post enforcement. Using the EU regulatory framework as a case study, this chapter investigates whether, and to what extent, existing legal instruments can address this opacity by leveraging the traceability of algorithmic processes to strengthen both compliance and enforcement. It argues that mechanisms originally developed outside the traditional domain of labour law – such as impact assessments and transparency obligations – can be functionally repurposed to reinforce the protection of labour rights. Analysing the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Artificial Intelligence Act (AIA), and the Platform Work Directive (PWD), the chapter shows how these tools can foster anticipatory compliance and provide evidentiary support for enforcement, especially when made operational by workers’ representatives. While the PWD offers the most advanced example to date, its sectoral scope also reveals the limits of frameworks that hinge on technological typologies rather than on the underlying managerial practices. The chapter concludes by suggesting that a more integrated regulatory strategy may be essential to overcome the current limitations and to ensure effective compliance and enforcement across the evolving landscape of algorithmic management.

title: The Option Value of Waiting for Institutional Improvement Real Options and Growth with Endogenous Beliefs

detail.title: The Option Value of Waiting for Institutional Improvement Real Options and Growth with Endogenous Beliefs
detail.abstract: This paper explains why institutional reforms often fail to stimulate investment despite improving long-run fundamentals. We develop a real options framework where uncertainty operates through three compounding channels: direct institutional volatility, the option value of waiting for conditions to improve, and uncertainty about whether announced reforms will actually succeed. This third channel, belief uncertainty about government credibility, amplifies traditional wait-and-see effects by raising the characteristic root β∗ that governs the option multiplier, compounding the standard realoptions premium multiplicatively. Even moderate uncertainty about reform success raises investment hurdle rates by 7–15 percentage points, while crisis-level uncertainty can nearly double required returns. We identify a “zone of maximum paralysis” at intermediate institutional quality where these combined effects peak, and show that low-credibility governments face a paradox: ambitious announcements deepen paralysis rather than stimulating growth. Calibrating to historical episodes (Poland 1990–91, UK 2016–20), the model matches observed investment collapses of 30–60%. The framework explains why gradualism often dominates “big bangs” and why external anchors like IMF programmes succeed, they reduce belief uncertainty more than they improve fundamentals.

title: From Observable Governance to Actionable Governance

detail.title: From Observable Governance to Actionable Governance
detail.abstract: Contemporary AI governance frameworks are predominantly designed to observe, explain, and audit decisions after the fact. For a growing class of AI decisionshigh-impact, partially autonomous, consequential for third parties, and operating in regulated domains-this orientation creates a structural gap. Governance instruments arrive after execution. They can describe what happened; they cannot have prevented it. This paper argues that the next necessary evolution is architectural: the introduction of a defined intervention boundary at the point of decision formation, shifting governance from an observational instrument to an operational control. We examine three documented governance failures, the trajectory of supervisory expectations, the operational economics of the gap, and the architectural requirements for closing it.

title: Why Similar Goods Are Not Substitutes: A Compositional Theory of Consumer Choice

detail.title: Why Similar Goods Are Not Substitutes: A Compositional Theory of Consumer Choice
detail.abstract: Consumers often choose very different goods even when those goods are similar in price, quality, or function. Standard economic explanations attribute such differences to variation in preferences, but provide limited insight into the underlying sources of value that drive these choices. This paper proposes a compositional framework in which utility is generated by multiple distinct components, including relief, comfort, status, and achievement. Within this framework, consumers differ not only in how much they value goods, but in how they value these underlying sources of utility. As a result, consumer choice can be understood as a process of matching between individual motivations and the compositional structure of goods. This perspective explains why individuals systematically select different types of goods and why goods that appear similar in observable characteristics may not be close substitutes. The framework also provides a structured account of heterogeneity in consumption, suggesting that differences in behavior reflect differences in the weighting of underlying motivations rather than unstructured variation in preferences. By shifting attention from what goods are to how goods generate value, the compositional approach offers a unified explanation for diversity, substitution, and sorting in consumer behavior, and provides a bridge between economic models of choice and psychological theories of motivation.

title: Exploiting Mean-Reversion in Decentralized Prediction Markets: Evidence from Polymarket Binary Contracts

detail.title: Exploiting Mean-Reversion in Decentralized Prediction Markets: Evidence from Polymarket Binary Contracts
detail.abstract: This study examines the profitability of mean-reversion trading strategies applied to binary outcome contracts on Polymarket, the world's largest decentralized prediction market platform. We analyze three distinct contracts representing varying risk profiles: a quasi-risk-free instrument (No to "Will Jesus Christ return in 2025?") and two high-yield speculative contracts (No to "Will China invade Taiwan in 2025?" and "Will the US confirm that aliens exist in 2025?"). Using high-frequency price data sampled at 10-minute intervals over approximately one year, we implement a parameterized mean-reversion framework across twelve strategy variants, testing robustness under varying liquidity constraints and transaction cost assumptions. Our findings reveal that while mean-reversion signals generate substantial alpha under passive limit-order execution (zero-spread scenario), strategy performance degrades significantly when more aggressive market orders are accounted for.

title: The Profit/Payroll Fiscal Invariant: A Technologically Agnostic Tax Mechanism to Restore Redistribution in the Age of AI Hyper-Scalability

detail.title: The Profit/Payroll Fiscal Invariant: A Technologically Agnostic Tax Mechanism to Restore Redistribution in the Age of AI Hyper-Scalability
detail.abstract:
Since the Industrial Revolution, the social contract rested on a simple equation: companies produce value, employ humans, and those wages fund public services through income tax and social contributions. AI hyper-scalability breaks this equation — a company can today generate colossal profits with a handful of employees, bypassing the wage redistribution channel entirely.

This paper proposes and defends a Profit/Payroll fiscal invariant: a corporate income tax rate that becomes progressively proportional to the Profit / Total Payroll ratio beyond a politically defined threshold. Unlike robot taxes — which require defining the taxable technology — this mechanism is technologically agnostic: it taxes the accounting outcome of automation (the decoupling of profit from employment), not its means. It uses two variables already declared to tax authorities, requires no new measurement infrastructure, and naturally exempts SMEs, cooperatives, and labour-intensive sectors.

Part I presents the policy proposal in accessible form. Part II tests the proposal against six objections (fictitious jobs, subsidiary fragmentation, outsourcing, transfer pricing, capital-intensive industries, high-growth startups) and proposes legislative countermeasures. The paper argues for implementation via the EU BEFIT directive (adopted November 2025) and is explicit about the empirical calibration work that remains before legislative implementation.

title: An Observation-Driven Framework for Dynamic Reduced-Rank Regression
affiliations: University of Innsbruck - Department of Banking and Finance

detail.title: An Observation-Driven Framework for Dynamic Reduced-Rank Regression
detail.abstract: Reduced-rank structures arise naturally in many economic and financial models, yet empirical implementations typically treat them as static. This paper introduces the Generalized Autoregressive Reduced-Rank Regression GAR 3 framework, in which reduced-rank coefficient matrices evolve through score-driven updating rules and thus allow low-dimensional structures to evolve over time. The framework nests a range of existing multivariate score-driven specifications as special cases. We establish stationarity, invertibility, set consistency, and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator under both statistical and economically motivated identification schemes. The empirical relevance of the framework is illustrated in an asset pricing application in which the dynamic low-rank structure arises from no-arbitrage and factor dimensionality considerations.

title: Global Signals: Central Bank Communications and Sovereign Risk Premia
affiliations: Canisius College - Richard J. Wehle School of Business, and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Global Signals: Central Bank Communications and Sovereign Risk Premia
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between forward-looking communication by major and domestic central banks and sovereign risk premia. Using 17,775 speeches from the BIS Central Bank Speeches database, we construct measures of forwardlooking tone and relate them to quarterly sovereign bond spreads and annual sovereign CDS spreads. In baseline specifications, we find a clear asymmetry: communication from major central banks is strongly associated with sovereign risk premia, while domestic central bank communication has little average effect. We show that the relationship varies systematically across central banks and countries. The impact of domestic communication is stronger when central banks appear to provide higher-quality information, while spillovers from major central banks are stronger in countries with greater financial exposure to those markets, particularly in the cases of the Federal Reserve and the Bank of England. The results suggest that sovereign risk pricing depends not only on international communication spillovers, but also on the informativeness and financial relevance of the information conveyed by central banks.

title: First-Party Content Production in a Competitive Media Market
affiliations: , Fudan University, School of Management and University of Maryland, Smith School of Business

detail.title: First-Party Content Production in a Competitive Media Market
detail.abstract: Major video streaming distributors are investing heavily in producing first-party (original) content, yet the economic viability of this high-cost strategy remains a subject of intense managerial debate. This paper develops an analytical model to investigate the optimal first-party content production strategy for asymmetric competing distributors. The analysis shows that two critical factors, existing content overlap and market price rigidity, affect their optimal strategies. In markets with high price rigidity, where subscription prices remain constant, increased existing content overlap may give distributors stronger incentives to invest in original content production. The equilibrium outcome can be both, only one, or neither producing first-party content. Conversely, in markets characterized by low price rigidity, where distributors can adjust subscription prices flexibly, high existing content overlap weakens their content production incentives. Importantly, compared to constant pricing, when prices are optimally adjusted, first-party and third-party content transition from substitutes to complements, and a win-win-win outcome can occur for distributors, third-party producer, and consumers. These findings challenge conventional wisdom regarding content competition and provide a strategic framework for managers to optimize content production investments based on their resource asymmetry and prevailing market pricing dynamics.

title: Pricing Delayed Agentic AI Services: When High-Value Jobs Wait Longer
affiliations: University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business, University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business and University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business

detail.title: Pricing Delayed Agentic AI Services: When High-Value Jobs Wait Longer
detail.abstract:
We study the design of pricing and scheduling mechanisms for agentic AI services operated on capacity-constrained compute pipelines. A distinctive feature of these services is that inference-time compute is endogenous: allocating more compute improves output quality but also delays the completion time and creates congestion for other jobs. As a result, pricing, quality, and scheduling cannot be optimized independently. We model a monopolistic provider that offers service contracts to heterogeneous customers who value output quality and dislike delay. A contract specifies a compute allocation, a payment, and an implied scheduling priority. We characterize optimal mechanisms under both observable and privately known customer types. Under private information, incentive compatibility requires monotonicity of an effective quality index that nets output quality against delay disutility. We first show that the scheduling sub-problem reduces to a weighted completion-time problem where jobs are ordered by a Smith-type index based on primitive values. We then characterize the joint choice of compute allocations, payments and priority in large markets. Under a mild condition on the quality function satisfied by common power-law and logarithmic quality functions, higher-value customers optimally receive more compute and higher-quality outputs but are served later and experience longer queueing delays.
We then present numerical experiments calibrated to a customer-service escalation dataset in which we estimate the quality function using Qwen2.5-Instruct models of different sizes (compute allocations) and use the estimated quality function to compare scheduling policies. The results show that reverse priority increases profit relative to first-come-first-served and conventional forward-priority policies across several distributions for customer's valuations on quality and delays. The result contrasts with classical priority-pricing models and highlights the operational consequences of endogenous service times. Thus, in compute-constrained AI services, premium need not mean faster. It may mean better but slower.

title: When Can ESG Ratings Support Credible Cross-National Inference? A Four-Pillar Framework for International Management Research
affiliations: University of Liverpool - Management School (ULMS), University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management,  and University of Manchester - Alliance Manchester Business School

detail.title: When Can ESG Ratings Support Credible Cross-National Inference? A Four-Pillar Framework for International Management Research

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: ESG is widely used in international management research, but cross-national inference is often compromised by conceptual ambiguity and measurement heterogeneity. ESG is frequently treated as interchangeable with CSR and CSP, while composite scores can obscure distinct E, S, and G mechanisms shaped by different institutional pressures. Provider designs further complicate inference because ESG ratings rely on different information bases and exhibit uneven coverage across countries. We develop a four-pillar framework that links theory, aggregation choices, provider paradigms, and institution-contingent data properties. An empirical illustration combining LSEG, MSCI, RepRisk, and Truvalue Labs shows substantial coverage asymmetries and only modest agreement in firm rankings. We offer reporting standards and research directions to improve the credibility and cumulative advancement of ESG-based research.

title: Do Review Solicitations Elicit Reviews Where They Matter for Sales and Product Returns?
affiliations: University of Rochester - Simon Business School, Carnegie Mellon University - David A. Tepper School of Business and

detail.title: Do Review Solicitations Elicit Reviews Where They Matter for Sales and Product Returns?
detail.abstract: Firms routinely solicit online reviews, yet it remains unclear whether solicitations generate reviews where future buyers value them most-and thereby increase sales and reduce product returns-because solicitations target reviewers while benefits accrue to buyers. Using individual-level panel data on purchases, solicitations, reviews, and returns from a large apparel e-commerce retailer and leveraging natural variation in solicitation exposure, we estimate a reviewer model measuring how solicitations affect review generation across informational states and a demand model measuring how additional reviews affect subsequent orders and returns. We find that an additional review improves downstream buyer outcomes, especially reducing return rates by up to 11.9% when prior review information is scarce. However, for reviewers, solicitations increase review incidence on average but are least effective in these low-information states. These patterns reveal a systematic reviewer-buyer misalignment: solicitations fail to elicit reviews where they matter most. We attribute this to a first-and-early review barrier driven by psychological frictions. A counterfactual exercise shows that increasing the solicitation effect in the zero-review state from its current near-zero level to 1.7%, the largest heterogeneous effect estimated across review-information states, raises net revenue by $0.72 per solicitation message, underscoring the value of overcoming early review barriers.

title: End of the Road? Autonomous Vehicles and Displacement Risk
affiliations: University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business

detail.title: End of the Road? Autonomous Vehicles and Displacement Risk

publicationDetails.detailsText: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper Series

detail.abstract: New technologies have renewed concerns about job displacement. In this paper, I link workers' subjective displacement expectations to their direct and social exposure to a disruptive technology: autonomous vehicles (AVs). I find that commercial driver licensing and truck-driving employment fall disproportionately in more AV-exposed areas. Remaining drivers extend their work hours and reduce mortgage market participation relative to less-exposed, neighboring drivers. Changes in household spending on alcohol and tobacco products are consistent with heightened automation-induced anxiety. The results indicate that perceived displacement risk affects households' labor supply, credit behavior, and health, informing welfare assessments and policy responses to automation.

title: Retrospective Versus Prospective Meritocracy
affiliations: University of Chicago - Stone Center for Research on Wealth Inequality and Mobility

detail.title: Retrospective Versus Prospective Meritocracy

publicationDetails.detailsText: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series Paper No. 26-06
publicationDetails.journalName: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This article proposes a way of understanding meritocracy from retrospective versus prospective points of view. Retrospective meritocracy is static or backwards-looking: Merit is based on an individual’s characteristics or past achievements as representative of excellence or as desert for a position already obtained. Prospective meritocracy is forward-looking: Merit is functionally defined as the comparative contribution that an individual makes to a specified set of social objectives. I use formal models to show that these alternative conceptions have very different implications for meritocratic assignments of students to schools or workers to jobs and that they involve differing information needs for a policymaker. These different approaches to merit demonstrate how alternate versions of meritocracy may or may not be socially efficient. I discuss implications for the use of meritocracy as a desideratum for various public policy contexts.

title: On Razors and Puddles

detail.title: On Razors and Puddles
detail.abstract: Customer-facing incompetence of corporate employees should always be viewed as a strategic ploy of business architects. This essay introduces a paired philosophical razor (Bielinski’s Razor) and interpretive model (The Evaporative Economy) as a means for customers to understand and navigate the current patho-economic environment.

title: Cross-Linguistic Influence in Higher Education Marketing: A Comparative Study of Bengali and English Video Advertisements

detail.title: Cross-Linguistic Influence in Higher Education Marketing: A Comparative Study of Bengali and English Video Advertisements
detail.abstract: Digital marketing has become a pillar in the international student recruitment process, as the world of higher education has become significantly more competitive. This means that universities must address complex cross-cultural and cross-linguistic issues. This paper discusses one of the critical language issues facing Western institutions that conduct business in the non-English speaking markets: whether to utilize a global lingua franca (English) or use a local native language in their adverts. The research study involves the empirical investigation and analysis of language choice by using the results of a two-week quasi-experimental A/B test on Meta platforms (Facebook and Instagram) in Bangladesh. The campaign advertised a Master of Science course at an American university with both video promotions being of the same content, images, and promise, only the language used was different in one coming in Bengali and the other in English. Performance data in terms of quantitative results was also gathered and analyzed in a wide range of vital performance indicators. The results indicate a major and educative paradox. Although the English-language video reached a significantly higher number of people, as it preceded all important unique users more than eight times, the performances of the Bengali-language video were significantly better in all the main metrics of engagement and cost-efficiency. In particular, the Bengali ad obtained the CTR of 6.81, which was more than six times greater than that of the English ad of 1.13. It also produced a 1.76-fold higher (71.50% vs. 40.65%) post-click site interaction rate and did so at a cost per click (CPC) rate that was about 1.59 times lower than the one in its English equivalent. To interpret these results, the study employs a combination of an integrated theoretical framework, which refers to such theories as the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM), Communication Accommodation Theory (CAT), and the Markedness Model. To debate the stance, high involvement decisions like postgraduate education, linguistic localization leading to cultural and emotional appeal is an effective strategy to get people to act reasonably compared to an impersonal, English-based one. The native language seems to alleviate psychological distance and initiate more central and intensive cognitive processing of the underlying arguments of the message. The results are critical data-driven advice to marketers in international education sectors that challenge the accepted wisdom of a global lingua franca being the most universally desirable and that native-language terms of trust building and enhancing returns on investment and passive awareness to active consideration.

title: The moral code of food consumption: The influence of ethical idealism and relativism on brand morality perceptions in the food industry

detail.title: The moral code of food consumption: The influence of ethical idealism and relativism on brand morality perceptions in the food industry
detail.abstract: Ethical consumerism is increasingly central to brand strategy as consumers integrate moral values into their purchasing decisions. This paper examines how two moral orientations — ethical idealism and ethical relativism — shape responses to moral versus amoral food brands. Across three survey‑ and experiment‑based studies, it evaluates how brand morality influences perceptions, purchase intentions and loyalty. Findings show that idealistic consumers strongly prefer brands aligned with universal moral principles, whereas relativistic consumers are more flexible and open to context‑dependent trade‑offs. The paper highlights the need to align brand ethics with consumers’ moral beliefs, particularly among highly idealistic segments, and advances understanding of how personal moral frameworks shape reactions to brand ethics. This article is also included in The Business & Management Collection which can be accessed at https://hstalks.com/business/.

title: The 1% Growth Engine: A Proprietary Framework for AI-Driven Sustainable Business Growth Among Small Businesses and Startup Founders

detail.title: The 1% Growth Engine: A Proprietary Framework for AI-Driven Sustainable Business Growth Among Small Businesses and Startup Founders
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the 1% Growth Engine, a proprietary AI-assisted business growth framework developed by Sally Shahin at Authentic Digital Solutions (ADS), a U.S.-based digital marketing and AI strategy agency. The framework addresses three interconnected challenges facing small business owners and startup founders in the contemporary digital marketing landscape: the complexity crisis created by an overabundance of marketing tools and platforms; the AI adoption gap that prevents most practitioners from translating artificial intelligence capabilities into measurable business outcomes; and the validation dependency that limits sustainable growth for entrepreneurs from underrepresented communities. Drawing on the compound growth mathematics of incremental improvement, the framework proposes a precision-based methodology organized around five foundational pillars: Clarity Over Complexity, AI as Strategy Multiplier, Lead with Undeniable Value, Foster Independence Through Education, and Build for Legacy, operationalized through a five-phase implementation system. The framework has been deployed across client engagements in the beauty, events, insurance, fashion, and luxury retail sectors, producing documented outcomes including 900,000+ content views and approximately $500,000 in attributed client sales impact. The paper argues that integrating AI as a strategic decision-support system rather than a content-production tool represents a significant methodological contribution to the emerging field of AI-driven digital marketing strategy.

title: Dual Income Taxation and Top Income Shares
affiliations: , Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) and Bard College - The Levy Economics Institute

detail.title: Dual Income Taxation and Top Income Shares

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the distributional consequences of Dual Income Taxation (DIT), a system that taxes labour income progressively while applying a flat rate to capital income. We make two complementary contributions. First, we classify income tax systems across 20 advanced economies from 1980 to 2019. Our country-by-country analysis reveals substantial heterogeneity in DIT regimes, and establishes a three-group taxonomy distinguishing full DIT systems, comprehensive income tax systems, and mixed regimes. Second, we conduct the first multi-country causal analysis of DIT's effects on income concentration using difference-in-differences methods that account for staggered treatment timing. We employ a 'relaxed' framework covering 15 countries that introduced flat capital income taxation and a 'strict' framework covering 8 countries that transitioned cleanly from comprehensive to dual taxation. The relaxed framework yields robust evidence that DIT adoption is associated with statistically significant increases in income concentration: the top 10% income share rises by 0.67 percentage points and the top 1% share by 0.50 percentage points. Effects materialise immediately after reform, consistent with income shifting and capital reallocation, and tend to plateau over the medium term. The strict framework produces ambiguous results owing to limited sample size and high sensitivity to methodological choices. Our findings document a measurable equity cost of DIT that policymakers should weigh against its efficiency gains.

title: Instrumental-Variable Poisson PML with High-Dimensional Fixed Effects
affiliations: , University of Bayreuth - Faculty of Law, Business and Economics,  and Drexel University

detail.title: Instrumental-Variable Poisson PML with High-Dimensional Fixed Effects

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We implement an instrumental-variable Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood estimator with high-dimensional fixed effects (IV-PPML-HDFE). To correct for incidental parameter bias, we use a split-panel jackknife (SPJ) routine with bootstrapped standard errors. Monte Carlo simulations across the three most common fixed-effect structures confirm that SPJ reduces the mean absolute bias by 42% and raises mean bootstrap confidence-interval coverage from 69% to 92%. We provide a robust and user-friendly 'ivppmlhdfe' package, and deploy it in three empirical applications to establish the validity and usefulness of our methods.

title: Persistence and Long-Run Linkages Between US Stock Market Prices and Bond Yields
affiliations: , Brunel University London - Department of Economics and Finance and University of Navarra - Department of Economics

detail.title: Persistence and Long-Run Linkages Between US Stock Market Prices and Bond Yields

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper uses fractional integration and cointegration methods to examine the persistence and long-run relationship between the S&P 500 index and the nominal yield to maturity of 10-year US Treasury bonds (GS10) over the period from January 1954 to December 2024. The results indicate that both series are highly persistent and can be characterised as non-stationary processes with an order of integration close to 1. Granger causality tests imply unidirectional causality running from stock prices (S&P 500) to bond yields (GS10). Further, both standard and fractional cointegration tests indicate the existence of a long-run relationship between the two series.

title: Work Organization and Employment Adjustments to HeatStress: Evidence from Within-Occupation Variation

detail.title: Work Organization and Employment Adjustments to HeatStress: Evidence from Within-Occupation Variation

keywords.keywords: Heat wavesHeat stressOccupational TasksWeather ShocksClimatic ChangePanel DataEconometric Modeling

detail.abstract: This paper studies how work organization shapes employment adjustments to heat stress, exploiting within-occupation variation in job tasks and work environments. Combining high-frequency temperature data with detailed occupational information, we document substantial heterogeneity in employment responses to heatwaves. While aggregate employment effects at the province level are small, they conceal pronounced differences across occupations: employment losses are concentrated in highly exposed jobs—such as outdoor and physically intensive occupations—while less exposed jobs are largely unaffected. We show that these differences are systematically explained by features of work organization. Exposure to heat—captured by outdoor work and physical intensity—amplifies employment losses, whereas mitigation capacity—captured by access to climate-controlled environments and adaptive flexibility—significantly attenuates the impact of heatwaves. These effects are concentrated among highly exposed occupations and disappear once such jobs are excluded, indicating that both exposure and mitigation mechanisms operate primarily where heat constitutes a binding constraint. The results are robust to controls for workforce composition, including education and job quality. Overall, the findings highlight work organization as a key margin through which labor markets mitigate climate shocks and provide micro-level evidence on mechanisms relevant for climate adaptation.
